t: Bias–variance: the decomposition behind every debugging session
sum: Why a model's error splits into bias, variance and irreducible noise; how to read a train/validation gap and a learning curve; which levers fix which problem; and how double descent changes the picture for very large models.
prereq: ml1
A model has parameters chosen to minimise average training loss (such as mean squared error); what we care about is error on new data, estimated with held-out validation and test sets.
why:
A team is building a model to predict delivery times. Their first version, a simple linear model, is off by an average of 14 minutes both on the orders it was trained on and on orders it has never seen. Someone suggests a much more powerful model. They try it and training error drops to 2 minutes — a triumph — but on new orders it is off by 19 minutes, worse than before. A third engineer suggests collecting another year of data; that takes two months and, for the linear model, changes nothing at all. A fourth wants to add weather features. Everyone has an idea and nobody has a way to decide which idea addresses the actual problem.

The bias–variance decomposition is that way. It says a model's error on new data comes from exactly three sources: the model being too rigid to represent the pattern (bias), the model being so sensitive to its particular training data that it learns quirks rather than the pattern (variance), and randomness in the data that no model can remove (noise). Each source has different symptoms and different cures. The linear model's problem was bias, which is why more data did nothing and weather features might help. The powerful model's problem was variance, which is why it looked brilliant on training data and poor elsewhere, and why more data or regularisation would help it.

This is the reasoning behind nearly every "my model isn't good enough, what now?" conversation, and interviewers use it constantly: "train error is 2%, validation is 25%, what do you do?" A candidate who answers from the decomposition sounds like someone who has debugged real models; one who lists every technique they know sounds like someone who hasn't.

This lesson builds the idea from scratch: the intuition, the formula and where it comes from, a worked example with four training sets computed by hand, how to diagnose a real model from its training and validation errors and its learning curve, which levers fix which problem, why averaging models reduces variance (with the formula), the public story of Google Flu Trends — a model that searched 50 million candidate features to fit 1,152 data points — and double descent, the modern wrinkle that explains why enormous neural networks don't behave the way the classical picture predicts.
primer:
Darts, thrown by many different players

Picture a dartboard. Now imagine not one throw but many: each throw is a model trained on a different random sample of data from the same world. Where the darts land relative to the bullseye (the truth) tells you everything.

If the darts cluster tightly but away from the bullseye, the thrower is consistently wrong: that is bias. If they are centred on the bullseye on average but spread all over the board, each individual throw is unreliable: that is variance. A good model is both centred and tight. And even a perfect thrower faces a board that wobbles a little on every throw — randomness in the data itself — which is the irreducible noise.

The analogy breaks in one important way: in real life you only throw one dart. You train one model on one dataset, and you cannot see the cloud. That is why the practical tools in this lesson — comparing training and validation error, and learning curves — exist: they infer the shape of the cloud from a single throw.

Underfitting and overfitting

A model with high bias is underfitting: it is too simple for the pattern. Fitting a straight line to data that curves, it is wrong in the same way whichever sample it sees, and it does badly even on its own training data. A model with high variance is overfitting: it is so flexible it bends to fit every point, including the noise. A curve of degree 15 through 16 points passes through every one of them and swings wildly between them; train it on a slightly different 16 points and it swings differently. It does brilliantly on training data and badly on new data.

Capacity: the dial between them

A model's capacity is how wide a range of functions it can represent. A straight line has little capacity; a degree-10 polynomial, a deep decision tree or a large neural network has a lot. Raising capacity typically lowers bias (the model can now represent the true shape) and raises variance (it can now also represent the noise). Somewhere in between is the capacity that makes the total error on new data smallest. You find it by trying several capacities and measuring on a validation set, not by reasoning about it in advance.

How you notice, with numbers

Compare error on the training set with error on a validation set the model never trained on (ml1), and against an estimate of the best achievable error — often how well humans do:

  • Train 30% error, validation 32%, humans 5%: both far above what's achievable, small gap → underfitting (bias).
  • Train 2% error, validation 25%: big gap → overfitting (variance).
  • Train 5%, validation 6%, humans 5%: you are near the best achievable; improvements must come from the data.
body:
1. The setup: a true function, noise, and many possible training sets

To make "bias" and "variance" precise we need a model of how data is produced. Assume each label is a true, unknown function of the features plus random noise:

y = f(x) + ε        where ε has mean 0 and variance σ²

f is the pattern we want to learn — how delivery time really depends on distance, time of day and so on. ε (epsilon) is everything the features can't explain: a driver stopping for fuel, a lift that's out of order. Its average is zero and its variance σ² (sigma squared, the average squared distance from its mean) measures how big it typically is. No model can predict ε from x, by definition.

A training set is a random sample of such (x, y) pairs. Had we collected data a month later we'd have a different sample, and training the same kind of model on it would give a slightly different fitted function, f̂ ("f-hat"). So f̂ is itself random — it depends on which training set we happened to get. The notation E[·] means expected value: the long-run average over all the training sets we might have drawn (and over the noise). E[f̂(x)] is therefore "the average prediction at x, averaged over all the models we could have trained" — the centre of the dart cloud.

2. The decomposition in words, then as a formula

In words: when you predict a new point, your squared error comes from three places. How far the average model is from the truth (bias). How far your particular model is from the average model (variance). And how far the actual observed label is from the truth (noise). For squared error these three add up exactly:

E[(y − f̂(x))²]  =  (E[f̂(x)] − f(x))²   +   E[(f̂(x) − E[f̂(x)])²]   +   σ²
expected error      bias²                   variance                     noise

Where it comes from, in three lines. Write the error as the sum of three pieces: y − f̂ = (f − E[f̂]) + (E[f̂] − f̂) + ε. Square it. The square of a sum of three terms is the three squares plus cross terms. Take the average: the cross terms vanish, because ε has mean zero and doesn't depend on the training set, and E[f̂] − f̂ averages to zero by definition. What remains is the three squared terms — bias², variance and σ². That is the whole derivation; the only assumption that matters is the squared loss, which is why the clean version holds only for squared error.

Bias is squared because it enters through a square: a model that is systematically 2 minutes too high and one that is 2 minutes too low contribute the same.

3. A worked example with four training sets

Take one test point where the true value is f(x₀) = 2.0 and the noise variance is σ² = 0.25. Imagine the world could have given us any of four training sets, equally likely. We train three models of different capacity on each set and record their predictions at x₀:

ModelSet ASet BSet CSet DAverage
Simple (e.g. a constant)1.01.20.81.01.0
Medium (e.g. a cubic)2.01.72.11.81.9
Flexible (e.g. degree 10)2.61.42.81.22.0

Now compute each term by hand.

  1. Simple. Bias² = (1.0 − 2.0)² = 1.00. Variance: deviations from the average 1.0 are 0, +0.2, −0.2, 0; squares 0, 0.04, 0.04, 0; average 0.02. Expected error = 1.00 + 0.02 + 0.25 = 1.27.
  2. Medium. Bias² = (1.9 − 2.0)² = 0.01. Deviations from 1.9: +0.1, −0.2, +0.2, −0.1; squares 0.01, 0.04, 0.04, 0.01; average 0.025. Expected error = 0.01 + 0.025 + 0.25 = 0.285.
  3. Flexible. Bias² = (2.0 − 2.0)² = 0. Deviations from 2.0: +0.6, −0.6, +0.8, −0.8; squares 0.36, 0.36, 0.64, 0.64; average 0.50. Expected error = 0 + 0.50 + 0.25 = 0.75.

Check the flexible model directly, without the formula: its errors against the truth are 0.6, 0.6, 0.8, 0.8 in size, whose squares average 0.50; add the noise the label carries, 0.25, and you get 0.75 — the decomposition is just bookkeeping. The pattern is the whole lesson in miniature. The simple model is consistently wrong (all bias). The flexible model is right on average but unreliable (all variance). The medium model is slightly wrong and slightly unreliable, and has by far the lowest total. And none of them can get below 0.25, the noise floor.

4. The U-curve: sweeping capacity

Repeat that calculation for every capacity from very simple to very flexible and plot the pieces. Bias² falls as capacity rises; variance rises; noise is flat; their sum — expected test error — is U-shaped. Training error, meanwhile, keeps falling, because a more flexible model can always fit the training points at least as well.

The lab reproduces this with real numbers. Fitting polynomials to 25 noisy points from a sine wave, over 500 resampled training sets, gives:

DegreeBias²VarianceNoiseTest MSETrain MSE
00.5890.0240.0900.7040.563
10.1460.0230.0900.2580.263
30.0030.0130.0900.1060.078
50.0000.0470.0900.1370.070
70.0000.0770.0900.1670.061

Degree 3 wins. Degrees 5 and 7 have essentially zero bias — they can represent the sine perfectly — but lose because of variance, even though their training error is lower. That is overfitting in one table.

5. Diagnosing a real model from one training run

In practice you have one dataset, so you can't compute bias and variance directly. You infer them from three numbers: training error, validation error, and an estimate of the Bayes error — the lowest error any model could achieve, set by the noise. For tasks humans do well (reading images, transcribing speech), human-level error is the usual proxy; otherwise, disagreement between repeated measurements or between annotators on the same items.

  • Avoidable bias ≈ training error − Bayes estimate. How much better the model could fit even the data it has seen.
  • Variance ≈ validation error − training error. The generalisation gap: how much worse it does on new examples.

Worked: Bayes estimate 1%, training error 8%, validation 10% → avoidable bias 7 points, variance 2 points; work on bias first. Bayes 1%, training 1.5%, validation 10% → avoidable bias 0.5, variance 8.5; work on variance. Always attack the bigger gap first. And note what this reasoning needs: without a floor, "training error 8%" could be terrible or perfect.

A fourth and fifth gap matter in production. If you have tuned many times against the validation set, the test set may come in worse — you have overfitted to validation (ml9). And if production data differs from training data, a further gap opens that bias and variance don't describe at all, because the decomposition assumes the test point comes from the same distribution. That is distribution shift (ml14, ml16), and its fix is data, not capacity.

6. Learning curves: will more data help?

A learning curve plots training and validation error against the number of training examples. It answers the most expensive question in the field — "should we collect more data?" — before you spend the money.

Why the shapes: with 10 examples almost any model can fit them all, so training error starts low and rises as more examples make a perfect fit impossible; validation error starts high (the model has seen too little) and falls. Both head towards the same value — the best error this model class can achieve. If that value is too high, you have a bias problem and the remedy is capacity or features; if the curves are still far apart at your current data size, you have a variance problem and more data will close the gap.

7. The levers, sorted by what they fix

ProblemLeversWhat not to do
High biasMore capacity (bigger model, deeper trees, higher degree), better features, weaker regularisation, train longer, boosting (ml10)Collect more of the same data
High varianceMore data, stronger regularisation (ml3), data augmentation, early stopping, fewer features, simpler model, bagging/ensemblesAdd capacity
At the noise floorBetter labels, new informative features, better measurementKeep tuning the model

Several levers help both: a genuinely informative new feature reduces bias (the model can now explain more) without adding much variance, and more data reduces variance without adding bias. The "trade-off" is what happens when you turn the single capacity dial; good features and more data move you to a better curve altogether.

8. Why averaging models reduces variance

If you could train on many independent training sets and average the models, the average would have the same bias but much less variance — that is the centre of the dart cloud. You can't get independent datasets, but you can approximate them. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains each model on a bootstrap resample — rows drawn from the original data with replacement — and averages them. The models are not independent, though; they share most of their data. For B models each with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the variance of their average is:

Var(average) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ² / B

Plug in the flexible model from section 3 (σ² = 0.50). Ten models with correlation 0.2: 0.2 × 0.5 + 0.8 × 0.5 / 10 = 0.10 + 0.04 = 0.14. Expected error falls from 0.75 to 0 + 0.14 + 0.25 = 0.39. A thousand models: 0.10 + 0.0004 ≈ 0.10, so error 0.35 — and no further, because the first term doesn't shrink with B. The floor ρσ² is why random forests go out of their way to decorrelate their trees (ml10), and why ensembles of near-identical models are disappointing.

9. The modern wrinkle: double descent

Classical theory says: past the sweet spot, bigger models only get worse. Deep learning practice says the opposite — enormous networks that fit their training data perfectly still generalise well. Belkin and colleagues reconciled the two in 2018 with the double descent curve. As capacity grows, test error first follows the U. It peaks at the interpolation threshold: the capacity at which the model can just fit every training point exactly. There, only one contorted function fits the data, so noise is baked into it. Keep growing and many different functions fit the training data exactly; the training procedure — gradient descent starting from small weights — tends to pick among them one that is smooth (small in size), and test error falls again, sometimes below the classical minimum.

Nakkiran and colleagues showed the same shape for deep networks as a function of model size and of training epochs, and found a surprising corollary: near the threshold, more data can hurt, because adding examples moves the threshold to where your model currently sits. For interviews, the takeaway is: the U-curve is the classical, data-limited half of the picture; massively over-parameterised models live on the second descent; and good regularisation largely removes the peak.
deep:
Implicit regularisation

Why does the training procedure prefer smooth solutions when many exact fits exist? For linear models trained by gradient descent from zero, the answer is provable: gradient descent converges to the solution with the smallest weights (the minimum-norm solution), which is the smoothest. For neural networks the picture is less exact but similar: small initial weights, small-batch stochastic gradient descent and large learning rates bias training towards "flat" solutions — ones where the loss changes little if the weights move — which tend to generalise. This is called implicit regularisation: the algorithm itself restrains capacity, even though nothing in the loss function asks it to. It is why "number of parameters" is a poor measure of effective capacity for deep networks.

Networks can memorise random labels

Zhang et al. (2016) trained standard image classifiers on data whose labels had been replaced with random ones. The networks still reached zero training error — they memorised pure noise. So their capacity is enormous, and classical bounds that promise good generalisation only for low-capacity models say nothing useful. Yet the same networks generalise on real labels. The resolution is that generalisation depends on the data and the algorithm together: on real data, gradient descent finds simple patterns that explain many examples at once, whereas random labels can only be fitted example by example (the paper found this took longer, though only by a small constant factor), and real labels are explainable by simple patterns.

Classification and the 0–1 loss

The additive decomposition is exact only for squared error. For 0–1 loss (a prediction is either right or wrong), several decompositions exist (Domingos, and James, among others), but bias and variance interact rather than add. The striking consequence: when the average model is wrong at a point, variance can help, because a model that occasionally flips to the right class beats one that is consistently wrong. The practical diagnosis — compare training error, validation error and a floor — carries over unchanged; the clean equation does not.

The ensemble formula, more carefully

The formula ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B assumes every member has the same variance σ² and every pair the same correlation ρ. Its message is robust: adding members helps with diminishing returns, and the floor is set by how correlated they are. Random forests lower ρ by giving each tree a bootstrap sample and a random subset of features at each split, which raises each tree's own variance slightly but lowers the correlation more — a net gain. Stacking diverse model types (trees, linear models, neural nets) lowers ρ further, which is why competition-winning ensembles mix model families (the Netflix Prize is the classic example; see ml10).

Bias, variance and regularisation strength

Regularisation (ml3) is a continuous capacity dial. For ridge regression — least squares plus a penalty λ times the sum of squared weights — increasing λ shrinks the weights towards zero, adding bias and removing variance; the test-error curve against λ is the U-curve mirrored. That continuity is what makes regularisation strength the most common hyperparameter to tune: it moves smoothly along the trade-off without changing the model family. Early stopping in iterative training acts the same way, with the number of training steps as the dial.

Scaling laws reframe the question

For very large language models, the relevant question is no longer "am I overfitting?" — they usually see each training token once or a few times — but "how should a fixed compute budget be split between model size and data?". Empirically, loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute; the Chinchilla study found compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 tokens per parameter. In bias–variance language: at that scale the models are data-limited and capacity-limited together, and both are relieved by scale — which is why the classical trade-off is rarely the binding constraint in LLM pretraining, though it very much is when fine-tuning on a few thousand examples.

Variance from the training procedure itself

Two models trained on the same data can differ because of random initialisation, data ordering and non-deterministic GPU arithmetic. This "training variance" adds to the data variance in the decomposition. It matters in practice: a 0.3-point improvement from a change may be smaller than the spread between random seeds. Senior engineers train several seeds before believing a small gain, and report the mean and spread.
prod:
The public case: Google Flu Trends

In 2008 Google launched Flu Trends (GFT), which estimated the prevalence of influenza-like illness from search queries, published ahead of the official surveillance reports of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). It was hailed as a triumph of big data. By February 2013 it was predicting more than double the proportion of doctor visits for influenza-like illness that the CDC reported. Lazer and colleagues' analysis in Science (2014), "The Parable of Google Flu", is a textbook study in variance and overfitting:

  • Too many candidate features for too little data. The original method searched for the best matches among 50 million search terms to fit 1,152 data points. With that many candidates, some terms will match the flu curve by coincidence. The authors describe the original GFT as "part flu detector, part winter detector" — it had picked up seasonal searches (they cite terms such as high-school basketball) that correlated with winter, not with flu.
  • It failed when the pattern changed. The original model completely missed the non-seasonal 2009 H1N1 ("swine flu") pandemic, which peaked outside the usual winter season, exactly what a winter detector would do.
  • Systematic errors afterwards. After updates, GFT overestimated flu prevalence in 100 of the 108 weeks starting August 2011, and its errors were correlated from week to week — a sign of structure the model was missing.
  • A simple model did better. Over the paper's out-of-sample period, mean absolute error was 0.486 for GFT, 0.311 for a simple model using the CDC's own lagged (two-week-old) data, and 0.232 for GFT combined with lagged CDC data.

Two lessons map directly onto this lesson. Selecting features from an enormous candidate pool against a small number of targets is a variance machine: in-sample fit looks superb and generalisation suffers. And the problem was compounded by drift — Google kept changing its search product, which changed how people searched — a production gap that bias and variance don't describe but that monitoring would have caught. The combined model winning is the ensemble lesson: blending two error sources with different errors beat either one.

What overfitting looks like in production systems

Offline wins that vanish online. A model that beats the current one by 0.5% on the validation set, after dozens of tuning rounds against that same set, often shows nothing in an A/B test (ml16). The validation set has been overfitted by repeated selection. Defences: a held-out test set that is truly used once, or a fresh validation set periodically.

Great on the benchmark, worse on the long tail. High-capacity models can memorise frequent patterns and still vary wildly on rare segments with little data. Slice metrics — error per country, per device, per customer tier — reveal variance that the overall average hides.

Instability between retrains. High-variance models produce noticeably different predictions after each retraining even when the data barely changed, which confuses users and downstream systems ("why did my credit limit change?"). Tracking prediction churn between model versions is a practical variance metric.

The debugging routine teams actually use

First, establish a floor (human-level or annotator agreement) and a trivial baseline. Second, overfit a small subset on purpose — if a model cannot reach near-zero error on 100 examples, there is a bug or a bias problem, not a variance problem. Third, train on the full data and compare training error, validation error and the floor, attacking the larger gap first. Fourth, draw a learning curve before deciding to buy data. Fifth, before celebrating a small improvement, repeat the run with several random seeds to see whether the gain exceeds run-to-run variation. This routine answers most "what do I try next?" questions in a few hours.
myths: Low training error means a good model.

Training error measures how well the model fits examples it has already seen, and a flexible enough model can drive it to zero by memorising — including the noise. In the lab, a degree-7 polynomial has lower training error than a degree-3 one but higher test error. Only error on held-out data says anything about new examples; the gap between the two is the variance signal.
More data always helps.

More data reduces variance. If the model is limited by bias — train and validation errors are close together and both too high — more rows of the same kind change almost nothing, because the model already cannot represent the pattern. A learning curve that has flattened is the evidence. The remedy there is more capacity or better features, not a bigger dataset.
A more complex model always overfits.

Complexity raises variance only relative to the amount of data and the regularisation used. A deep network with millions of parameters can generalise well on millions of examples with the right regularisation and training procedure, and past the interpolation threshold test error can even fall as models grow (double descent). The question is always capacity relative to data, not capacity alone.
Bias and variance can be measured directly on a real dataset.

Both are defined as averages over many hypothetical training sets drawn from the same world, and in practice you have one. You can estimate them in simulations (as in the lab), approximate variance with bootstrap resampling, and use train and validation errors as proxies — but the train/validation diagnosis is an inference, not a measurement of the terms in the formula.
The bias–variance trade-off means you must always sacrifice one for the other.

Many improvements lower both: better features reduce bias without adding variance, more data lowers variance without adding bias, and averaging many models (bagging) lowers variance at almost no cost in bias. The trade-off describes what happens when you turn a single capacity dial, not a law that every change must obey.
If validation error is much worse than training error, the model is broken.

Some gap is normal and expected: training error is always optimistic. The question is whether the validation error is good enough for the task and whether the gap is shrinking as you add data or regularisation. A gap can also come from something other than variance — a validation set drawn from a different distribution, or leakage in the training features — so check the split before blaming the model.
lab:
Goal: measure bias², variance and noise directly by simulation — possible only because we invent the true function. NumPy only; tested with Python 3.12.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
f = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)          # the true function
SIGMA, N, TRIALS = 0.3, 25, 500              # noise sd, points per training set, resamples
x_test = np.linspace(0.1, 0.9, 50)

print("degree   bias^2  variance   noise   expected test MSE   mean train MSE")
for degree in (0, 1, 3, 5, 7):
    preds, train_mse = [], []
    for _ in range(TRIALS):
        x = rng.uniform(0, 1, N)
        y = f(x) + rng.normal(0, SIGMA, N)
        coef = np.polyfit(x, y, degree)
        preds.append(np.polyval(coef, x_test))
        train_mse.append(np.mean((np.polyval(coef, x) - y) ** 2))
    preds = np.array(preds)                          # TRIALS x 50
    bias2 = np.mean((preds.mean(axis=0) - f(x_test)) ** 2)
    var = np.mean(preds.var(axis=0))
    print(f"{degree:>6} {bias2:8.3f} {var:9.3f} {SIGMA**2:7.3f} "
          f"{bias2 + var + SIGMA**2:14.3f} {np.mean(train_mse):16.3f}")

What to look for. Bias² collapses from 0.589 (degree 0) to about zero by degree 5, variance climbs from degree 3 on, and expected test error is lowest at degree 3 (0.106) while training error keeps falling. Then experiment: raise N to 200 and watch variance shrink for the high degrees (more data fixes variance, not bias); set SIGMA to 0 and the floor disappears; add degree 9 and some training sets with a gap in x make the curve explode — variance in its purest form. None of this is possible on real data, where the true function is unknown; that is why section 5's train/validation diagnosis exists.
recap: For squared error, the expected error of a model at a point splits exactly into bias squared, variance and irreducible noise.

Bias is how far the average model — averaged over possible training sets — is from the truth; variance is how much individual trained models scatter around that average; noise is the part no model can remove.
Increasing capacity typically lowers bias and raises variance, which gives the classic U-shaped test-error curve while training error keeps falling.

High training error with a small train–validation gap signals bias; low training error with a large gap signals variance; both near a known noise floor means the model is nearly as good as the data allows.
Bias is reduced by more capacity, better features and weaker regularisation; variance by more data, stronger regularisation, simpler models and averaging many models.
A learning curve — error against training-set size — shows whether more data will help: converged curves mean no, a shrinking gap means yes.
Averaging B models with correlation ρ leaves variance ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B, so ensembles help most when members disagree.
Very large models trained past the point where they fit the training set exactly can see test error fall again — double descent — so the U-curve is only the classical left half of the picture.
glossary: The gap between training error and the best achievable error (often estimated by human-level performance); the part of bias you could still remove.
Training many models on bootstrap resamples of the data and averaging their predictions to reduce variance.
The lowest error any model could achieve on a task, because of noise in the labels or information missing from the features.
The error of the average model, over many possible training sets, relative to the true function; caused by the model class being too rigid.
Creating a new dataset by sampling rows from the original with replacement, used to estimate how much a result varies between datasets.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose surveillance reports were the ground truth Google Flu Trends tried to anticipate.
How wide a range of functions a model can represent; raised by more parameters, deeper trees, higher-degree polynomials or more features.
The observation that test error can rise near the point where a model just fits its training data, then fall again as capacity keeps growing.
The long-run average of a random quantity; here, averages over possible training sets and noise.
Validation (or test) error minus training error.
Google's 2008-2015 service that estimated flu prevalence from search queries; this topic's public case of overfitting.
Graphics processing unit: the parallel processor used to train neural networks; its arithmetic is not always bit-for-bit repeatable.
A setting chosen by the engineer rather than learned, such as polynomial degree, tree depth or regularisation strength.
The capacity at which a model can just fit every training example exactly.
The part of the error caused by randomness in the labels that no model can remove, written σ².
A plot of training and validation error against the number of training examples.
A very large neural network pretrained by next-token prediction on text (ml1).
The average absolute difference between predictions and labels.
The average squared difference between predictions and labels (ml1).
Fitting the training data so closely, noise included, that performance on new data suffers; the symptom of high variance.
The highest power of x in a polynomial model; degree 1 is a straight line, degree 3 can bend twice.
Any technique that restrains a model's flexibility to reduce variance, such as penalising large weights (ml3).
Being too simple to capture the real pattern, so error is high even on the training data; the symptom of high bias.
How much a model's predictions change when it is trained on a different sample of data from the same world.
drill:
Work it out

Two models, same data. Diagnose each and say what you would change.

A: train MAE 0.12, validation MAE 0.41.
B: train MAE 0.38, validation MAE 0.40.
You also know repeated measurements of the same input disagree by about 0.10 MAE (MAE is mean absolute error — the average size of the error).

Answer

That 0.10 is the noise floor — no model can beat it, so it is the number both should be read against.

A is variance-limited. A 0.29 gap with training error near the floor means it has memorised. Get more data, regularise harder, simplify, augment, or stop earlier; a learning curve will show how much more data would buy. Note what would not help: more capacity.

B is bias-limited. Almost no gap, but both errors sit 0.28 above the floor — the model class cannot represent the signal. Add capacity, add features, train longer, weaken regularisation. More data will do nothing here, which is the counter-intuitive half.

The reason to state the floor first: without it you cannot tell "B is underfitting" from "B is done and the task is just noisy".
qa: E
What are bias and variance, in one sentence each?

Bias is the systematic error from the model being too simple to represent the true pattern — the average model, over many possible training sets, is still wrong. Variance is the error from the model being too sensitive to the particular training set — train it on a different sample and its predictions change a lot. Together with irreducible noise they make up the expected squared error.
E
Train error 2%, validation error 25%. Diagnosis and fixes?

Overfitting: a large gap with low training error is the variance signature. Fixes, roughly in order of cost: stronger regularisation, a simpler model or fewer features, early stopping, data augmentation, and more training data. Adding capacity would make it worse. Also check the validation set comes from the same distribution as training — a distribution mismatch produces the same gap.
E
Train error 30%, validation error 32%, humans get 5%. Diagnosis and fixes?

Underfitting: both errors are high and close together, and far above the 5% human-level estimate of what is achievable, so avoidable bias is about 25 points. Add capacity (a bigger or more flexible model), better features, train longer, or weaken regularisation. More data of the same kind would barely help.
M
Write down the bias–variance decomposition and explain each term.

For y = f(x) + ε with noise variance σ² and a model f̂ trained on a random dataset: E[(y − f̂(x))²] = (E[f̂(x)] − f(x))² + E[(f̂(x) − E[f̂(x)])²] + σ². The first term is bias squared, the distance of the average model from the truth; the second is variance, the scatter of individual models around their average; the third is noise. The expectations are over training sets and noise, and the cross terms vanish because the noise has mean zero and is independent of the training set.
Follow-up: Why squared bias? — Because the decomposition comes from expanding a square; bias itself can be positive or negative, but only its size contributes to squared error.
M
Does the bias–variance decomposition hold for classification?

Not as clean algebra. It is exact only for squared error. For 0–1 loss (right or wrong) several decompositions have been proposed, but bias and variance are not additive, and variance can even help when the average model is wrong — a model that sometimes flips to the correct class does better than one that is consistently wrong. The intuition carries over; the equation does not, so say that rather than claiming a clean decomposition.
Follow-up: What about log-loss? — Probabilistic losses have their own decompositions, but in interviews the practical diagnosis via train/validation gaps is what matters.
M
How do you estimate the irreducible noise floor on a real dataset?

Measure disagreement between repeated observations of the same input: duplicate rows with different labels, two annotators labelling the same items, or repeated measurements. Human-level performance is the usual proxy for classification. Without a floor you cannot tell 'the model is underfitting' from 'the task is just noisy' — a model at 12% error might be terrible or perfect.
Follow-up: What if humans are worse than the model? — Then human-level is no longer a useful floor; use label-agreement studies or accept that you can't bound the remaining avoidable error.
M
What does a learning curve tell you that a single train/validation pair doesn't?

Whether more data will help. If training and validation errors have converged at a high value as the training set grows, the model is bias-limited and more data won't help. If there is a gap that is still shrinking at the largest size, the model is variance-limited and more data will help — and extrapolating the curve estimates roughly how much. That answers the expensive question 'should we buy more labels?'

Follow-up: Why does training error rise as data grows? — With few examples a model can fit them all; more examples are harder to fit simultaneously, so training error increases towards the validation error.
M
Why do ensembles like random forests reduce error?

Averaging reduces variance. If B models each have variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, their average has variance ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B. With independent models (ρ = 0) variance falls as 1/B; with correlated ones it floors at ρσ². Bias is essentially unchanged, since the average of similar models has similar bias. That is why random forests decorrelate trees by sampling rows and features, and why diversity matters more than the number of members.
Follow-up: Which ensemble method reduces bias instead? — Boosting, which fits each new model to the errors of the ensemble so far (ml10).
M
Which common techniques reduce bias and which reduce variance?

Bias: bigger or more flexible models, better features, less regularisation, longer training, boosting. Variance: more data, stronger regularisation (weight penalties, dropout), data augmentation, early stopping, feature selection, simpler models, bagging and ensembling. Some, like better features and more data, can improve one without hurting the other.
H
What is double descent and why does it matter?

If you keep increasing capacity past the interpolation threshold, where the model can exactly fit the training set, test error often peaks and then falls again rather than continuing to rise. Near the threshold there is essentially one way to fit the data and it is contorted; far beyond it there are many exact fits, and the training procedure tends to pick a smooth one. It matters because it explains why massively over-parameterised networks generalise, and it means the classical U-curve is only the left half of the picture. Nakkiran et al. showed it also occurs over training epochs, and that near the threshold more data can temporarily hurt.
Follow-up: Does this mean regularisation is obsolete? — No; well-tuned regularisation largely removes the peak, and data-limited problems still behave classically.
H
Your model's validation error is fine but production error is much worse. Where does that fit in the bias–variance picture?

It usually doesn't: bias and variance assume test data comes from the same distribution as training data. A production gap is typically distribution shift (the world changed), a training/serving difference in features, or leakage that made validation optimistic. Break error into four gaps: human-to-train (avoidable bias), train-to-validation (variance), validation-to-test (overfitting to the validation set by repeated tuning) and test-to-production (shift or pipeline bugs) — each has different fixes.

Follow-up: How do you tell shift from a pipeline bug? — Compare the feature values the model received in production with the same features recomputed offline for the same requests; if they differ, it's the pipeline.
H
Why can deep networks fit random labels yet generalise on real ones?

Zhang et al. showed standard image networks reach zero training error even when labels are replaced by random ones, so their capacity is enormous and classical capacity-based bounds are vacuous. On real data they generalise because the training procedure — gradient descent from small random weights, with implicit and explicit regularisation — finds simple, smooth solutions first, and real labels have structure that such solutions capture. So generalisation depends on the data and the training algorithm, not only on the model class.

Follow-up: What does that imply for capacity-based theory? — Measures based on the model class alone, such as parameter count, can't explain generalisation for these models; the explanation has to involve the training algorithm and the structure of real data.

t: Regularisation: L1, L2, and everything that behaves like them
sum: How a penalty on weight size trades a little bias for a lot less variance; why L1 zeroes coefficients while L2 only shrinks them (the algebra and the geometry); choosing λ; the Bayesian reading; and the many techniques — early stopping, dropout, weight decay, augmentation — that regularise without saying so.
prereq: ml1
Training chooses parameters that minimise the average loss on training data, such as mean squared error; what matters is error on new data.
ml2
Expected error = bias² + variance + noise; flexible models overfit (high variance), and techniques that restrain flexibility trade a little bias for less variance.
why:
A bank wants to predict which small-business loans will default. It has 800 past loans and, thanks to an enthusiastic data team, 3,000 candidate features: every ratio from every financial statement, several months of account balances, industry codes, postcode statistics. A straightforward linear model fitted to all of it achieves almost perfect accuracy on the 800 training loans and does little better than guessing on the next 200. With more features than examples, the model can find some combination of columns that explains every past default, including all the coincidences. Removing features by hand would take weeks and would be guesswork.

ml2 explained what is happening: this is variance. The model has so much freedom that it fits the noise, and the fitted weights would change completely if a slightly different set of 800 loans had been collected. What ml2 didn't provide was a precise, adjustable way to take some of that freedom away. Regularisation is that tool. The most common form adds a second term to the training objective that charges the model for having large weights. The model can still use any feature it likes, but every unit of weight has to "pay for itself" by reducing the error enough to justify the cost. A single number, λ, sets the price.

Two choices of price behave very differently. Charging for the squares of the weights (L2, ridge) shrinks everything a little. Charging for their absolute values (L1, lasso) sets most of the 3,000 weights to exactly zero, leaving a model the bank can read: these twelve features matter. Understanding why the two differ — algebraically and geometrically — is one of the most common interview questions in machine learning, and the answer reaches all the way to how large language models are trained, where "weight decay" is regularisation under another name.

This lesson builds regularisation from the objective up: what the penalty does to a single weight (worked by hand for both L1 and L2), the diamond-versus-circle geometry with a computed example, choosing λ, why features must be standardised, the Bayesian reading, elastic net, and the many techniques that regularise without looking like a penalty — early stopping, dropout, data augmentation, weight decay in AdamW, label smoothing and LoRA. The public case reproduces a classic published comparison on real prostate-cancer data, where lasso keeps three of eight clinical measurements and still beats unregularised least squares on held-out patients.
primer:
A budget for complexity

Imagine giving a contractor a job and paying them only for how well the result matches your specification. They will use every trick available, including fragile ones, to hit every measurement exactly — and the result might fall apart the first time conditions change. Now add a second rule: every material they use costs money, deducted from their fee. They will still use whatever genuinely improves the result, but they will stop adding things that help only marginally. The result is simpler and more robust. That second rule is regularisation.

In machine learning the "materials" are the model's weights. The training objective becomes:

total cost  =  how badly the model fits the training data  +  λ × how large the weights are
                (the loss, e.g. squared error)                (the penalty)

λ (lambda) is the regularisation strength, a hyperparameter chosen by you, not learned. At λ = 0 there is no penalty and you get the ordinary fit. As λ grows, large weights become expensive, and the model uses only the features that reduce error enough to justify their cost. At enormous λ, every weight is driven towards zero and the model predicts roughly the average for everything.

Why small weights mean a simpler model

A weight says how strongly the output reacts to a feature. With large weights, a small change in an input causes a big change in the output, so the model can bend sharply to pass through every training point — including the noisy ones. With small weights, the model's output changes gently as inputs change; it can capture broad patterns but not every wiggle. Limiting weight size therefore limits how contorted the fitted function can be, which is exactly the capacity that ml2 identified as the source of variance. The price is a little bias: the model may now be too gentle to capture a pattern that really is sharp. That is why λ must be tuned rather than set high.

Two ways to measure "how large"

  • L2 penalty (ridge): the sum of squared weights, w₁² + w₂² + …. Large weights are punished heavily (doubling a weight quadruples its cost), small ones hardly at all. Effect: all weights shrink, none reach zero.
  • L1 penalty (lasso): the sum of absolute weights, |w₁| + |w₂| + …. Every unit of weight costs the same, whether the weight is large or tiny. Effect: weights that only help a little are set to exactly zero, so the model selects features.
  • Elastic net: a mix of both.

One practical rule before anything else: standardise the features (rescale each to mean 0 and standard deviation 1) before penalising weights. The penalty sees only the numbers in the weight vector, and those depend on each feature's units. Without standardising, the penalty would favour or punish features according to whether they happened to be recorded in millimetres or kilometres.
body:
1. The penalised objective

For a linear model ŷ = w₁x₁ + … + w_px_p + b with squared-error loss, the three standard objectives are:

ordinary least squares:  minimise  Σᵢ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²
ridge (L2):              minimise  Σᵢ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²  +  λ Σⱼ wⱼ²
lasso (L1):              minimise  Σᵢ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²  +  λ Σⱼ |wⱼ|

The sums over j run over the weights but not the intercept b, which sets the average level of predictions and is not a source of complexity. Libraries scale these differently, which matters when you copy a λ from one to another: scikit-learn's Ridge minimises exactly the ridge line above (calling λ alpha), while its Lasso divides the squared-error term by 2n (twice the number of rows), so the same alpha means a much stronger penalty in lasso than in ridge. LogisticRegression uses C, the inverse of the strength: small C means strong regularisation.

2. One weight, worked by hand

The fastest way to see the difference is a model with a single feature and no intercept (both x and y centred to mean zero). Take three points: x = −1, 0, 1 and y = −2, 0.5, 1.5. Two sums are all we need: Σxy = 2 + 0 + 1.5 = 3.5 and Σx² = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2.

Ordinary least squares. Setting the derivative of Σ(y − wx)² to zero gives w = Σxy / Σx² = 3.5 / 2 = 1.75.

Ridge. The derivative of Σ(y − wx)² + λw² is −2Σxy + 2wΣx² + 2λw. Setting it to zero:

w_ridge = Σxy / (Σx² + λ) = 3.5 / (2 + λ)
λ = 1   → 3.5 / 3   = 1.167
λ = 2   → 3.5 / 4   = 0.875
λ = 10  → 3.5 / 12  = 0.292
λ = 100 → 3.5 / 102 = 0.034     (never exactly zero)

Ridge divides: λ adds to the denominator, so the weight is scaled down by the factor Σx² / (Σx² + λ). It gets smaller and smaller but only reaches zero as λ goes to infinity.

Lasso. The absolute value has a corner at zero, so we handle the positive side (w > 0, where |w| = w and its slope is 1). The derivative of Σ(y − wx)² + λw is −2Σxy + 2wΣx² + λ. Setting it to zero:

w_lasso = (Σxy − λ/2) / Σx² = (3.5 − λ/2) / 2
λ = 1 → 3.0 / 2 = 1.50
λ = 2 → 2.5 / 2 = 1.25
λ = 7 → 0.0 / 2 = 0          and for any λ ≥ 7 the weight stays exactly 0

Lasso subtracts: the evidence for the feature, Σxy = 3.5, is reduced by a fixed λ/2 before dividing. Once λ/2 exceeds the evidence, the formula would give a negative weight, but a negative weight would pay the penalty and fit the data worse, so the best choice is exactly zero. That is soft-thresholding: shrink towards zero by a threshold, and snap to zero anything that was within the threshold. The general rule (for standardised, uncorrelated features) is w = sign(z) · max(|z| − t, 0), where z is the unregularised weight and t the threshold. It is what the diagram in the primer draws.

3. The same thing through gradients

Most models are trained iteratively by gradient descent — repeatedly moving each weight a small step in the direction that reduces the loss (ml4 covers it fully). The gradient is the slope of the objective with respect to each weight. The penalty adds its own slope to the data's:

  • L2 penalty λw² has slope 2λw: proportional to the weight. A weight of 4 is pulled back eight times harder than a weight of 0.5. As the weight shrinks, so does the pull, so it approaches zero ever more slowly and never arrives.
  • L1 penalty λ|w| has slope λ·sign(w): the same size whatever the weight. A weight of 0.01 is pulled towards zero just as hard as a weight of 4, so small weights get pushed all the way.

Because |w| has a corner at zero, plain gradient descent tends to make lasso weights jitter around zero rather than land on it. Lasso solvers therefore use coordinate descent (update one weight at a time, applying soft-thresholding exactly) or proximal gradient methods (take a gradient step on the loss, then soft-threshold), which the lab implements in six lines.

4. The geometry: diamond versus circle

There is an equivalent way to state each problem: minimise the loss subject to the penalty being at most some budget t. Every λ corresponds to some t. With two weights, the ridge budget w₁² + w₂² ≤ t is a disc; the lasso budget |w₁| + |w₂| ≤ t is a diamond with its corners on the axes. The loss has its minimum at the ordinary least-squares solution, and its level sets — the points of equal loss — are rings around that minimum. The regularised solution is the first point where an expanding ring touches the budget region.

Worked example. Suppose the unregularised solution is (w₁, w₂) = (2, 0.5) and, to keep the arithmetic simple, the loss is plain squared distance from that point (circular rings). With a budget of 1:

  • L2 disc of radius 1. The closest point on a disc is along the straight line to the centre: divide (2, 0.5) by its length √(4 + 0.25) = 2.062, giving (0.970, 0.243). Both weights shrink by the same proportion; neither is zero.
  • L1 diamond with |w₁| + |w₂| ≤ 1. The closest point is found by soft-thresholding both coordinates by the same amount τ until they sum to 1. Try τ = 0.75: (1.25, −0.25) — but the second can't go negative, so it clips at 0. With w₂ = 0, w₁ must be 1: τ = 1 gives (2 − 1, max(0.5 − 1, 0)) = (1, 0), the corner. The small weight has been removed entirely.

Real loss rings are ellipses (stretched when features are correlated), which changes where they touch but not the key fact: a region with corners on the axes is touched at a corner far more often than a smooth one is touched on an axis. In high dimensions the effect is stronger, because the L1 ball has corners and edges in every combination of axes.

5. Standardise first — with numbers

Suppose a house-price model finds that each extra metre of garden adds £2,000, so the weight is 2,000 per metre. Record the same length in millimetres and the weight becomes 2 per millimetre. The fit is identical, but the L2 penalty on that weight drops from λ × 4,000,000 to λ × 4 — a factor of a million — so the regulariser would barely touch the millimetre version while crushing the metre version. The choice of units, not usefulness, would decide which features survive. Standardising every feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 removes this arbitrariness: a weight then means "the change in prediction per standard deviation of the feature", comparable across features. Compute the means and standard deviations on the training data only, and apply those same numbers to validation and test data, or information leaks from the held-out sets (ml9).

6. Choosing λ

λ is a hyperparameter, so it is chosen on held-out data. The usual procedure is cross-validation (splitting the training data into k parts and rotating which part is held out; ml9 covers it) over a grid on a log scale, such as 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100 — the useful values span orders of magnitude. Plotting each coefficient against λ gives the regularisation path: for ridge, curves that glide smoothly towards zero; for lasso, curves that hit zero one after another, so reading the plot from right to left shows the order in which features enter the model.

A common refinement is the one-standard-error rule. Cross-validation scores are noisy estimates, so instead of the λ with the very best score, take the largest λ whose score is within one standard error of the best. It gives a simpler model whose performance is statistically indistinguishable. The public case below shows the rule at work.

The lab shows what the sweep looks like on synthetic data with 40 training rows, 30 features, and only 3 features that truly matter:

Lasso λTrain MSEValidation MSENon-zero weights

Training error rises steadily with λ (more bias); validation error falls, bottoms out, then rises (the U-curve of ml2 mirrored, because large λ means low capacity). At λ = 20 lasso keeps exactly the three true features. In the same data ridge never beats the unregularised fit, because the truth is sparse and shrinking all 30 weights a little doesn't help — which penalty suits a problem depends on the structure of the truth. If many features each contribute a little (a dense truth), the ranking reverses: lasso throws away real signal, and ridge's gentle shrinkage of everything wins. Since you rarely know which world you are in, trying both, or elastic net, under cross-validation is the practical answer.

7. Elastic net: the best of both

Lasso has two weaknesses. When features are strongly correlated — say, three different measurements of company size — it tends to keep one and drop the others, and which one it keeps changes with small changes in the data. And when there are more features than rows, it can select at most as many features as there are rows. Elastic net adds both penalties: λ₁ Σ|wⱼ| + λ₂ Σwⱼ². The L2 part prefers to spread weight across correlated features (for a fixed total, squared weights are smallest when the weight is shared), so correlated groups enter and leave together; the L1 part still produces zeros. In scikit-learn the mix is set by l1_ratio (1 = pure lasso, 0 = pure ridge). With 3,000 correlated financial features and 800 loans, elastic net is the natural first choice.

8. The Bayesian reading

There is a second, probabilistic way to arrive at the same objectives. Suppose labels are the model's prediction plus Gaussian noise of variance σ², and before seeing data you believe each weight is probably small: a prior distribution centred on zero. The MAP estimate (maximum a posteriori) — the weights that are most probable given the data and the prior — minimises the negative log of (likelihood × prior):

Gaussian prior, variance τ²:   Σ(y − ŷ)² / (2σ²) + Σw² / (2τ²)
multiply by 2σ²:               Σ(y − ŷ)² + (σ²/τ²) Σw²      ← ridge with λ = σ²/τ²

A Laplace prior — a distribution with a sharp peak at zero — gives the lasso penalty instead. This reading explains λ: it is the ratio of noise to prior spread. Noisy data (large σ²) or a strong belief that weights are small (small τ²) both mean a larger λ. And the sharp peak of the Laplace prior at zero is the probabilistic counterpart of the diamond's corners: it puts real preference on weights being exactly zero.
deep:
Ridge fixes ill-conditioned problems

Ridge regression has a closed-form solution, w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹ Xᵀy, where I is the identity matrix. Without the λI, least squares needs to invert XᵀX, which fails or becomes numerically unstable when features are perfectly or nearly collinear, or when there are more features than rows. Adding λ to every diagonal element makes the matrix invertible and well-behaved. That was ridge's original purpose (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970): stabilising regression with correlated predictors. In terms of the data's principal directions (ml13), ridge shrinks the weight along each direction by d²/(d² + λ), where d² measures how much the data varies along it — directions the data barely explores, where estimates are least reliable, are shrunk the most.

Weight decay versus L2 under adaptive optimisers

With plain gradient descent and step size η, the L2 penalty (λ/2)‖w‖² contributes λw to the gradient, so each step multiplies every weight by (1 − ηλ) before the data's update: with η = 0.1 and λ = 0.01, that is 0.999 per step, and after 1,000 steps with no data pressure a weight would be down to 0.999¹⁰⁰⁰ ≈ 0.37 of its value. That multiplicative shrink is weight decay, and for plain gradient descent it is identical to L2. Adaptive optimisers such as Adam divide each parameter's gradient by a running estimate of its typical size. If the L2 term is inside the loss, its gradient is divided too, so parameters that have large gradients receive far less decay than intended. Loshchilov and Hutter's AdamW applies the decay directly to the weights, outside the adaptive scaling, which restores uniform shrinkage and improved generalisation in their experiments. AdamW with weight decay is the default optimiser for transformer training (dl5 covers optimisers).

Dropout

Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) sets each hidden unit's output to zero with some probability p (often 0.1–0.5) at every training step, and rescales the rest to keep the expected total unchanged. A unit can't rely on particular other units being present, which discourages fragile co-adaptations. Two readings explain why it regularises: training with dropout approximately trains an ensemble of exponentially many "thinned" networks that share weights, and averaging reduces variance (ml2's ensemble formula); and for linear models, dropout in expectation is equivalent to an L2 penalty weighted by each feature's variance. At inference time dropout is switched off.

Data augmentation and label smoothing

Augmentation creates new training examples by transformations that shouldn't change the label — flipping, cropping or colour-shifting an image; adding noise to audio; paraphrasing text. It encodes knowledge ("a cat flipped left-to-right is still a cat") that rules out many functions which fit the original data but violate the invariance. When the invariance is real, it is often the strongest regulariser available; when it isn't (flipping digits turns some into other digits), it hurts. Label smoothing replaces a one-hot target (1 for the right class, 0 for the others) with, for example, 0.9 and small shares for the others, so the model is never pushed towards infinite confidence; it tends to improve calibration (ml15) and generalisation.

Low-rank constraints in fine-tuning

Fine-tuning all billions of weights of a large model on a few thousand examples invites overfitting. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the original weights and learns only a small update to each weight matrix, expressed as the product of two thin matrices of rank r (say 8 or 16). That cuts trainable parameters by orders of magnitude and constrains the update to a low-dimensional space — a structural regulariser, analogous to limiting a linear model to a few principal directions.

Sparsity beyond lasso

The L1 penalty is the convex stand-in for what one often really wants: to count non-zero weights (the "L0" penalty) and keep few. Counting is combinatorial and intractable for many features; L1 is its closest convex relaxation, which is why it's used. Group lasso penalises the L2 norm of predefined groups (for example, all the dummy columns of one categorical variable), so whole groups are kept or dropped together. For trees and boosting (ml10), regularisation takes other forms — maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf, shrinkage (learning rate), subsampling — but the principle is the same: limit how closely the model can follow the training data.
prod:
The public case: lasso on the prostate-cancer data

The textbook The Elements of Statistical Learning (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman) uses a real clinical dataset to compare regression methods: 97 men about to undergo prostate surgery, eight clinical measurements (such as log cancer volume, log prostate weight, age and seminal-vesicle invasion), and the target, log prostate-specific antigen (lpsa). The data and its fixed split — 67 men for training, 30 for testing — are published on the book's website. We reproduced the comparison in NumPy with standardised features:

Method (λ by 10-fold cross-validation)Test MSEFeatures used
Predict the training mean1.0570
Least squares, no penalty0.5218
Ridge, best CV λ0.4908 (all shrunk)
Lasso, best CV λ0.4927
Lasso, one-standard-error rule0.4783 (+ one near zero)

The least-squares figure, 0.521, matches the book's table exactly, which confirms the reproduction uses the same data and split. The one-standard-error lasso kept log cancer volume, log prostate weight and seminal-vesicle invasion (plus a weight of 0.007 on one more), dropping age, the Gleason score and the others entirely — and it predicted the 30 held-out patients better than the full least-squares model. Three lessons carry over to industry. A small dataset with several correlated measurements is exactly where regularisation pays. The simpler, sparser model is not only easier to explain to a clinician but also more accurate on new patients. And the choice between "best CV score" and "one standard error" changed the model from seven features to three with no loss — because with 67 rows, cross-validation differences smaller than one standard error are noise. (With only 30 test patients, the ranking between ridge and lasso here is itself within noise; the robust conclusion is that both beat unregularised least squares.)

Where regularisation goes wrong in production

Scaling mismatch between training and serving. A model trained on standardised features must receive features standardised with the same training means and standard deviations at serving time. Recomputing them on live data, or forgetting to apply them, silently shifts every prediction. Store the scaler with the model as one artefact (ml14).

λ tuned on the wrong split. If the scaler or feature selection was fitted on all data before cross-validation, the chosen λ is optimistic. Put scaling, selection and the model inside one pipeline that cross-validation refits in each fold.

Interpreting lasso's selection causally. Teams report "lasso found that feature X doesn't matter" when X was simply correlated with a feature lasso kept. Check selection stability across bootstrap samples before telling anyone which features matter.

Weight decay on the wrong parameters. In deep-learning recipes, biases and normalisation parameters are usually excluded from weight decay. Decaying them can hurt training, and frameworks don't exclude them automatically — the parameter groups have to be set up explicitly.

What to monitor and tune

Track the regularisation strength alongside the model version, the number of non-zero coefficients for sparse models (a sudden change after retraining often signals a data problem), and the train–validation gap over retrains. When the gap grows as data drifts, increasing λ is a quick mitigation while the underlying shift is investigated.
myths: Regularisation always improves a model.

It trades bias for variance. If a model is underfitting — high training error close to validation error — adding a penalty makes it worse, because it restrains a model that is already too rigid. Regularisation helps when variance dominates: many features relative to rows, a flexible model, noisy labels. That is why its strength is tuned on validation data rather than set high by default.
L1 regularisation reliably finds the features that truly matter.

Lasso finds a small set of features that predict well, which is not the same thing. When features are correlated it picks one from each group more or less arbitrarily, and a different bootstrap sample of the data can pick a different one. Treat lasso's selection as a compact predictive model, not as evidence of which variables are causal or even uniquely important; elastic net or stability selection give more trustworthy groups.
L2 regularisation eventually sets weights to zero if you make λ big enough.

It shrinks every weight by a proportion, so weights approach zero but never reach it exactly (unless the unregularised weight was already zero). In the one-feature example, ridge takes the weight from 1.75 to 0.29 at λ = 10, and to 0.03 at λ = 100 — never zero. Exact zeros come from penalties with a corner at zero, like L1.
You can regularise without scaling features first.

The penalty acts on the numbers in the weight vector, and those depend on each feature's units. The same distance measured in millimetres needs a weight 1,000 times smaller than in metres, so its squared-weight penalty is a million times smaller and the penalty effectively ignores it. Standardise features (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) so the penalty compares like with like.
Adding an L2 term to the loss is the same as weight decay in every optimiser.

It is the same for plain gradient descent: the L2 gradient shrinks each weight by a fixed fraction per step. Adaptive optimisers such as Adam divide each parameter's gradient by a running estimate of its size, which also divides the L2 part, so weights with large gradients are barely regularised. AdamW applies the decay directly to the weights instead, which is why it generalises better and is the default for training transformers.
Deep networks are so over-parameterised that explicit regularisation doesn't matter.

Implicit effects of the training procedure do a lot, but explicit regularisation still matters in practice: weight decay is on by default in nearly every large-model recipe, data augmentation is essential in vision, dropout remains standard in many architectures, and fine-tuning on a small dataset overfits quickly without early stopping or a low-rank constraint such as LoRA.
lab:
Goal: watch ridge shrink and lasso select, on data where you know the truth. NumPy only; tested with Python 3.12.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 60, 30                                   # few rows, many features
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
w_true = np.zeros(p); w_true[:3] = [3.0, -2.0, 1.5]   # only 3 features matter
y = X @ w_true + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n)
Xtr, ytr, Xva, yva = X[:40], y[:40], X[40:], y[40:]
mse = lambda w, X, y: np.mean((y - X @ w) ** 2)

print("ridge:  lambda   train    val   |w|2")
for lam in [0, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]:
    w = np.linalg.solve(Xtr.T @ Xtr + lam * np.eye(p), Xtr.T @ ytr)
    print(f"{lam:>13} {mse(w, Xtr, ytr):6.2f} {mse(w, Xva, yva):6.2f} {np.linalg.norm(w):6.2f}")

def lasso(X, y, lam, steps=5000):               # ISTA: gradient step, then soft-threshold
    L = np.linalg.norm(X, 2) ** 2               # step size 1/L keeps it stable
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(steps):
        z = w - X.T @ (X @ w - y) / L
        w = np.sign(z) * np.maximum(np.abs(z) - lam / L, 0)
    return w

print("lasso:  lambda   train    val  nonzero")
for lam in [0.1, 1, 5, 20, 80]:
    w = lasso(Xtr, ytr, lam)
    print(f"{lam:>13} {mse(w, Xtr, ytr):6.2f} {mse(w, Xva, yva):6.2f} {np.sum(w != 0):6d}")
print("lasso weights at lambda=20:", np.round(lasso(Xtr, ytr, 20)[:6], 2))

What to look for. Ridge's weight norm falls from 4.37 to 1.17 but validation error only rises — shrinking all 30 weights doesn't help when the truth is sparse. Lasso's non-zero count falls from 29 to 3, and validation error bottoms out at 1.13 (λ = 5); at λ = 20 the surviving weights are the three true features (2.24, −1.93, 0.97), shrunk towards zero. Try making w_true dense (all 30 non-zero and small) and ridge becomes the winner.
recap: Regularisation restrains a model's flexibility to reduce variance, usually by adding λ times a penalty on weight size to the training loss.

L2 (ridge) penalises the sum of squared weights and shrinks every weight by a proportion; L1 (lasso) penalises the sum of absolute weights and subtracts a constant, pushing small weights to exactly zero.

Geometrically, the L1 constraint region is a diamond with corners on the axes, so the best point inside it often sits on a corner where some weights are zero; the L2 region is a circle with no corners.
Elastic net combines the two to get sparsity while keeping groups of correlated features together.
λ is chosen by cross-validation over a log-scale grid, often taking the largest λ within one standard error of the best score for a simpler model.
Features must be standardised first, and the intercept is not penalised.
In Bayesian terms, L2 is a Gaussian prior on weights and L1 a Laplace prior; λ encodes how strongly you believe weights are small.

Early stopping, dropout, data augmentation, weight decay, label smoothing and low-rank fine-tuning are all regularisers, and with adaptive optimisers weight decay must be decoupled from the gradient, as AdamW does.

An optimisation method that updates one weight at a time while holding the others fixed; the standard solver for lasso.

The constant added to a linear model's prediction; it sets the baseline level and is not penalised.

The count of non-zero weights; penalising it directly is the ideal of feature selection but is computationally intractable, which is why L1 is used as a stand-in.
Training a classifier against slightly softened targets (for example 0.9 for the right class instead of 1.0) so it doesn't become over-confident.

A probability distribution with a sharp peak at its centre and heavier tails than a Gaussian; as a prior it corresponds to L1.
Low-rank adaptation: fine-tuning a large model by learning small low-rank updates to its weight matrices instead of changing all weights.

A plot of each coefficient against λ, showing how weights shrink (and, for L1, drop to zero) as the penalty grows.
Linear regression with an L2 penalty; shrinks all weights and stabilises fits with correlated features.

Having many weights exactly equal to zero.
