t: Loss functions: what each one punishes
sum: How the loss defines what a model learns: MSE vs MAE vs Huber and the outlier question, quantile loss for intervals and asymmetric costs, cross-entropy and why it pairs with softmax, focal loss for extreme imbalance, losses as noise models, and the difference between the loss you train and the metric you report.
prereq: ml1
Training chooses parameters that minimise the average loss over the training examples; regression predicts numbers, classification predicts categories.
ml4
Gradient descent moves parameters against the gradient of the loss, so the loss's slope decides how strongly each example pushes on the model.
why:
An online estate agent trains a model to estimate house prices. It performs well on validation data by the team's chosen measure, mean squared error, and ships. Within a week, sellers of ordinary three-bedroom homes complain that the estimates are consistently too high. The cause is a small number of mansions in the training data. Because the model was trained to minimise squared error, a £2 million miss on one mansion counted as much as a £20,000 miss on ten thousand ordinary houses, so the model shifted its predictions upward everywhere to reduce the mansion errors. It did exactly what it was told. It was told the wrong thing.

A loss function is the instruction. It turns "how wrong was this prediction?" into a number, and training (ml4) adjusts the parameters to make the average of that number small. Everything the model learns — whether it predicts averages or typical values, whether it cares more about rare cases or common ones, whether its probabilities can be trusted, how it trades one kind of mistake against another — follows from the choice of loss. Choose it carelessly and the model optimises the wrong objective very precisely.

Interviewers probe this constantly because it separates people who have trained models from people who have called fit(). "Why cross-entropy and not MSE for classification?" "What does MAE estimate?" "Your forecast has asymmetric costs — what do you train on?" "Why does PyTorch want logits, not probabilities?" Each has a crisp answer that comes straight from what the loss punishes.

This lesson works through the losses you will meet, each with numbers: MSE, MAE and Huber on the same data with an outlier (including what a constant model predicts under each); quantile loss and how a cost ratio becomes a percentile; cross-entropy computed through a softmax by hand, with its p − y gradient; why MSE fails for classifiers, with the gradients compared; focal loss and the public case where it made a new kind of object detector work; the idea that every loss is a noise model; and the gap between the loss you train and the metric you report.
primer:
A loss is a pricing policy for mistakes

Think of a loss function as a fine schedule. A traffic authority could fine speeding by a fixed amount per kilometre per hour over the limit, or by the square of the excess, or by a flat fee for anything over. Each schedule changes driver behaviour differently: squared fines make drivers terrified of large excesses and relaxed about small ones; flat fees make them indifferent to how much they exceed once they do. A model is a driver who minimises its total fine across the training data. Change the schedule and you change what it learns to avoid.

Three regression losses on the same five numbers

True values 10, 10, 10, 10, 50 (one outlier). A model predicts 10 for all of them, so the errors are 0, 0, 0, 0 and 40.

  • Mean squared error (MSE) = (0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 40²)/5 = 1,600/5 = 320. The one outlier supplies the entire loss.
  • Mean absolute error (MAE) = (0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 40)/5 = 8. The outlier counts, but only in proportion.
  • Root mean squared error (RMSE) = √320 ≈ 17.9 — back in the original units, but still outlier-driven.

The deepest way to remember the difference: if a model could only output a single constant for all five examples, the constant that minimises MSE is the mean (18), and the constant that minimises MAE is the median (10). A feature-based model trained with MSE predicts the average outcome for inputs like this one; trained with MAE it predicts the typical outcome. For the estate agent, the median was what sellers expected.

Classification: cross-entropy in one line

A classifier outputs a probability for each class. Cross-entropy (also called log loss) charges −log(probability given to the correct class):

  • Correct class given 0.9 → −ln 0.9 ≈ 0.105.
  • Given 0.5 → 0.693.
  • Given 0.01 → 4.61. Being confidently wrong is punished severely, and the fine grows without limit as the probability approaches zero.

Loss versus metric

The loss is what training optimises; because training follows the slope of the loss (ml4), it must be smooth. The metric is what you report and decide with — accuracy, F1, revenue — and it can be anything. Accuracy can't be trained directly: nudging a weight slightly changes no prediction's class, so accuracy's slope is zero almost everywhere. So models are trained on a smooth loss that tends to improve the metric, and then checked, and tuned, against the metric itself.

Keep one question in mind through the rest of the lesson: what decision will this prediction drive, and what does each kind of mistake cost? Totals call for means, typical cases for medians, stock levels for percentiles, and risk calculations for honest probabilities. The loss is where that answer gets written down.
body:
1. The regression family: what each loss's slope does

Write the residual as r = y − ŷ. What matters for training is the gradient — how hard each example pulls the prediction:

LossPer examplePull (gradient w.r.t. ŷ)A constant model predicts
MSEr²−2r: grows with the errorthe mean
MAE|r|−sign(r): the same for every errorthe median
Huber (δ)½r² if |r| ≤ δ, else δ(|r| − ½δ)−r, capped at ±δbetween mean and median

Under MSE, an example 40 away pulls 40 times harder than one 1 away; under MAE they pull equally; under Huber with δ = 5, the far one pulls 5 times harder and no more. MAE's constant pull has two costs: it is not differentiable at zero, and it doesn't shrink as the prediction gets close, so gradient-based training can oscillate near the optimum. Huber fixes both while keeping robustness, which is why it's a common production choice.

Worked example: a constant model on skewed prices. House prices in £ thousands: 100, 110, 120, 130, 1,000. The best single constant under each loss:

  • MSE → mean = 1,460 / 5 = 292. Above every ordinary house: the model is wrong about 80% of the data to be less wrong about one point.
  • MAE → median = 120. Unmoved by the outlier; it would stay at 120 if the mansion cost £100 million.
  • Huber, δ = 50 → 127.5. Suppose the answer c lies near the four ordinary prices, within 50 of each. Those four pull with force (c − yᵢ) each; the mansion, far beyond δ, pulls with a fixed force of 50. At the optimum the pulls balance: (c − 100) + (c − 110) + (c − 120) + (c − 130) = 50, so 4c − 460 = 50 and c = 127.5. Check: 127.5 is within 50 of all four, as assumed. The outlier nudges the answer up by 7.5 rather than 172.

Before switching losses, ask whether the outlier is an error (fix the data), a real but unwanted influence (use a robust loss), or a real segment the model lacks features for (add features — a "number of bedrooms" or "is detached" feature explains mansions better than any loss). And if the target is multiplicative — prices, incomes, durations — training MSE on log(target) is often the best of all: it treats a 10% error the same at every price level. Note that exponentiating a prediction of the mean log gives the geometric mean, which is closer to a median than a mean; correct for that if totals matter.

2. Quantile loss: predicting a percentile

Sometimes the question isn't "what's the expected demand?" but "how much stock should I hold so I run out only 10% of the time?". That is the 90th percentile of demand, and quantile (pinball) loss trains a model to predict it directly:

pinball_τ(r) = τ · r          if r ≥ 0   (under-prediction: actual above forecast)
             = (τ − 1) · r    if r < 0   (over-prediction)

With τ = 0.9, under-predicting by 10 costs 9 and over-predicting by 10 costs 1. The forecast that balances these is the one exceeded by actual demand only 10% of the time — the 90th percentile. Train one model at τ = 0.1 and another at τ = 0.9 and you get an 80% prediction interval instead of a single point. And the link to business costs is exact: if running out costs 4 per unit and overstocking costs 1, the cost-minimising stock is the percentile τ = 4/(4 + 1) = 0.8 (the "newsvendor" critical ratio). Train at τ = 0.8 and the model's output is the order quantity.

3. Cross-entropy, from probabilities to gradients

A multi-class classifier produces one raw score per class, called a logit. Softmax turns logits into probabilities that are positive and sum to 1: pₖ = exp(zₖ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ). Cross-entropy is then −log of the probability of the true class.

Worked, three classes. Logits z = (2, 1, 0), true class 0.

  1. Exponentials: e² = 7.389, e¹ = 2.718, e⁰ = 1. Sum = 11.107.
  2. Probabilities: 7.389/11.107 = 0.665, 2.718/11.107 = 0.245, 1/11.107 = 0.090.
  3. Loss: −ln 0.665 = 0.408.
  4. Gradient with respect to the logits: p − y = (0.665 − 1, 0.245 − 0, 0.090 − 0) = (−0.335, +0.245, +0.090).

That last line is the key fact. Combining softmax and cross-entropy, the derivative of the loss with respect to each logit is just "predicted probability minus target". Gradient descent therefore raises the true class's logit in proportion to how much probability it is missing, and lowers each wrong class's logit in proportion to the probability it wrongly received. The more wrong the model, the stronger the correction — no saturation, no vanishing signal.

For two classes, the same thing with a sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) is binary cross-entropy: −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)], with gradient p − y with respect to z. Cross-entropy is also the negative log-likelihood of the labels: minimising it is choosing the parameters under which the observed labels were most probable. (ml6 derives this for logistic regression.)

4. Why not MSE for classifiers? The gradients compared

Take a positive example (y = 1) that the model gets badly wrong, with logit z = −5, so p = σ(−5) = 0.0067.

  • Cross-entropy: gradient with respect to z is p − y = −0.993. Strong push in the right direction.
  • MSE on the probability, (p − y)²: by the chain rule the gradient is 2(p − y) · σ′(z), and σ′(z) = p(1 − p) = 0.0066. Gradient = 2 × (−0.993) × 0.0066 = −0.013.

The MSE gradient is about 75 times weaker exactly when the model is most wrong, because the sigmoid is flat (saturated) out there and MSE multiplies by its slope. Cross-entropy's logarithm cancels that slope. So MSE-trained classifiers learn slowly from their worst mistakes, and cross-entropy is the standard.

5. Focal loss: when easy examples drown the signal

Suppose 99.9% of examples are easy negatives the model already gets right with probability 0.9. Each contributes a small cross-entropy (0.105), but there are so many that together they dominate the total loss and gradient, and the rare hard examples barely register. Focal loss multiplies cross-entropy by (1 − p_t)^γ, where p_t is the probability given to the true class:

  • Easy example, p_t = 0.9, γ = 2: factor (0.1)² = 0.01 → loss 0.105 × 0.01 = 0.00105, cut 100-fold.
  • Hard example, p_t = 0.1: factor (0.9)² = 0.81 → loss 2.303 × 0.81 = 1.87, barely changed.

The easy example's weight relative to the hard one drops from about 1:22 to about 1:1,800. Training attention moves to the examples that still have something to teach. This is the public case below. Focal loss reweights by difficulty, while class weights reweight by class (every negative counts, say, one-tenth as much); both change the model's optimum and therefore its probabilities, which is the subject of ml8 and ml15.

6. Other losses you will meet

  • Hinge loss, max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) with labels ±1: zero once an example is on the right side with a margin; used by support vector machines. It doesn't produce probabilities.
  • Poisson and Tweedie deviance: for counts (orders per day) and non-negative skewed targets with many zeros (insurance claims). They penalise errors relative to the expected variance, so a miss of 5 on an expected count of 2 matters more than a miss of 5 on 2,000.
  • KL divergence: compares two probability distributions; used in knowledge distillation (a small "student" model matches a large "teacher's" probabilities) and in variational autoencoders.
  • Contrastive losses (InfoNCE): a cross-entropy over "which of these candidates is the true match?", used to train embedding models such as CLIP (ml1).
  • Ranking losses: pairwise (score the relevant item above the irrelevant one) and listwise losses for search and recommendation, where the metric is order, not value.

7. Weights, and losses that combine several goals

Every loss above is an average over examples, and averages can be weighted. A sample weight multiplies an example's loss: weight 2 means it counts as if it appeared twice. Weights are how you encode that some examples matter more (high-value customers), correct for sampling (if you kept only 1 in 10 negatives to save compute, give each kept negative weight 10 to restore the original balance), or emphasise recent data when the world changes. Worked: 900 negatives and 100 positives, and you want each class to contribute equally. Give positives weight 900/100 = 9. The weighted loss now treats the data as if it were balanced — which also means the model's predicted probabilities will be inflated for positives (it believes positives are 50% of the world, not 10%), a trap covered in ml8.

Many real models optimise several things at once. A recommendation model may predict click, purchase and return from shared features, with a total loss L = L_click + 0.5·L_purchase + 2·L_return. The weights decide how much each head influences the shared layers, and they interact with the losses' scales: a cross-entropy of about 0.7 and an MSE of about 10,000 on prices can't be added naively, or the MSE term will take over. Normalise targets, or choose weights so each term contributes a comparable share of the gradient, and track each component separately in training logs, never just the sum.

Regularisation (ml3) is another added term: the full objective is data loss plus λ × penalty, and everything said here about scales applies — a penalty that is tiny next to a loss measured in millions of pounds does nothing.

8. How to evaluate the choice

Loss choice is itself a hyperparameter, judged on validation data against the metric that matters. A practical routine: train the candidates (say MSE, Huber and MSE on log-target), then compare them on the business metric, on the median error, and on error by slice — cheap versus expensive items, frequent versus rare customers. MSE-trained models usually win on the mean error and lose on the median; robust losses the reverse. If the slice that matters most to the business is the tail, a robust loss may be exactly wrong. Plotting predictions against actuals, or residuals against predictions, often shows immediately whether a model is being dragged by a few extremes.

9. Numerical stability: never compute log(softmax) in two steps

Softmax of large logits overflows: exp(1,000) is infinity in floating point. Subtracting the largest logit first changes nothing mathematically (it cancels in the ratio) but keeps every exponent ≤ 0. Separately, the log of a tiny probability can underflow to log(0) = −∞. Fused implementations compute log_softmax(z) = z − max(z) − log Σ exp(z − max(z)) directly — the log-sum-exp trick — so both problems disappear. That is why PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits, and why BCEWithLogitsLoss is preferred over applying a sigmoid and then binary cross-entropy. Passing probabilities into a loss that expects logits is a classic silent bug: training runs, just badly.
deep:
Every loss is a noise model

Suppose labels are the model's prediction plus Gaussian noise of fixed variance. The likelihood of the data is a product of Gaussian densities, and its negative log is, up to constants, the sum of squared residuals. So minimising MSE is maximum-likelihood estimation under Gaussian noise. Laplace noise (sharper peak, heavier tails) gives MAE; a Bernoulli or categorical distribution over labels gives cross-entropy; Poisson counts give Poisson deviance. This reading turns loss choice into a modelling question: how do the observations scatter around the truth? Heavy tails suggest Laplace or Student-t style losses; variance growing with the mean suggests Poisson, gamma or Tweedie; multiplicative noise suggests modelling the logarithm.

Proper scoring rules

A loss on probability forecasts is proper if, when the true probability of an event is q, the expected loss is minimised by forecasting exactly q. Log loss: expected loss is −[q log p + (1 − q) log(1 − p)], whose minimum over p is at p = q. The Brier score (squared error on probabilities) is also proper. Accuracy is not — any forecast on the right side of 0.5 scores the same — and neither is hinge loss. Training on a proper loss aligns the model with producing honest probabilities, which is what expected-cost decisions, risk ranking and calibration need. Reweighting classes or focusing on hard examples deliberately breaks this, so the outputs must be recalibrated before being read as probabilities (ml15).

Surrogates and consistency

The losses we actually want to minimise — 0–1 error, F1, NDCG — are discontinuous. We train on smooth surrogate losses instead. Theory on "classification-calibrated" or consistent surrogates says when minimising the surrogate also minimises the true error in the limit of infinite data: cross-entropy, hinge and exponential losses all are for 0–1 error. For set-based metrics like F1 there is no simple consistent per-example surrogate, and the reliable approach is to train with cross-entropy and then choose the decision threshold that maximises F1 on validation data (ml7).

Label smoothing and what it trades

Label smoothing replaces the one-hot target (1 for the true class) with 1 − ε and ε/(K − 1) for the other K − 1 classes, for example 0.9 and small shares. The optimal logits under smoothed targets are finite, so the model never tries to push logits to infinity; this regularises (ml3) and often improves calibration. The cost: the model's outputs cluster tightly by class, discarding information about which wrong classes are similar, which can make a smoothed model a worse teacher for distillation.

Asymmetric and business-derived losses

When errors have different costs, put the costs in the loss or in the decision rule. For regression, quantile loss at the critical ratio implements asymmetric linear costs exactly. For classification, it is usually better to train an honest probability model with cross-entropy and apply the cost-sensitive threshold afterwards (predict positive when p × cost of a miss exceeds (1 − p) × cost of a false alarm), because then one model serves many cost settings and its probabilities stay interpretable. Changing the loss for each cost setting bakes the costs into the model and makes it harder to reuse.

Robust losses and the influence of a single point

Statisticians describe robustness through the influence of one observation: how much the fitted model moves if that point is changed. Under MSE the influence is unbounded — push one label to infinity and the fit follows it. Under Huber and MAE it is bounded by δ or by 1, so no single point can move the fit arbitrarily far. The robust version has a cost: when the noise really is Gaussian and there are no outliers, MSE is the most efficient estimator, and Huber loses a little accuracy (with the conventional δ ≈ 1.35 standard deviations, about 5%). That's the trade: a small loss of efficiency on clean data for protection against contaminated data.

The loss of language models

LLM pretraining minimises average next-token cross-entropy, usually reported in nats (natural log) or bits per token, and as perplexity = exp(mean cross-entropy). A mean of 2.0 nats per token gives perplexity e² ≈ 7.39. Because the loss is per token, perplexities are comparable only between models with the same tokeniser; across tokenisers, compare bits per byte of text. Preference optimisation such as DPO uses a logistic loss on the difference between the model's log-probability ratios (relative to a frozen reference model) for a preferred and a rejected response — still a cross-entropy, applied to pairs.
prod:
The public case: focal loss and RetinaNet

Object detectors find and label every object in an image. In 2017 the most accurate ones were "two-stage": a first stage proposed a few thousand candidate regions, and a second stage classified them. "One-stage" detectors, which classify a dense grid of candidate boxes directly, were faster and simpler but consistently less accurate. Lin and colleagues at Facebook AI Research asked why, and concluded in "Focal Loss for Dense Object Detection" that the central cause was extreme foreground–background class imbalance: a dense detector evaluates on the order of 100,000 candidate locations per image, almost all of them easy background. Under ordinary cross-entropy, those easy negatives each contribute a small loss but together overwhelm the gradient, so the detector learns little from the rare, hard examples.

Their fix was purely a change of loss: reshape cross-entropy so that it "down-weights the loss assigned to well-classified examples" — focal loss, with γ = 2 and a class weight α = 0.25 working best in their experiments. With it, their simple one-stage detector, RetinaNet, matched the speed of previous one-stage detectors while surpassing the accuracy of all existing two-stage detectors, in the paper's words. The architecture was deliberately ordinary; the loss made the difference. The general lesson for engineers: when the data's composition is badly skewed, look at what the loss is actually spending its gradient on before reaching for a bigger model.

Failure modes in production

Mean versus median surprises. An MSE model reports the expected value, which for skewed targets is above what most users experience (delivery times, prices, waiting times). If the product displays the prediction as "typical", use a median (MAE, or quantile 0.5) or show a range.

Metric–loss mismatch. Teams optimise log loss offline and are judged online on revenue or clicks. A model can improve log loss mostly on examples that don't affect the decision (very low-probability items that are never shown). Evaluate offline with a metric close to the decision, such as ranking metrics for recommendation, and keep an eye on the online metric (ml16).

Reweighted losses and broken probabilities. Class weights, focal loss and negative subsampling all shift predicted probabilities away from true frequencies. Downstream systems that multiply probabilities by values (expected revenue from an ad click, expected loss from fraud) are then systematically wrong unless the outputs are recalibrated (ml15).

Numerical bugs. Passing probabilities to a loss that expects logits, applying softmax twice, or computing log(softmax) separately in low precision produces NaNs or quietly slower learning. Unit-test the loss on a hand-computed example like section 3's.

Choosing a loss in practice

Start from the decision: is it about totals (mean, MSE or a deviance matching the target's noise), typical cases (median, MAE/Huber), thresholds and stock levels (quantiles), or probabilities feeding expected-value calculations (cross-entropy, kept proper)? Then check the target's distribution — skew, zeros, counts, outliers — and whether a transformation such as the logarithm makes it well behaved. Finally, evaluate with the business metric, not just the training loss, and log both.
myths: MSE is the default regression loss, so it's always a safe choice.

MSE makes the model estimate the conditional mean and weights each error by its square, so a handful of extreme values can dominate training. For heavy-tailed targets — prices, durations, claim sizes — that can pull predictions away from the typical case. Whether that's wrong depends on what the business needs: if it pays on averages (total revenue), the mean is right; if it cares about the typical case or is exposed to data errors, MAE or Huber may be better.
You should train on the metric you care about.

Many metrics — accuracy, F1, precision at a threshold, NDCG — change only when a prediction crosses a boundary, so their gradient is zero almost everywhere and gradient descent gets no signal. You train a smooth surrogate (cross-entropy, a ranking loss) that tends to improve the metric, then tune thresholds or post-process to optimise the metric itself on validation data.
Cross-entropy and log loss are different things.

For classification they are the same quantity: the negative log of the probability the model gave to the correct class, averaged over examples. 'Log loss' is the common name in scikit-learn and Kaggle, 'cross-entropy' in deep learning, and 'negative log-likelihood' in statistics.
A classifier can be trained with MSE on its probabilities just as well.

It can be trained, but badly. With a sigmoid or softmax output, the MSE gradient is multiplied by the output's own slope, which is nearly zero when the model is confidently wrong — in the lesson's example the MSE gradient is about 75 times smaller than cross-entropy's for a badly wrong prediction. Cross-entropy's gradient with respect to the logits is simply p − y, so confident mistakes get the strongest correction.
Focal loss is the fix for class imbalance.

Focal loss down-weights easy examples, which helps when the imbalance is extreme and the majority class is mostly trivial — dense object detection with ~100,000 candidate boxes per image is its origin. For ordinary tabular imbalance, a well-trained model with cross-entropy plus a tuned decision threshold is usually as good, and focal loss distorts the predicted probabilities, so they need recalibrating (ml8, ml15).
The choice of loss is a technical detail separate from business requirements.

The loss is the model's definition of 'good'. Choosing the 90th-percentile quantile loss instead of MSE turns a demand forecast into a stock-level recommendation; weighting classes changes which errors the model avoids. The loss should come from the decision the prediction drives and the cost of each kind of error.
lab:
Goal: compute each loss on the same data, find the best constant under each, and compare cross-entropy and MSE gradients. NumPy only; written for Python 3.12.

import numpy as np

y = np.array([100., 110., 120., 130., 1000.])
grid = np.linspace(50, 1100, 10501)
def best(loss):                                  # brute-force the best constant
    return grid[np.argmin([loss(y - c).mean() for c in grid])]
mse   = lambda r: r ** 2
mae   = lambda r: np.abs(r)
huber = lambda r, d=50: np.where(np.abs(r) <= d, 0.5 * r**2, d * (np.abs(r) - 0.5 * d))
pinball = lambda r, t=0.9: np.maximum(t * r, (t - 1) * r)
for name, f in [("MSE", mse), ("MAE", mae), ("Huber", huber), ("pinball 0.9", pinball)]:
    print(f"{name:12s} best constant = {best(f):.1f}")

z = np.array([2., 1., 0.])                        # softmax + cross-entropy, true class 0
p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
print("probs", p.round(3), "CE", round(-np.log(p[0]), 3), "grad", (p - [1, 0, 0]).round(3))

zc = -5.0; pc = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-zc))             # badly wrong positive example
print("CE grad", round(pc - 1, 3), " MSE grad", round(2 * (pc - 1) * pc * (1 - pc), 4))

What to look for. The best constants: MSE 292 (mean), MAE 120 (median), Huber 127.5, and pinball at τ = 0.9 lands on 1,000: with five points, anything below the mansion is exceeded by 20% of the data, more than the 10% a 90th percentile allows (moving up past 130 saves 0.9 per unit on the mansion and costs only 4 × 0.1 on the others). The softmax line should print probabilities 0.665, 0.245, 0.090, loss 0.408, gradient −0.335, 0.245, 0.090. The last line shows cross-entropy's gradient (−0.993) about 75 times larger than MSE's (−0.0132).
recap: A loss function scores each prediction's error, and training minimises its average, so the loss defines what the model considers good.
Mean squared error squares errors, so large errors dominate and a constant model trained on it predicts the mean; mean absolute error counts errors linearly and its constant predicts the median.
Huber loss is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, combining MSE's smoothness near the optimum with MAE's robustness to outliers.
Quantile (pinball) loss penalises under- and over-prediction asymmetrically, producing a chosen percentile rather than the mean, which gives prediction intervals and encodes asymmetric costs.
Cross-entropy is the negative log of the probability given to the correct class; it punishes confident mistakes heavily, and combined with softmax its gradient with respect to the logits is p − y.
Focal loss multiplies cross-entropy by (1 − p_t)^γ to down-weight easy examples, which made one-stage object detectors competitive.
Each common loss is the negative log-likelihood of a noise model: MSE for Gaussian noise, MAE for Laplace, cross-entropy for categorical outcomes, Poisson deviance for counts.
The training loss must be differentiable; the reported metric need not be, so models are trained on surrogates and tuned to the metric afterwards.
Fused, numerically stable implementations — log-softmax with cross-entropy, sigmoid with binary cross-entropy — should always be used instead of computing probabilities and then their logarithms.
glossary: Cross-entropy for two classes: −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)], where p is the predicted probability of class 1.
The mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and 0/1 outcomes; a proper scoring rule.
OpenAI's image-text model trained with a contrastive loss to match images with their captions (ml1).
The average (or middle value) of the target among examples with the same features; what MSE (or MAE) models learn to predict.
The negative log of the probability a model assigns to the true class, averaged over examples.
A generalisation of squared error for other noise models, such as Poisson or Tweedie, used for counts and skewed non-negative targets.
Direct Preference Optimisation: fine-tuning a language model with a logistic loss that favours preferred over rejected responses relative to a reference model.
A classification metric combining precision and recall into one number between 0 and 1 (ml7).
Cross-entropy multiplied by (1 − p_t)^γ, which shrinks the loss on examples the model already classifies well.
A distribution where extreme values are much more common than in a Gaussian, such as house prices or insurance claims.
max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) for labels ±1; zero once an example is on the right side of the margin, used by support vector machines.
A loss that is quadratic for errors smaller than δ and linear beyond, robust to outliers yet smooth.
Kullback–Leibler divergence: a measure of how one probability distribution differs from another; minimising cross-entropy to fixed targets is equivalent to minimising it.
A classifier's raw, unbounded score before sigmoid or softmax turns it into a probability.
A very large neural network pretrained by next-token prediction on text (ml1).

The average absolute difference between predictions and labels.
The average squared difference between predictions and labels.
The number you report and make decisions with (accuracy, F1, revenue); it need not be differentiable.
Normalised discounted cumulative gain: a ranking metric that rewards putting relevant items near the top of a list.
Minus the log of the probability a model assigns to the observed data; minimising it is maximum-likelihood estimation.
An example far from the bulk of the data, either a genuine extreme or an error.
exp(mean cross-entropy per token); for a language model, the effective number of equally likely choices it is 'confused' between.

A loss on probability forecasts that is minimised in expectation only by reporting the true probabilities, such as log loss or the Brier score.

drill:
Work it out

Five house prices, in thousands: 100, 110, 120, 130, 1000. You fit a model with no features — it can only output one constant. What does it predict under MSE, under MAE, and under Huber with δ = 50?

Answer

MSE → the mean = 292. Sum 1,460 ÷ 5. The single mansion drags the prediction above every ordinary house, so the model is wrong about 80% of the data to be less wrong about one point.

MAE → the median = 120. Completely unmoved by the outlier; it would give 120 whether the fifth house cost £1M or £100M.

Huber, δ = 50 → 127.5. Guess that the answer c sits within 50 of the four ordinary prices. Each of them pulls with force (c − yᵢ); the mansion is far beyond δ, so it pulls with a constant force of δ = 50. Balance: (c − 100) + (c − 110) + (c − 120) + (c − 130) = 50 → 4c = 510 → c = 127.5, which is indeed within 50 of all four. The outlier nudges the answer by 7.5 instead of dragging it by 172.

The interview line: MSE estimates the conditional mean, MAE the conditional median, Huber something in between controlled by δ. Then the real question — is the mansion an error to be robust against, or a real segment you are failing to model? If it is real, the fix is a feature, not a loss function.
qa: E
What is the difference between a loss function and a metric?

The loss is what training minimises, so it must be differentiable and is usually averaged per example — cross-entropy, MSE. The metric is what you report and decide with — accuracy, F1, revenue, latency-weighted error — and it need not be differentiable. A good loss is one whose improvement tends to improve the metric; you still evaluate and tune (for example, thresholds) against the metric itself.
E
MSE or MAE — when would you choose each?

MSE when large errors are disproportionately bad and the target is well behaved; it estimates the conditional mean, which is right when you care about totals. MAE when you want the typical case and robustness to outliers or data errors; it estimates the conditional median. Huber is the compromise: smooth like MSE for small errors, robust like MAE for large ones.
E
What does quantile loss give you that MSE does not?

A chosen percentile instead of the mean. Training at τ = 0.1 and τ = 0.9 gives a 10th- and 90th-percentile forecast, i.e. an 80% prediction interval, and a single high quantile encodes asymmetric costs — for stock levels, under-forecasting (lost sales) may cost several times more than over-forecasting, so you forecast a high quantile.
M
Why is cross-entropy used for classification instead of MSE?

Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the correct class, so it heavily punishes confident mistakes (−log 0.01 ≈ 4.6), and with a sigmoid or softmax output its gradient with respect to the logits is simply p − y. MSE on probabilities multiplies the error by the sigmoid's slope, which is nearly zero when the model is saturated: for a logit of −5 on a positive example, cross-entropy's gradient is −0.99 while MSE's is −0.013, so learning from confident mistakes almost stops.
Follow-up: Is MSE on probabilities ever used? — The Brier score is exactly that and is a good evaluation metric for calibration, but it trains more slowly as a loss.
M
Why is cross-entropy paired with softmax rather than applied after it?

Because the combined gradient with respect to the logits simplifies to p − y, and because computing log(softmax(z)) in two steps takes the log of a possibly tiny number, underflowing to log(0) = −∞. Fused implementations compute log-softmax directly with the log-sum-exp trick, subtracting the largest logit before exponentiating. That's why PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits and why BCEWithLogitsLoss is preferred over sigmoid followed by BCE.
M
What is Huber loss and how do you choose δ?

Huber is ½r² for residuals |r| ≤ δ and δ(|r| − ½δ) beyond, so small errors behave like MSE and large ones like MAE: the gradient is capped at δ. δ is the error size at which you stop trusting a point fully — set it from the scale of normal noise, for example around the typical absolute residual, or tune it on validation data. As δ → 0 Huber approaches MAE (scaled); as δ → ∞ it becomes MSE.

Follow-up: What does a constant Huber model predict on 100, 110, 120, 130, 1000 with δ = 50? — 127.5: the four normal points pull quadratically, the outlier adds a fixed pull of 50, and 4c − 460 = 50 gives c = 127.5.
M
When would you use focal loss instead of class weights?

When the imbalance is extreme and most negatives are trivially easy. Class weights reweight by class — every negative counts less — while focal loss reweights by difficulty, shrinking the loss on examples already classified confidently, whatever their class. Dense object detection, with ~100,000 candidate locations per image nearly all of which are easy background, is the canonical case. The price is distorted probabilities, which then need recalibration.

Follow-up: What do the α and γ parameters do? — γ controls how strongly easy examples are down-weighted (γ = 2 in the RetinaNet paper); α is a class-balancing weight applied on top (0.25 for the positive class there).
M
What noise model does each common loss assume?

Minimising MSE is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise of constant variance; MAE under Laplace noise, which has heavier tails; cross-entropy under a categorical (or Bernoulli) distribution of labels; Poisson deviance under Poisson counts, whose variance equals the mean; Tweedie deviance for non-negative targets with a spike at zero, like insurance claims. Choosing a loss is choosing an assumption about how data scatters around the truth.

Follow-up: Why does that matter in practice? — A count target with MSE treats an error of 5 on a count of 2 the same as on a count of 2,000; Poisson deviance scales the penalty to the expected variance.
H
What is a proper scoring rule and why does it matter?

A loss on probability forecasts is proper if its expected value is minimised by reporting the true probability. Log loss and the Brier score are proper; accuracy and hinge loss are not, since they only care which side of 0.5 a prediction falls. Models trained on proper scores produce probabilities that can be used for decisions — expected-cost calculations, ranking by risk, calibration — whereas models trained on improper losses (SVMs, heavily reweighted or focal losses) need calibration afterwards.

Follow-up: Are the probabilities of a cross-entropy-trained network automatically calibrated? — Not necessarily; modern networks are often over-confident despite a proper loss, because of overfitting of the logits, so calibration is checked on held-out data (ml15).
H
How would you choose a loss for a demand-forecasting model where stock-outs cost four times as much as overstock?

Use quantile (pinball) loss at the critical ratio τ = cost_under / (cost_under + cost_over) = 4 / (4 + 1) = 0.8, so the model forecasts the 80th percentile of demand — the stock level that minimises expected cost in the newsvendor problem. Forecasting the mean with MSE and then adding a fudge factor is worse, because the right margin depends on each item's uncertainty, which the quantile model learns. Evaluate with the pinball loss and with the business cost directly.

Follow-up: How would you get full uncertainty? — Train several quantiles (or a distribution such as Tweedie/negative binomial) and check their coverage on held-out data: 80% of outcomes should fall below the 80th-percentile forecast.
H
What loss are LLMs trained with, and how does it relate to perplexity?

Pretraining minimises the average cross-entropy of the next token: the negative log-probability the model gives to the actual next token, averaged over all positions. Perplexity is exp of that average: a mean cross-entropy of 2.0 nats per token is perplexity e² ≈ 7.4 — as uncertain as choosing uniformly among about 7 tokens. Fine-tuning uses the same loss on curated responses; preference optimisation methods such as DPO use a loss on the difference in log-probability between a preferred and a rejected response, relative to a reference model.

Follow-up: Why can't you compare perplexities across models with different tokenisers? — Cross-entropy is per token, and a different tokeniser splits text into a different number of tokens; compare bits per byte or per character instead.
H
Your regression model's MSE is dominated by a few huge errors. How do you decide what to do?

First look at the examples: are they data errors (a price with extra zeros), genuine rare cases, or a segment the model lacks features for? Data errors should be fixed or excluded; a missing segment needs features, not a different loss. If they're genuine and the business cares about typical cases, switch to Huber or MAE, or model log(target) — which turns multiplicative errors into additive ones — and remember that predicting exp of a mean log gives a median, not a mean. If the business cares about totals, keep MSE and accept the influence, because the mean is the right target.

t: Logistic regression: the model every interview starts from
sum: A linear model in log-odds space: the sigmoid, odds and odds ratios, training by maximum likelihood (one gradient step by hand), the linear decision boundary, separation, multi-class softmax, reading coefficients honestly, and why a 2014 Facebook ads system still ran on it.
prereq: ml1
A model has parameters chosen to minimise average training loss; classification predicts a category and a baseline predicts the most common one.
ml3
An L2 or L1 penalty with strength λ (scikit-learn's C = 1/λ) shrinks weights; features should be standardised and the intercept is not penalised.
ml4
Gradient descent updates weights by w ← w − η·gradient; the gradient of a mean loss is an average over examples.
ml5
Cross-entropy (log loss) is −log of the probability given to the true class; with a sigmoid output its gradient with respect to the score is p − y.
why:
A subscription business wants to know which customers are likely to cancel next month, so its retention team can call them. It needs more than a yes/no answer. Calling costs money, and the team can make only 2,000 calls, so it needs a ranking; the finance team wants to forecast revenue, so it needs a probability — "this customer has a 31% chance of leaving" — that can be multiplied by the customer's value; and a regulator may ask why a particular customer was treated differently, so the model's reasoning must be explainable in a sentence.

Logistic regression does all three, and it's why almost every classification interview starts with it. It is linear regression's sibling for yes/no outcomes: compute a weighted sum of the features, as linear regression does, then squash that sum into a probability. Each weight has a precise meaning ("each support ticket in the last month doubles the odds of cancelling"), the probabilities are well calibrated when the model fits, and training has a single best answer that every solver finds. It trains in seconds on millions of rows, and it is the last layer of nearly every neural-network classifier.

It also carries a set of subtleties that interviewers love, because they reveal whether a candidate has actually used it: odds versus probabilities (the most common misreading of any model in industry), why training uses cross-entropy, what happens when classes are perfectly separable, how to correct probabilities after downsampling negatives, and when coefficients mean what people think they mean.

This lesson builds the model from a score to a probability: the sigmoid, odds and log-odds with worked conversions, maximum-likelihood training with one gradient step computed by hand, the linear decision boundary and how to bend it with features, separation (with the loss going to zero as weights grow), multi-class softmax regression, honest interpretation, and the public case of Facebook's 2014 ad-click system — a logistic regression fed by boosted trees, retrained daily, trained on downsampled data and recalibrated with a one-line formula.
primer:
From a score to a probability

Logistic regression answers yes/no questions with a probability, in two steps:

  1. Compute a score exactly as linear regression would: z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + b. The score can be any number from −∞ to +∞.
  2. Squash it into the range 0 to 1 with the sigmoid (logistic) function: p = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)).

A few sigmoid values to remember: z = 0 → 0.5; z = 2 → 0.88; z = −2 → 0.12; z = 5 → 0.993. Large positive scores mean "very likely yes", large negative ones "very likely no".

A worked example

A churn model has learned z = −3 + 0.8 × (support tickets last month) − 0.05 × (months as customer). A customer with 4 tickets and 20 months of tenure: z = −3 + 3.2 − 1.0 = −0.8, so p = 1/(1 + e^0.8) = 1/(1 + 2.23) ≈ 0.31 — a 31% chance of cancelling. To act, the business chooses a threshold, say "call everyone above 0.25"; choosing it well is the subject of ml7.

Odds and log-odds: the key to reading the model

The odds of an event are p / (1 − p): a probability of 0.8 is odds of 4 ("4 to 1"); 0.5 is odds of 1; 0.2 is odds of 0.25. The logarithm of the odds, log(p / (1 − p)), is the log-odds or logit. Rearranging the sigmoid shows the central fact:

log( p / (1 − p) )  =  w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + b

Logistic regression is a linear model of the log-odds. Each weight is the change in log-odds per unit of its feature. In the churn model, each extra support ticket adds 0.8 to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds by e^0.8 ≈ 2.23 — the odds ratio. Our customer's odds are 0.31/0.69 = 0.45; one more ticket makes them 0.45 × 2.23 = 1.0, a probability of 0.50. Evidence adds on the log-odds scale; the sigmoid only converts the total into a probability at the end.

This additivity is what makes the model easy to explain. For our customer, the story is: start from the baseline log-odds of −3 (a customer with no tickets and no tenure), add 0.8 for each of the 4 tickets (+3.2), subtract 0.05 for each of the 20 months (−1.0), and land at −0.8. Each feature's contribution can be shown as a bar in a chart, and the explanation for any individual prediction is just that list of contributions — something much harder to produce for a large tree ensemble or neural network.

How it is trained, in one sentence

The weights are chosen to make the observed outcomes as probable as possible — maximum likelihood — which is the same as minimising the cross-entropy loss of ml5. There is no formula for the answer, so it is found iteratively (ml4), but the loss is a single smooth bowl (convex), so every solver finds the same best weights.
body:
1. The likelihood and why it becomes cross-entropy

For one example with label y ∈ {0, 1} and predicted probability p, the probability the model assigns to what actually happened is p if y = 1 and 1 − p if y = 0 — compactly, p^y (1 − p)^(1 − y). Assuming examples are independent (ml1's i.i.d.), the probability of the whole training set — the likelihood — is the product over examples. Products of many small numbers underflow, and logarithms turn products into sums, so we maximise the log-likelihood instead, or equivalently minimise its negative average:

L(w, b) = −(1/n) Σᵢ [ yᵢ log pᵢ + (1 − yᵢ) log(1 − pᵢ) ]      pᵢ = σ(w·xᵢ + b)

That is binary cross-entropy exactly (ml5). So "maximum likelihood" and "minimise log loss" are the same instruction, and the loss has a statistical justification rather than being an arbitrary choice.

The simplest case, by hand. With no features, the model is just p = σ(b). If 30 of 100 customers churned, the likelihood is maximised at p = 0.30 — the observed rate — so b = log(0.3/0.7) = −0.847. With features, the model distributes that 30% across customers according to their features, but a version of this property survives: at the optimum, the average predicted probability equals the observed positive rate (section 6).

2. The gradient, and one training step by hand

Differentiating the loss for one example with respect to the score z, using the sigmoid's derivative σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), everything cancels to:

∂L/∂z = p − y      →      ∂L/∂w = (p − y)·x      ∂L/∂b = p − y

Prediction error times input — the same shape as linear regression's gradient in ml4. A positive example predicted at 0.2 pushes its weights up by 0.8 × x; one predicted at 0.95 barely pushes at all.

Worked step. Four students; the feature is hours studied, centred at its mean (ml4 showed why centring helps): x = −1.5, −0.5, +0.5, +1.5. Passed the exam: y = 0, 0, 1, 1. Start at w = 0, b = 0 with learning rate η = 1.

  1. Predict. z = 0 for everyone, so p = 0.5 for everyone. Loss = −log 0.5 = 0.693 each, mean 0.693.
  2. Errors p − y: +0.5, +0.5, −0.5, −0.5.
  3. Gradient for w: mean of (p − y)·x = (0.5 × −1.5 + 0.5 × −0.5 − 0.5 × 0.5 − 0.5 × 1.5)/4 = (−0.75 − 0.25 − 0.25 − 0.75)/4 = −0.5. Gradient for b: mean of (p − y) = 0.
  4. Update: w = 0 − 1 × (−0.5) = 0.5; b stays 0.
  5. Check: scores −0.75, −0.25, 0.25, 0.75 give p = 0.321, 0.438, 0.562, 0.679. The losses are −log(1 − 0.321) = 0.387, −log(0.562) = 0.576, and the same two again for the passing students: mean 0.481. One step cut the loss from 0.693 to 0.481.

3. The decision boundary

With a threshold of 0.5, the model predicts "yes" when p > 0.5, which is when z > 0. So the decision boundary is the set of points where w·x + b = 0: a straight line with two features, a flat plane (hyperplane) with more. Logistic regression is therefore a linear classifier. Changing the threshold moves the boundary parallel to itself — a threshold of 0.2 puts it where z = log(0.2/0.8) = −1.39 — but never bends it.

To learn a curved boundary, you give the model curved features. Adding x₁², x₂² and x₁x₂ lets the boundary be an ellipse or parabola in the original inputs; binning a continuous feature (age 18–25, 26–35, …) lets its effect be any step shape; an interaction feature (tickets × is_new_customer) lets tickets matter more for new customers. That manual feature work is exactly what decision trees and neural networks automate, and it's why "logistic regression on good features" can be remarkably strong.

4. Perfect separation: when the best weights are infinite

The four students above are perfectly separable: every non-passer studied less than every passer. Make w larger and every prediction moves further in the right direction, so the loss keeps falling: at w = 1 (b = 0) it is 0.338, at w = 2 it is 0.181, at w = 5 it is 0.040, at w = 10 it is 0.0034 and at w = 20 it is 0.00002. There is no finite minimum; the weights run towards infinity, and a solver either stops at an iteration limit with enormous weights or reports it failed to converge. Predicted probabilities of exactly 0 or 1 are the symptom.

Separation is common with many features and few examples, or when one rare category occurs only among positives. Regularisation (ml3) fixes it: the penalty makes large weights costly, so there is a finite best trade-off. This is why scikit-learn's LogisticRegression applies an L2 penalty by default (C = 1.0) — it isn't only about overfitting; without it the problem may have no answer.

5. More than two classes

Softmax (multinomial) regression gives each of K classes its own weight vector, computes K scores and converts them to probabilities with softmax (ml5), trained with categorical cross-entropy. The probabilities sum to one and the gradient for each class's score is again p − y. One-vs-rest instead trains K separate binary models ("class k versus everything else") and picks the highest score; it's simple and parallelisable, but the K scores aren't coordinated and don't sum to one. Modern libraries default to softmax. The final layer of a neural classifier is exactly softmax regression on the features the network has learned.

6. Calibration by construction

At the optimum, the gradient with respect to b is zero, and that gradient is mean(p − y). So the average predicted probability equals the observed positive rate on the training data — automatically. The same holds for every binary feature in the model: among customers with a support ticket, predicted and actual churn rates agree. That's why logistic regression's probabilities are usually trustworthy when the model is correctly specified. They go wrong when the true log-odds aren't linear in the features (a missing interaction makes some groups over- and others under-predicted), when regularisation is strong (predictions are shrunk towards the base rate), or when training data was reweighted or resampled.

7. Downsampling and the intercept

With a click-through rate of 0.1%, a dataset of a billion ad impressions contains a million clicks and 999 million non-clicks. Keeping only a fraction w of the negatives cuts training cost dramatically. Because logistic regression is linear in log-odds, discarding negatives at random multiplies the odds of a positive by 1/w and so adds log(1/w) to every score — only the intercept changes. Predictions made in the downsampled world, p, are converted back with:

q = p / ( p + (1 − p) / w )

Worked: after keeping 1% of negatives (w = 0.01), the model predicts p = 0.10 for a typical ad. Then q = 0.10 / (0.10 + 0.90/0.01) = 0.10 / 90.1 ≈ 0.0011 — back to the true 0.1% base rate. Forget this correction and every predicted click probability is 90 times too high, which in an ads auction means bidding wildly wrong. This exact formula appears in the Facebook paper that is this lesson's public case.

8. Regularised logistic regression and choosing C

In practice logistic regression is almost always fitted with a penalty: minimise the log loss plus λ times an L2 penalty (the sum of squared weights) or an L1 penalty (the sum of absolute weights), as in ml3. scikit-learn expresses the strength as C = 1/λ, so small C means strong regularisation. With L2 the weights shrink smoothly and predicted probabilities are pulled towards the base rate; with L1 many weights become exactly zero, which is useful with thousands of sparse features such as words or hashed identifiers. C is chosen by cross-validation on a log-scale grid (0.001, 0.01, …, 100), judged by log loss if you need probabilities or by the metric you care about otherwise. Two practical notes: the intercept is never penalised, so the base rate is always fitted; and because the penalty depends on units, features must be standardised first.

9. Class weights and imbalanced data

With 5% positives, a common reflex is to weight each positive more heavily in the loss (scikit-learn's class_weight="balanced" gives positives weight 0.95/0.05 = 19 here). For logistic regression this has an effect very like downsampling: the model behaves as if positives were 19 times more common, so the intercept rises by about log 19 ≈ 2.9 and every predicted probability is inflated — a customer with a true 5% risk gets a prediction around 50%. The ranking of customers barely changes, which is all a threshold decision needs, but the probabilities are no longer probabilities. If you weight classes, correct the outputs the same way as in section 7 (with w = 1/19) or recalibrate (ml15). Often it is better not to reweight at all and instead choose the decision threshold from costs, as ml7 and ml8 explain.

10. Evaluating the fit

Log loss on held-out data is the natural measure, but its raw value depends on the base rate: predicting the base rate itself already scores well when positives are rare. So compare against that trivial baseline. With a 30% positive rate, the baseline log loss is −(0.3 ln 0.3 + 0.7 ln 0.7) = 0.361 + 0.250 = 0.611. A model scoring 0.45 has a normalised entropy of 0.45/0.611 = 0.74 — it removes 26% of the uncertainty — which is exactly the metric Facebook used in the public case below. Alongside it, check ranking — how well the scores put positives above negatives, measured with ROC (receiver operating characteristic) and precision–recall curves in ml7 — and calibration (ml15).

Finally, always compare with the two baselines of ml1: predicting the base rate for everyone, and a logistic regression on the obvious features. If a complex model can't beat the second by a margin that justifies its cost, the complex model shouldn't ship. Logistic regression is so often the model that survives this comparison in production that many teams treat "beats a well-regularised logistic regression on the same features" as the entry ticket for anything fancier.

11. Reading a fitted model honestly

  • Report odds ratios, e^w, with confidence intervals, and translate into probabilities at realistic baselines (the drill below).
  • Standardise before comparing sizes. A weight of 0.8 per support ticket and 0.05 per month of tenure aren't comparable until both are per standard deviation.
  • Coefficients are conditional. Each is the effect "holding the other features fixed". With correlated features (multicollinearity), individual coefficients are unstable and can flip sign while predictions barely change.
  • Association is not causation. Support tickets predict churn, but calling customers so they file fewer tickets won't prevent it; tickets may be a symptom of a product problem. Causal claims need experiments (ml16).
deep:
How solvers find the optimum

The log loss is convex and smooth, so any sensible method converges to the same answer, but they differ in speed and in which penalties they support. Newton's method uses the Hessian — for logistic regression, XᵀSX with S a diagonal matrix of p(1 − p) — and converges in a handful of steps; statisticians call it IRLS (iteratively reweighted least squares) because each step is a weighted linear regression. L-BFGS approximates the Newton step from recent gradients and is scikit-learn's default (L2 only). liblinear handles L1 on small data; saga, a stochastic method, handles L1 and elastic net on large data. At web scale, models are trained online with stochastic methods and per-coordinate learning rates — FTRL-Proximal (Google) and per-coordinate SGD (Facebook) — because each sparse feature appears at a very different frequency, and a single global learning rate would under-train rare features or overshoot common ones.

A generalised linear model

Logistic regression belongs to the family of generalised linear models (GLMs): a linear score, a link function connecting it to the mean of the outcome, and a noise distribution. Linear regression is the identity link with Gaussian noise; logistic regression is the logit link with Bernoulli outcomes; Poisson regression is the log link with count outcomes (ml5's noise-model view). The shared machinery — maximum likelihood, IRLS, standard errors, deviance — is why statistics packages report p-values and confidence intervals for logistic coefficients, which rely on the model being correctly specified and on there being no separation.

Generative versus discriminative: Naive Bayes

Naive Bayes models how features are generated within each class and uses Bayes' rule to get P(class | features); with its independence assumption, its log-odds are also linear in the features. Logistic regression models P(class | features) directly. Ng and Jordan's classic analysis found Naive Bayes can reach its (higher) asymptotic error with fewer examples, while logistic regression reaches a lower error given enough data — the general trade between a generative model's strong assumptions and a discriminative model's flexibility.

Firth's correction and rare events

Maximum-likelihood estimates of logistic coefficients are biased away from zero in small samples, and badly so with rare outcomes or near-separation. Firth's penalised likelihood adds a penalty (based on the Jeffreys prior) that removes the first-order bias and guarantees finite estimates even under separation. In ML practice the ordinary L2 penalty plays the same stabilising role; in clinical or epidemiological work with small samples, Firth's method is the standard answer.

The scorecard tradition

Credit scoring is a long-standing production use. Continuous variables are binned, each bin is encoded by its weight of evidence — log of the ratio of good to bad rates in the bin — and a logistic regression is fitted on those encodings. The result is turned into points (for example, 20 points double the odds), so a loan officer can see exactly which attributes contributed how many points. The appeal is regulatory: monotone, explainable effects and a transparent reason for every decision, at a small cost in accuracy compared with boosted trees.

Standard errors and what "significant" means here

Statistics packages report a standard error for each coefficient, derived from the curvature (Hessian) of the log-likelihood at the optimum: a sharply curved likelihood means the data pins the coefficient down tightly. The ratio of coefficient to standard error gives a Wald test and a p-value. Three cautions matter in ML settings: with millions of rows almost every coefficient is "significant" while being practically tiny; with correlated features standard errors inflate and individual tests become meaningless; and after any feature selection or tuning on the same data, the reported p-values are optimistic. Use confidence intervals on odds ratios to communicate uncertainty, and bootstrap resampling when the assumptions are doubtful.

Where it lives inside modern systems

The final layer of a neural classifier is softmax regression on learned features; a "linear probe" — logistic regression on frozen embeddings — is the standard way to measure how much information an embedding contains; Platt scaling calibrates another model's scores with a one-feature logistic regression; and in LLM work, simple logistic classifiers on embeddings are used for routing, safety filtering and data quality scoring because they are fast and easy to audit. Even the reward models used to align LLMs are trained with a logistic loss: the probability that response A is preferred to response B is modelled as the sigmoid of the difference in their scores (the Bradley–Terry model).
prod:
The public case: Facebook's ad-click model (2014)

In "Practical Lessons from Predicting Clicks on Ads at Facebook" (He et al., 2014), Facebook's ads team described the model that predicted click probabilities for an audience of over 750 million daily active users and over 1 million active advertisers. Calibrated probabilities mattered because the ads auction multiplies the predicted click probability by the bid: a model that over-predicts by 2× distorts the whole marketplace. The core was logistic regression, and several of this lesson's ideas appear directly:

  • Features are what matter. The paper's first lesson is that the right features — especially historical ones, such as the ad's or user's past click-through rate — dominate everything else. Removing historical features cost 4.5% in prediction accuracy; removing contextual features cost less than 1%.
  • Bending the boundary with trees. Instead of hand-crafting non-linear features (section 3), they trained boosted decision trees and fed the index of the leaf each example lands in, as one-hot features, into logistic regression. The hybrid improved normalised entropy — their log-loss metric, normalised by the loss of always predicting the average click rate — by over 3% relative to either model alone (NE 96.58% of the trees-only model, versus 99.43% for logistic regression alone), where typical feature-engineering wins were a fraction of a percent.
  • Freshness. Accuracy degraded as the gap between training and serving grew; moving from weekly to daily retraining reduced normalised entropy by about 1%. The logistic-regression layer was trained online, with per-coordinate learning rates performing best of the schemes they compared.
  • Downsampling and recalibration. They trained on data with most negatives removed (a negative sampling rate of 0.025 performed best) and corrected predictions with q = p / (p + (1 − p)/w) — the formula of section 7 — giving the example of a 0.1% true rate that becomes about 10% after 1% negative downsampling.

The lessons generalise: in production, a simple, well-calibrated model on strong features, retrained frequently and corrected for sampling, beats a sophisticated model trained once on stale data.

Failure modes in production

Forgetting to recalibrate after sampling or reweighting. Predictions come out inflated by the sampling factor; anything multiplying them by a value (bids, expected loss) is wrong by the same factor.

Misreading coefficients. "A coefficient of 0.7 means +70% churn" leads to wrong business cases. Always convert through odds at a realistic baseline.

Silent separation. A new categorical value that appears only among positives in a retrain gets a huge weight; predictions for that group jump to near-certainty. Regularisation limits the damage; monitoring coefficient magnitudes between retrains catches it.

Stale scalers and encodings. Standardisation parameters and category encodings must travel with the model; recomputing them on serving data shifts every score (ml14).

What to monitor

Track calibration (predicted versus observed rate, overall and by segment), log loss or normalised entropy over time, the distribution of scores, and coefficient drift between retrains. A sudden change in the average predicted probability with no change in the observed rate usually means a feature pipeline broke. And keep the logistic-regression baseline running in shadow next to any more complex replacement: if the complex model's advantage shrinks over time, that is an early sign it is decaying faster.
myths: Logistic regression is a regression model, so the name is a mistake.

It is a regression — of the log-odds of the outcome on the features — which is why it's called that. It becomes a classifier only when you apply a threshold to the predicted probability. Its native output is a probability, and many of its best uses (risk scores, expected-value calculations, calibration) use the probability directly, never thresholding it.
A coefficient of 0.7 means the probability goes up by 0.7 (or by 70%) per unit.

A coefficient is a change in log-odds. e^0.7 ≈ 2.0, so one extra unit doubles the odds. What that does to the probability depends on where you start: from 10% it becomes 18%, from 50% it becomes 67%, from 80% it becomes 89%. Probability effects are not constant because the sigmoid squashes both ends.
Logistic regression can only learn linear patterns, so it's obsolete.

Its decision boundary is linear in whatever features you give it. Add squared terms, interactions, bins or tree-derived features and the boundary becomes non-linear in the original inputs. Facebook's 2014 ad-click system fed boosted-tree leaf indicators into logistic regression and beat either model alone. It remains the standard baseline, the calibration layer (Platt scaling), and the linear probe for evaluating embeddings.
A large coefficient means the feature is important, and its sign says which way the feature causes the outcome.

Coefficient size depends on the feature's units unless features are standardised, and every coefficient is conditional on the other features in the model: with correlated features, coefficients can be unstable or even flip sign while predictions stay the same. And association in observational data isn't causation — a feature can predict churn because it's a symptom, not a cause.
If the optimiser doesn't converge, the data must be bad.

A classic cause is perfect separation: if some combination of features splits the classes exactly, the likelihood keeps improving as weights grow, so there is no finite best answer and weights run towards infinity. That's a property of the data and model together, not bad data. Regularisation, which libraries apply by default, gives a finite solution.
Logistic regression's probabilities are always well calibrated.

They are calibrated on average by construction — with an intercept, the mean predicted probability equals the training positive rate — and often well calibrated overall when the model is correctly specified. Missing interactions or non-linearities, strong regularisation, class reweighting or negative subsampling all distort them, and they must then be checked and corrected (ml15).
lab:
Goal: implement logistic regression from scratch, check its coefficients against the truth, watch separation make weights diverge, and apply the downsampling correction. NumPy only; written for Python 3.12.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def fit(X, y, lr=0.5, steps=3000, lam=0.0):
    w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w + b)))
        w -= lr * (X.T @ (p - y) / len(y) + lam * w)   # intercept not penalised
        b -= lr * np.mean(p - y)
    return w, b

# 1. Recover known coefficients
n = 20000; X = rng.normal(size=(n, 2))
w_true, b_true = np.array([1.5, -0.7]), -1.0
y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w_true + b_true)))).astype(float)
w, b = fit(X, y)
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w + b)))
print("fitted", w.round(2), round(b, 2), "| mean p", p.mean().round(3), "rate", y.mean().round(3))

# 2. Separation: weights grow without a penalty, stay finite with one
xs = np.array([[-1.5], [-0.5], [0.5], [1.5]]); ys = np.array([0., 0., 1., 1.])
for steps in (100, 1000, 10000):
    print(steps, "no penalty w =", fit(xs, ys, steps=steps)[0].round(2),
          " L2 w =", fit(xs, ys, steps=steps, lam=0.1)[0].round(2))

# 3. Downsampling correction
keep = (y == 1) | (rng.random(n) < 0.1)            # keep 10% of negatives
w2, b2 = fit(X[keep], y[keep])
p2 = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w2 + b2)))
q = p2 / (p2 + (1 - p2) / 0.1)
print("raw mean", p2.mean().round(3), "corrected", q.mean().round(3), "true", y.mean().round(3))

What to look for. Part 1 recovers weights near (1.5, −0.7) and intercept near −1.0, and the mean predicted probability equals the observed rate. Part 2's unpenalised weight keeps growing with more steps while the L2 version settles. Part 3's raw predictions are far too high; the corrected mean matches the true rate, and the fitted slopes (unlike the intercept) are nearly unchanged by downsampling.

It is trained by maximum likelihood, which is the same as minimising cross-entropy; the loss is convex, so every solver reaches the same optimum.

If the classes can be separated perfectly, unregularised weights diverge to infinity; regularisation makes the solution finite.
Multi-class problems use softmax regression (one weight vector per class) or one-vs-rest binary models.

Undersampling negatives by a rate w shifts the log-odds by −log w, and predictions are corrected with q = p / (p + (1 − p)/w).

drill:
Work it out

A churn model has coefficient 0.693 on had_support_ticket (binary). A customer without a ticket has a 10% churn probability. What is it with a ticket? A stakeholder guesses "about 20%, since it doubles".

Answer

What doubles is the odds, not the probability: e^0.693 = 2.0.

Baseline odds = 0.10 / 0.90 = 0.111. With a ticket: 0.111 × 2 = 0.222. Convert back: p = 0.222 / 1.222 = 18.2%.

So the stakeholder is close — but only by accident of starting at 10%. Start at 50% instead: odds 1.0 → 2.0 → 66.7%, not 100%. Start at 80%: odds 4 → 8 → 88.9%. The same coefficient moves probability by 8, 17 or 9 percentage points depending where you start, because the effect is linear in log-odds and probability is squashed at both ends.

This is the single most common misreading of a logistic regression, and being able to correct it politely is worth more than deriving the loss.
qa: E
What does logistic regression model, and what is the sigmoid for?

It models the probability of a binary outcome. It computes a linear score z = w·x + b, which can be any real number, and passes it through the sigmoid 1/(1 + e^(−z)) to get a value between 0 and 1. Equivalently, it says the log-odds of the outcome is a linear function of the features.
E
How do you interpret a coefficient?

A coefficient w is the change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding the others fixed; e^w is the odds ratio. A coefficient of 0.693 doubles the odds. It is not a constant change in probability: from a 10% baseline, doubling the odds gives 18.2%, from 50% it gives 66.7%.
E
Does logistic regression need feature scaling?

Not for correctness — without regularisation the predictions are the same whatever the units. It matters for optimiser speed (ml4's condition-number argument), and it matters a lot once you regularise, because an unscaled penalty punishes features in small units more than those in large ones. Standardise before fitting a regularised model or comparing coefficient sizes.
M
Why is logistic regression trained with cross-entropy rather than squared error?

Cross-entropy is its negative log-likelihood, so minimising it is maximum likelihood; it is convex in the weights, so there's one optimum and every solver finds it; and its gradient is (p − y)x, which doesn't vanish when the model is confidently wrong. Squared error on the sigmoid output is non-convex in the weights and its gradient is multiplied by the sigmoid's slope, which is tiny when predictions saturate.
Follow-up: Is there a closed-form solution? — No; unlike linear regression, the optimum must be found iteratively, with gradient descent, Newton's method (IRLS) or L-BFGS.
M
What is perfect separation and why does it break logistic regression?

When a combination of features splits the classes exactly, making all the weights larger always makes predictions more confident and correct, so the log-likelihood keeps improving and approaches its limit only as weights go to infinity — there is no finite maximum. In the lesson's four-point example, the loss is 0.34 at w = 1, 0.04 at w = 5 and 0.00002 at w = 20. Any regularisation makes the problem well-posed, which is why it's not optional here.
Follow-up: How would you notice? — Coefficients or standard errors that are huge and grow with more iterations, and predicted probabilities of exactly 0 or 1.
M
What is the decision boundary of logistic regression, and how can it learn non-linear patterns?

With a 0.5 threshold, the boundary is where z = w·x + b = 0 — a straight line in two dimensions, a flat hyperplane in more. It's linear in the features it's given, so non-linear boundaries need non-linear features: squares and interactions, binned continuous variables, splines, or learned features such as boosted-tree leaves or neural-network embeddings.
Follow-up: What happens to the boundary if you change the threshold to 0.2? — It shifts parallel to itself to where z = log(0.2/0.8) ≈ −1.39; its direction doesn't change.
M
How do you extend logistic regression to more than two classes?

Multinomial (softmax) regression trains one weight vector per class, computes K scores and turns them into probabilities with softmax, trained with categorical cross-entropy; the probabilities are properly normalised. One-vs-rest trains K independent binary models; it's simple and parallel, but the scores don't sum to one and can be inconsistent. Softmax is the default in modern libraries.
M
You trained on data where you kept only 1% of negatives. How do you get correct probabilities?

Downsampling negatives by rate w multiplies the odds of a positive by 1/w, which in logistic regression shifts only the intercept by log(1/w). Correct predictions with q = p / (p + (1 − p)/w), or subtract log(1/w) from the intercept. For example, p = 0.10 in the downsampled world with w = 0.01 becomes q = 0.10 / (0.10 + 90) ≈ 0.0011 — about the original 0.1% base rate, the example Facebook gives.
Follow-up: Why downsample at all? — It cuts training cost when negatives vastly outnumber positives; Facebook found a negative sampling rate of 0.025 performed best on their data.
H
Why are logistic regression's probabilities often well calibrated, and when aren't they?

At the maximum-likelihood optimum the gradient with respect to the intercept is the average of (p − y), so it is zero: the mean predicted probability equals the observed positive rate, and the same holds within any group defined by a binary feature in the model. If the model is correctly specified, calibration holds more broadly. It breaks when the true log-odds aren't linear in the features, when regularisation is strong (shrinking predictions towards the base rate), and when training data was reweighted or resampled.
Follow-up: How do you check? — A reliability diagram or expected calibration error on held-out data (ml15).
H
Why can coefficients flip sign when you add a correlated feature?

Each coefficient measures the effect of its feature holding the others fixed. If two features are strongly correlated, the data contains few examples where one changes and the other doesn't, so the split of effect between them is poorly determined; adding the second can move weight between them and even reverse the first's sign, while predictions barely change. It's multicollinearity, and the fix for interpretation is to combine or drop redundant features, regularise, or report effects of groups rather than individual coefficients.
Follow-up: Does it hurt prediction? — Usually not much, as long as the correlation is stable in production; it hurts interpretation and robustness when the correlation changes.
H
When would you choose logistic regression over gradient-boosted trees in 2026?

When interpretability or regulation requires explainable, monotone effects (credit scorecards); when data is small or very high-dimensional and sparse (text with millions of n-gram features, hashed ad features), where a regularised linear model is fast and hard to beat; when calibrated probabilities matter and you want minimal post-processing; when latency or memory is extremely tight; and as a baseline to show a complex model earns its cost. Trees usually win on dense tabular data with non-linear interactions.
Follow-up: Can you combine them? — Yes: Facebook's hybrid fed boosted-tree leaves into logistic regression and reported an improvement of over 3% in normalised entropy compared with either alone.
H
Implement logistic regression from scratch and explain each line.

Initialise w and b to zero. Repeat: compute z = Xw + b, p = sigmoid(z); compute the gradient of mean cross-entropy, ∇w = Xᵀ(p − y)/n + λw and ∇b = mean(p − y); update w −= η∇w, b −= η∇b. Use a numerically stable sigmoid (or compute the loss from logits with log-sum-exp), standardise features, stop when the loss changes by less than a tolerance, and don't regularise the intercept. Test on a separable toy set to see the weights grow without regularisation and stay finite with it.
