why:
A bank builds a model to predict which small-business loans will default. Two percent of past loans defaulted. The first model scores 98% accuracy, and the team is briefly delighted until someone notices it predicts "no default" for every single application. Someone suggests the textbook remedy: balance the classes. They throw away most of the good loans until defaults make up half the training set, retrain, and now the model flags plenty of applications. It goes to production, where the risk team uses its predicted probabilities to price loans — and every applicant looks about 25 times riskier than they are, because the model learned a world where half of all loans default.

That story contains most of what goes wrong with class imbalance, the situation where one class is much rarer than the other. The rare class is almost always the one that matters: fraud, disease, equipment failure, churn, a click on an ad. The folklore says imbalance is a modelling problem to be fixed by rebalancing the data. The evidence says something more nuanced. Most of the trouble comes from measuring the wrong thing (accuracy) and deciding with the wrong threshold (0.5). Standard training on the natural distribution often ranks the rare class perfectly well. And the popular fixes — oversampling, undersampling, SMOTE, class weights — all distort the model's probabilities in a predictable way that has to be corrected.

Interviewers ask about imbalance constantly, and the strongest answer is not a list of techniques but an order of operations with reasons: fix the metric, move the threshold, then consider weights or resampling if the model genuinely underweights positives — and correct the probabilities if anything uses them.

This lesson builds that answer: what imbalance actually breaks, with a threshold sweep on loan data; why cross-entropy self-balances once the model learns the base rate (with the gradient arithmetic); class weights, undersampling and oversampling and exactly how each shifts probabilities, with the correction formula worked; how SMOTE creates points and why it must stay inside cross-validation folds; evaluating with few positives; prevalence shift in production; and the public case — a 2022 simulation and ovarian-cancer study finding that imbalance corrections made calibration much worse without improving discrimination.
primer:
What "imbalanced" means

A dataset is imbalanced when one class is much rarer than the others: card fraud (around 0.1–0.2% of transactions in public datasets), disease screening (1%), equipment failures, ad clicks (around 1–2%), loan defaults (2%). The rare class is called the minority class and the common one the majority class. It's usually the minority we care about.

An analogy: a smoke alarm in a kitchen

A smoke alarm hears thousands of harmless events (toast, steam) for every real fire. If you judged it by accuracy — "fraction of moments it was right" — an alarm that never sounds would score 99.99%. What you actually care about is two things: does it go off when there's a fire (recall), and when it goes off, is there usually a fire (precision)? And how sensitive to set it is a choice you make based on costs: a kitchen that burns toast daily wants a less sensitive setting than a server room. Imbalance doesn't make the alarm's sensor worse; it makes the naive way of scoring the alarm useless and makes the sensitivity setting crucial. The analogy breaks in one respect: a machine-learning model's sensor is trained from examples, and with very few fires to learn from, the sensor itself can be undertrained — which is a data-quantity problem, not a proportion problem.

Why it causes trouble

  • Accuracy lies. Always predicting the majority class scores 98% on 2% defaults.
  • The default threshold is wrong. A well-calibrated model gives a rare-class example a probability above 0.5 only when it is more likely positive than not. With a 2% base rate that's uncommon, so at 0.5 the model flags almost nothing — not because it hasn't learned, but because 0.5 is the wrong cut.
  • Few examples to learn from. 200 defaults among 10,000 loans is only 200 examples of what default looks like.
  • Noisy evaluation. With few positives, metrics like recall jump around between splits.

A worked threshold sweep

10,000 loan applications, 200 defaults (2%). At threshold 0.5 the model flags 20 applications, 18 of them defaults: precision 90%, recall 18/200 = 9% — it misses 91% of defaults. At threshold 0.1 it flags 400, 140 of them defaults: precision 35%, recall 70%. At 0.03 it flags 1,500, 180 of them defaults: precision 12%, recall 90%. Nothing about the model changed; only the threshold. Which row is right depends on what a missed default costs compared with a rejected good customer — the cost-based threshold of ml7.

The tools, in the order to try them

  1. Measure properly: precision, recall, PR curves and expected cost, not accuracy.
  2. Move the threshold to match the costs or capacity.
  3. Class weights in the loss, if the model genuinely under-weights positives.
  4. Resampling: undersample the majority (especially when there's far too much of it) or oversample the minority, including synthetic methods such as SMOTE.
  5. Change the data or the problem: collect more positives, add features, or use a cascade or anomaly detection.

And one rule that cuts across all of them: steps 3 and 4 change the model's probabilities, so if anything downstream uses those probabilities, correct them.
body:
1. What training does with rare positives

It's worth seeing why standard training copes better than the folklore suggests. Take logistic regression (ml6) trained with cross-entropy on data with 1% positives. For each example the gradient with respect to its score is p − y (ml5), so the size of its push is |p − y|.

  • At the very start, weights are zero and every prediction is p = 0.5. Every example pushes with size 0.5, so the 1% of positives supply 1% of the total push. This is the phase people worry about.
  • Once the intercept learns the base rate — which takes a few steps, because the intercept's gradient is mean(p − y) — typical predictions are p ≈ 0.01. A negative now pushes with |0.01 − 0| = 0.01; a positive with |0.01 − 1| = 0.99. Per 100 examples: 99 negatives × 0.01 = 0.99 and 1 positive × 0.99 = 0.99. The two classes supply equal total push.

So after the first phase, cross-entropy is self-balancing: each rare example is worth about 99 common ones, exactly compensating for their frequency. The model isn't ignoring the minority. What remains is the fact that there are only so many positive examples to learn from, and the threshold. This is why strong, well-regularised models trained on natural data often rank rare positives very well — and why rebalancing tends to change probabilities much more than it changes ranking.

2. Measuring: metric, split and uncertainty

Evaluation comes first because most "imbalance problems" are measurement problems (ml7). Use precision and recall at a meaningful threshold, the precision–recall curve and average precision, or expected cost, and always include the trivial baseline. Two further habits matter specifically for rare classes:

Stratified splits. A random 20% test split of 10,000 loans with 200 defaults might contain 32 defaults or 48. Stratification keeps the class proportions equal in every split (exactly 40 here), and in cross-validation (ml9) it keeps each fold representative.

Uncertainty. With 50 positives in the test set, recall moves in steps of 2%, and at a measured recall of 0.80 its standard error is √(0.8 × 0.2 / 50) ≈ 0.057, so a 95% interval runs from about 0.69 to 0.91. Two models whose recalls differ by 5 points on this test set are statistically indistinguishable. Use repeated stratified cross-validation and bootstrap intervals, and choose between models only on differences larger than the noise.

3. Moving the threshold

If probabilities are calibrated, the cost-minimising threshold is C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN) (ml7). Suppose rejecting a good applicant loses £200 of profit and approving a defaulter loses £5,000. The threshold is 200 / 5,200 ≈ 0.038: reject any application with more than a 3.8% chance of default. In the sweep above that is close to the 0.03 row — 90% recall at 12% precision — which looks alarming by the precision number alone but is the cheapest policy given these costs. If instead the team can only review 400 applications a week, the threshold is whatever flags 400 (0.1 in the sweep). Neither of these involves retraining, and both can be changed tomorrow if costs or capacity change. This is why threshold tuning should come before any change to the training data.

4. Class weights

A class weight multiplies the loss of every example of that class. scikit-learn's class_weight="balanced" sets each class's weight inversely proportional to its frequency; with 2% positives, positives get weight 0.98/0.02 = 49 relative to negatives. In expectation, weighting positives by w is the same as showing the model each positive w times. The model's optimum moves: it now behaves as if positives were 49 times more common, so its predicted odds for every case are multiplied by about 49.

Worked. A borrower with a true 2% default risk has odds 0.02/0.98 = 0.0204. Multiplied by 49, the weighted model's odds are about 1.0 — a predicted probability of 50%. For ranking and a tuned threshold this is harmless: the ordering of borrowers is essentially unchanged, and you simply use a higher threshold. For pricing, it is a disaster: every borrower looks 25 times riskier. The correction divides the odds back by w:

q = p / ( p + (1 − p) · w )        weighted positives by w; p = model output, q = corrected

With p = 0.5 and w = 49: q = 0.5 / (0.5 + 24.5) = 0.02. For non-linear models the shift isn't exactly a constant on the log-odds scale, so recalibration on held-out data at the true prevalence (ml15) is the safer general fix.

When do weights genuinely help? When the model has limited capacity and must trade errors between classes — a weak or heavily regularised model will spend its capacity on the majority — and in neural networks trained on extreme imbalance, where weighting can speed up learning of the rare class. With large weights, each rare example produces a big gradient, which can make stochastic training noisier; moderate weights (square root of the ratio, for example) are a common compromise.

5. Undersampling and oversampling

Random undersampling keeps all positives and a random fraction w of negatives. Its main legitimate use is cost: with 500 million negatives, keeping 2.5% of them loses little information (most negatives are easy and redundant) and cuts training cost by 40 times. The probability shift is exact for a well-specified model — keeping a fraction w of negatives multiplies the odds of positive by 1/w — and is corrected with q = p / (p + (1 − p)/w) (ml6). With fraud at 1% and 1 in 99 negatives kept to reach 1:1, a model output of 0.5 corrects to q = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5 × 99) = 1%.

Random oversampling duplicates positives until the classes balance. It throws nothing away, but exact duplicates let flexible models memorise the rare examples, increasing variance (ml2), and — like weights — it inflates probabilities.

6. SMOTE, and why it must stay inside the fold

SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique, Chawla et al., 2002) oversamples without exact duplicates. For a minority example x, pick one of its k nearest minority neighbours, and create a new point a random fraction λ of the way along the line between them: new = x + λ·(neighbour − x). Worked: x = (2, 10), neighbour = (4, 14), λ = 0.25 gives new = (2 + 0.25 × 2, 10 + 0.25 × 4) = (2.5, 11).

The idea is that a wider cloud of minority points encourages a smoother, more generous boundary around the minority class, which helps weak learners such as a single decision tree or a nearest-neighbour classifier. Its limits: it assumes the space between two minority points is also minority territory, which is false when classes interleave; interpolating between categorical values or in very high dimensions creates unrealistic points; and it inflates probabilities like any oversampling. Elor and Averbuch-Elor (2022) compared balancing methods across many datasets and found that balancing helped weak learners but did not improve strong modern classifiers such as gradient-boosted trees.

The leakage trap. If SMOTE (or any oversampling) is applied to the whole dataset before splitting into training and validation, synthetic points built from validation examples end up in training. The model is then evaluated on points it has effectively seen, and scores look better than they will in production. Resampling must be part of the training pipeline, fitted separately inside each cross-validation fold (ml9), and validation and test data must never be resampled — they should reflect the real class proportions.

7. What rebalancing does to probabilities

Every technique in sections 4–6 moves the model towards predicting positives, and so every one of them breaks the link between output and true probability. This is the part of the folklore that causes real damage. If the scores feed only a threshold or a ranking, the damage is contained: choose the threshold on validation data drawn at the true prevalence. If the scores are used as probabilities — expected loss (probability × amount), pricing, capacity planning ("we expect 300 defaults"), combining with other models — they must be corrected with the formula (weights and random undersampling) or recalibrated on held-out data at the true prevalence (anything else).

8. Changing the data or the problem

When the limiting factor is the number of positives, the best investments are on the data side: collecting more history, pooling related positive types, targeted labelling of likely positives (active learning, ml1), and better features. Hard-negative mining keeps the negatives the model confuses with positives and drops the easy ones, focusing capacity where it matters. When positives are too rare or too varied to learn — novel fraud patterns, never-seen machine faults — anomaly detection models normal behaviour and flags departures from it, trading precision for the ability to catch the unseen. And at very large scale, a cascade of a cheap high-recall filter followed by an expensive precise model (or human reviewers) is the standard architecture.

9. The loan example, three ways

Put the pieces together on the bank's problem — 2% defaults, £200 lost per wrongly rejected good applicant, £5,000 lost per approved defaulter — comparing three teams.

Team A trains on the natural data and tunes the threshold. Its model's probabilities are calibrated, so the cost formula applies directly: reject above 200 / 5,200 ≈ 0.038. It validates that threshold on held-out data at the real 2% prevalence, reports precision and recall there, and hands the risk team probabilities they can use for pricing as-is.

Team B balances the classes with weights of 49 and keeps a 0.5 threshold. Its ranking is about as good as Team A's. Its threshold of 0.5 on inflated probabilities corresponds to a true risk of 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5 × 49) = 2% — so it rejects everyone above a 2% true risk, a stricter policy than the costs justify, rejecting many profitable customers. Its pricing uses probabilities 25 times too high. Nothing in its offline AUC warned of either problem.

Team C balances the classes, then corrects. It applies the weighting correction to every output (or recalibrates on a held-out set at 2%), then applies the cost threshold of 0.038 to the corrected probabilities. Its decisions and prices end up essentially the same as Team A's — after extra work, and with the risk that the correction isn't exact for its non-linear model.

The comparison is the whole lesson: rebalancing didn't buy Team C anything that threshold tuning didn't already give Team A, and without correction it made Team B's model wrong in two different ways. Rebalancing earns its place only when it improves the model itself — a limited-capacity learner, a neural network that learns the rare class too slowly, or a training set too big to use in full.
deep:
Why rebalancing seldom improves ranking

For a model that can represent the true relationship, reweighting or resampling classes changes the optimal scores only by a monotone transformation — for logistic regression, a constant shift in log-odds. Monotone transformations don't change which case scores higher, so AUC and average precision are unaffected in the limit of plenty of data. Where rebalancing does change ranking, it's through finite-sample effects on flexible models (duplicated points increase variance, discarded negatives lose information) or through capacity limits, where the model must trade errors between classes and the weights change the trade. This is the theoretical backbone of the empirical finding that corrections often don't improve discrimination.

Prior (label) shift in production

Class proportions change: fraud spikes during an attack, defaults rise in a recession, disease prevalence varies by clinic. If only the proportions change — each class still looks the same — this is label shift. A model trained at one prevalence is then systematically miscalibrated at another, and a fixed threshold produces a different volume of flags. Given the new prevalence, the same odds correction applies. When the new prevalence is unknown, it can be estimated from unlabelled production data using the model's own predictions — for example, with an expectation–maximisation procedure that alternates between re-estimating the prior and re-adjusting the predicted probabilities, or with black-box shift estimation using the model's confusion matrix.

Example-dependent costs

Not all positives are equally important: a £10,000 fraud matters 1,000 times more than a £10 one. Class weights treat them the same. Cost-sensitive approaches weight each example by its cost in training, or — usually better — keep the model probabilistic and apply the cost at decision time: flag when p × amount at risk exceeds the cost of review. The second approach keeps probabilities honest and lets the cost logic change without retraining.

Long-tailed multi-class problems

With thousands of classes — product categories, species, rare diagnoses — frequency varies across orders of magnitude, and models favour frequent classes. Logit adjustment (Menon et al.) corrects this by subtracting τ·log(prior) from each class's score at prediction time, or adding it to the loss during training, which targets balanced error (equal weight on every class) rather than overall error. Related methods include balanced softmax and training the representation on natural data but the final classifier on class-balanced samples. Evaluate with macro-averaged metrics and by frequency bucket.

Focal loss and hard examples

Focal loss (ml5) addresses a different aspect: not the class proportion but the dominance of easy examples. In dense object detection, most of the ~100,000 candidate boxes per image are trivially background; down-weighting well-classified examples let the detector learn from the hard ones. It shares the probability distortion of all reweighting schemes, and its benefit is largest when the majority class is overwhelmingly easy.

Negative subsampling as an efficiency tool

In systems with billions of examples, the question isn't balance but compute. Most negatives are easy and carry little information once the model has learned them; keeping a random fraction w of negatives reduces training cost roughly by 1/w with little loss in accuracy, and the exact log-odds correction restores calibration. The variance cost is concentrated in the negatives' contribution, so the optimal w depends on how informative typical negatives are. Refinements keep negatives with probability depending on how hard they are (importance sampling), then weight each kept negative by the inverse of its keep probability so the loss stays unbiased — a principled version of hard-negative mining.

Imbalance in LLM-era pipelines

The same issues appear in modern AI systems in new places. Safety and content classifiers face extreme imbalance (harmful requests are rare), so thresholds are tuned per category from the cost of a missed harmful request versus an unnecessary refusal. Retrieval-augmented systems train embedding models with contrastive losses where each query has one positive passage and many negatives, and the choice of hard negatives matters more than their number. And when fine-tuning a language model on labelled examples, a skewed label distribution teaches the model the prior as well as the task, so evaluation must look at per-class recall, not just overall accuracy.

Selective labels

Imbalance often comes with a biased label process. A lender observes defaults only on approved loans; a fraud team confirms fraud only on investigated transactions. The observed positive rate then reflects past policy, not the population, and training on it teaches the model the old policy's blind spots. Randomised exploration (approving a small random share below the cut-off), reject inference and auditing random samples of unflagged cases are the corrections (ml1).
prod:
The public case: "The harm of class imbalance corrections"

In 2022, van den Goorbergh, van Smeden, Timmerman and Van Calster tested the folklore directly for clinical risk prediction, where predicted probabilities are shown to doctors and patients. They trained standard and ridge-penalised logistic regression models with and without random undersampling, random oversampling and SMOTE, in Monte Carlo simulations and in a real case study on ovarian cancer diagnosis, and measured discrimination (AUC), calibration and classification. Their results, in their own summary:

  • All imbalance correction methods led to poor calibration — strong overestimation of the probability of belonging to the minority class.
  • They did not lead to better discrimination in terms of AUC.
  • They improved classification in terms of sensitivity and specificity — but similar results were obtained by shifting the probability threshold instead.

Their conclusion: outcome imbalance is not a problem in itself, and imbalance correction may even worsen model performance. For a doctor told "this patient has a 60% chance of a malignant tumour" when the true risk is 15%, that worsening is not academic. A separate large benchmark by Elor and Averbuch-Elor reached a compatible conclusion from the machine-learning side: balancing helps weak classifiers but not state-of-the-art ones. Together they justify the order of operations in this lesson: metric, then threshold, then — only if needed — weights or resampling, followed by probability correction.

Where rebalancing is the right call

Undersampling negatives is standard practice in very large-scale systems such as ad-click prediction, where there are billions of negatives and training cost matters; it is paired with an exact probability correction (Facebook's ad-click paper, ml6's case, found a negative sampling rate of 0.025 performed best and gives the correction formula). Weights or oversampling can help when a model's capacity is limited, or in deep-learning settings where the rare class is learned too slowly. The mistake is not using these tools; it's using them by reflex and forgetting what they do to probabilities.

Failure modes in production

Inflated probabilities reaching users. Risk scores shown to people, used in pricing or summed for forecasts, from a model trained on rebalanced data. Symptom: predicted counts far above observed counts. Fix: correct or recalibrate, and monitor the mean predicted probability against the observed rate.

Resampled validation sets. Tuning thresholds or reporting precision on a balanced validation set gives numbers production will never see. Validation and test data should have the real prevalence.

Leaky oversampling. SMOTE applied before cross-validation, producing optimistic offline scores and a disappointing launch.

Prevalence drift. The positive rate changes and alert volume swings. Monitor flagged volume, precision on audited samples and the score distribution; re-tune thresholds on recent labelled data.

A practical recipe

  1. Establish metrics at the true prevalence: PR curve, AP, precision and recall at candidate thresholds, with bootstrap intervals.
  2. Use stratified (and, for rare events, repeated) cross-validation.
  3. Train a strong model on the natural distribution; tune the threshold from costs or capacity on validation data.
  4. Only if the model underweights positives, or training cost demands it, try class weights or undersampling — inside the pipeline.
  5. Correct or recalibrate probabilities if anything consumes them, and verify calibration on held-out data.
myths: Imbalanced data must be balanced before training.

For most modern classifiers it needn't be. A model trained with cross-entropy on the natural distribution still ranks well and gives calibrated probabilities; the problems people attribute to imbalance are usually a wrong metric (accuracy) or a wrong threshold (0.5). Studies such as van den Goorbergh et al. (2022) found that undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE made calibration much worse without improving AUC, and that shifting the threshold achieved the same sensitivity and specificity.
SMOTE creates new information about the rare class.

It creates points on straight lines between existing rare examples. That can help a weak learner draw a wider boundary, but it adds no new facts about the world, can create unrealistic points in high-dimensional or categorical feature spaces, and inflates predicted probabilities. Elor and Averbuch-Elor found balancing helps weak learners but not state-of-the-art classifiers such as gradient-boosted trees.
A model that predicts almost no positives at threshold 0.5 hasn't learned anything.

With 1% prevalence, a calibrated model should rarely output probabilities above 0.5 — only cases that are more likely fraud than not. It may rank positives very well, which shows up as a good PR curve and high precision at a lower threshold. The fix is choosing the threshold from costs or capacity, not retraining.
Class weights and resampling only change which cases get flagged.

They change the model's predicted probabilities: weighting positives by w multiplies the predicted odds by about w. If anything downstream uses the probability — expected-loss decisions, pricing, alert budgets, combining models — it will be wrong by that factor unless you correct it or recalibrate on data at the true prevalence.
More negatives never hurt, and fewer never help.

Undersampling negatives is a legitimate engineering choice when there are hundreds of millions of them: training gets much cheaper, accuracy barely changes (most negatives are easy and redundant), and the probability shift is corrected exactly with a formula. Facebook's ad-click work found a negative sampling rate of 0.025 performed best. What matters is correcting the probabilities afterwards.
If the rare class is 0.1%, the data is the problem and nothing can be done.

Often the real limit is the number of positive examples, not their proportion. 500 frauds among 500,000 transactions is a small-data problem for the positive class. The high-value moves are getting more positives (targeted labelling, longer history, pooling related cases), better features, and evaluation that measures the rare class carefully with confidence intervals.
lab:
Goal: show that threshold tuning matches rebalancing on ranking and decisions, while rebalancing inflates probabilities until corrected. NumPy only; written for Python 3.12.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

n = 50000; X = rng.normal(size=(n, 3))
z = X @ np.array([1.2, -0.8, 0.5]) - 4.2            # about 2% positives
y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(float)
tr, te = slice(0, 40000), slice(40000, None)

def fit(X, y, wpos=1.0, lr=0.5, steps=3000):
    w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0
    sw = np.where(y == 1, wpos, 1.0); sw = sw / sw.mean()
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w + b)))
        g = sw * (p - y)
        w -= lr * X.T @ g / len(y); b -= lr * g.mean()
    return lambda X: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w + b)))

def auc(s, y):
    r = np.argsort(np.argsort(s)) + 1; npos = y.sum()
    return (r[y == 1].sum() - npos * (npos + 1) / 2) / (npos * (len(y) - npos))

wpos = (1 - y[tr].mean()) / y[tr].mean()             # "balanced" weight ≈ 49
plain, weighted = fit(X[tr], y[tr]), fit(X[tr], y[tr], wpos)
for name, m in [("plain", plain), ("weighted", weighted)]:
    p = m(X[te])
    print(f"{name:8s} AUC={auc(p, y[te]):.3f}  mean p={p.mean():.3f}  true rate={y[te].mean():.3f}")
pw = weighted(X[te]); q = pw / (pw + (1 - pw) * wpos)
print("weighted, corrected mean p =", q.mean().round(3))
for t in (0.5, 0.1, 0.05):
    f = plain(X[te]) >= t
    print(f"plain t={t}: flagged={f.sum()} recall={(f & (y[te]==1)).sum()/y[te].sum():.2f}")

What to look for. Both models have almost the same AUC — weighting didn't improve ranking. The weighted model's mean predicted probability is many times the true rate; the correction brings it back. The plain model flags few cases at 0.5, and lowering its threshold recovers recall with no retraining.
recap: A dataset is imbalanced when one class is much rarer; the rare class is usually the one that matters, and what breaks first is measurement, not learning.
Accuracy and the default 0.5 threshold mislead under imbalance, so use precision, recall and PR curves, and choose the threshold from costs, capacity or a required recall.
Cross-entropy on the natural distribution self-balances once the intercept learns the base rate, so strong models usually rank rare positives well without rebalancing.
Class weights and resampling push the model to flag more positives, but they inflate predicted probabilities: weighting positives by w multiplies predicted odds by about w.
Undersampling negatives at rate w is corrected exactly with q = p / (p + (1 − p)/w), or recalibration on held-out data at the true prevalence.
SMOTE interpolates new minority points between neighbours; it can help weak learners but rarely helps modern models, and it must be applied inside each cross-validation fold.
Evaluation is noisy when positives are few, so use stratified splits, repeated cross-validation and confidence intervals.
The most valuable fixes are usually more positive examples, better features, and a decision threshold matched to the costs of each error.
Prevalence changes over time, so monitor flagged volume and precision, and re-estimate thresholds and priors on recent data.
glossary: Modelling what normal data looks like and flagging what doesn't, used when positives are too rare or too varied to learn directly.
A summary of the precision–recall curve; its baseline is the prevalence (ml7).
Area under the ROC curve: the probability a random positive scores above a random negative; unaffected by class balance (ml7).
A large difference in how often classes occur, such as 1 fraud per 1,000 transactions.
Loss multipliers per class; weighting the rare class by w makes each of its examples count w times.
Training or deciding with explicit costs for each type of error, sometimes different for each example.
Keeping the negatives a model finds hardest and discarding easy ones, to spend training effort where it matters.
A change in class proportions between training and deployment while each class's feature distribution stays the same.
Adding (or subtracting) the log of class priors to a model's scores to correct for class frequency, used for long-tailed classes.
The rare and common classes in an imbalanced dataset.
Duplicating (or synthesising) minority examples so they make up a larger share of training data.
Adjusting predicted probabilities for a known change in class proportions, for example after undersampling.
Fitting a mapping from a model's scores to true probabilities on held-out data at the real prevalence (ml15).
Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique: creating new minority examples on line segments between a minority example and one of its minority neighbours.
A train/test or cross-validation split that keeps the class proportions the same in every part.
A cheap high-recall filter followed by an expensive, more precise model or human review on what passes.
Discarding a random fraction of majority examples to rebalance or to cut training cost.
drill:
Work it out

Fraud runs at 1%. You undersample negatives to train on a balanced 1:1 set. The model now outputs 0.5 for a transaction. What is the actual probability that it is fraud? And what else changes?

Answer

About 1%, not 50%.

In the original data there are 99 negatives per positive. To reach 1:1 you kept a fraction w = 1/99 of negatives, which multiplied the odds of fraud by 99 in the data the model saw. Undo it on the odds scale: model odds at p = 0.5 are 1.0; true odds = 1.0 / 99 = 0.0101; p = 0.0101 / 1.0101 ≈ 1.0%. Equivalently, q = p / (p + (1 − p)/w) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5 × 99) = 0.01.

Why it matters: the ranking is unaffected, so if you only need a top-N review queue, undersampling costs you little. But the moment anything computes expected value — p × loss for a decline decision, an alert budget, a forecast of fraud volume — a 50× inflated probability produces 50× wrong decisions. Either apply the correction, or recalibrate on a held-out set at the true prevalence.

What else changes: the validation set used to choose the threshold must be at the true 1% prevalence, not the balanced one, or precision will look far better than production. The same probability warning applies to class weights and to SMOTE, and SMOTE must be applied inside each cross-validation fold or synthetic neighbours of validation points leak into training.
qa: E
What problems does class imbalance actually cause?

Mainly measurement and decision problems: accuracy becomes meaningless (predicting the majority class scores highly), the default 0.5 threshold flags almost nothing, and metrics on the rare class are noisy because there are few positives. It can also mean too few positive examples to learn from, which is a data-quantity problem. With a proper loss and a strong model, the learning itself is often fine.
E
What is the simplest thing to try first for imbalance?

Use the right metric and move the decision threshold. Evaluate with precision, recall and the PR curve, then pick the threshold from the cost of each error or the review capacity. It's free, reversible, requires no retraining, and is usually most of the benefit.
E
What do undersampling and oversampling do?

Undersampling discards some majority examples; oversampling duplicates or synthesises minority examples. Both change the class proportions the model sees during training, pushing it to predict the minority class more often. Undersampling also cuts training cost with huge datasets; oversampling keeps all data but can overfit to duplicated points. Both shift predicted probabilities, which must be corrected if they're used.
M
Why must SMOTE go inside the cross-validation fold?

SMOTE creates synthetic points by interpolating between a minority example and its neighbours. If you apply it before splitting, synthetic points built from validation examples end up in training, so the model is effectively trained on near-copies of validation data and the score is optimistic. Put resampling inside a pipeline so it's fitted only on each fold's training part, and never resample validation or test data.
Follow-up: Does the same apply to plain oversampling? — Yes: a duplicated minority row that lands in both training and validation leaks directly.
M
You undersample negatives to a 1:1 ratio when fraud is 1%. The model outputs 0.5. What's the true probability?

About 1%. Keeping 1 in 99 negatives multiplies the odds of fraud by 99. The model's odds of 1.0 correspond to true odds of 1/99, so p = (1/99)/(1 + 1/99) = 1%. Equivalently q = p / (p + (1 − p)/w) with w = 1/99. Ranking is unaffected, so a top-N review queue is fine, but any expected-value calculation would be 50 times too high without the correction.
Follow-up: How would you correct if the relationship isn't this clean — say, after SMOTE? — Recalibrate on a held-out set at the true prevalence with Platt scaling or isotonic regression (ml15).
M
How do class weights relate to resampling?

In expectation, weighting each positive by w in the loss is the same as including each positive w times — oversampling without the duplicated rows. Both shift the optimum towards predicting positives, multiplying the predicted odds by about w. Weights avoid throwing data away (unlike undersampling) and avoid exact duplicates (unlike oversampling), but they have the same effect on probabilities and, with stochastic training, can make gradients noisier when rare examples carry large weights.
M
Does class imbalance always need fixing?

No. If the model is trained with a proper loss and you need ranking or calibrated probabilities, the natural distribution is usually best; a threshold chosen from costs handles the decision. It needs handling when the model genuinely underweights positives — weak learners, some neural networks with extreme imbalance — when training cost forces undersampling, or when the positive class is too small to learn from, in which case the fix is more data or a different framing.
M
How do you evaluate a model when there are only 50 positives in the test set?

Carefully and with intervals. Recall moves in steps of 2%, and its standard error at 80% recall is about √(0.8 × 0.2 / 50) ≈ 5.7 points, so a 95% interval is roughly ±11. Use stratified splits, repeated stratified cross-validation to use every positive, bootstrap intervals, and PR-based metrics. Avoid choosing between models on differences smaller than the noise.
Follow-up: Would you use AUC here? — Report it, but AP and precision at the operating threshold are more informative for a rare class, and all need intervals.
H
Why does cross-entropy handle imbalance better than people expect?

At the start of training every example has p ≈ 0.5, so each contributes about the same gradient and positives, at 1%, supply 1% of the signal. But the intercept quickly learns the base rate. Then negatives have p ≈ 0.01 and each contributes only |p − y| ≈ 0.01, while each positive contributes ≈ 0.99. With 99 negatives per positive, the two classes supply roughly equal total gradient. So after the first phase, the loss is effectively self-balancing; the minority isn't drowned out, and the remaining issues are the threshold and the sheer number of positive examples.
H
Fraud prevalence doubles after a new attack. What happens to your model and what do you do?

Recall and FPR at the same threshold may stay similar if the fraud looks like past fraud, but precision rises and flagged volume grows, and predicted probabilities are now too low on average, because the model learned the old base rate. If the new fraud looks different, recall drops too. Monitor flagged volume, precision on audited flags and score distributions; correct priors (re-estimate the base rate, adjust the intercept or recalibrate on recent labelled data); and retrain on data that includes the new pattern. Label delay means the evidence arrives late, so audits of recent flags are the early signal.

Follow-up: Can you estimate the new prevalence without labels? — Yes, under label shift: methods such as EM-based prior re-estimation or black-box shift estimation use the model's own predictions on the new data to infer the new class proportions.
H
Design a system for detecting a 0.01% event in 100 million daily events.

Frame it as a cascade: a cheap first stage (rules plus a fast model) with very high recall that passes perhaps 0.5% of traffic, then a more expensive model on what passes, then human review for the top cases within capacity. Train the first stage on heavily undersampled negatives with a probability correction; train later stages on the filtered distribution they actually see. Choose thresholds from review capacity and the cost of misses. Get more positives via longer history and pooled sources, audit a random sample of unflagged events to measure recall, and monitor prevalence and volumes continuously.
Follow-up: How do you evaluate the cascade? — End to end: recall of the whole system, precision of what reaches reviewers, and each stage's recall conditional on the previous stage.
H
How do you handle imbalance across thousands of classes, such as product categories with a long tail?

The head classes dominate training and the model's scores favour them. Remedies include logit adjustment (subtract the log of each class's prior from its score at prediction time, or add it during training), balanced or re-weighted loss, decoupling representation learning from training the final classifier on class-balanced samples, and collecting more tail data. Evaluate with macro-averaged metrics and by frequency bucket (head, torso, tail), because micro-averaged accuracy hides tail failures.

To SMOTE, or not to SMOTE?
Elor & Averbuch-Elor, 2022 — balancing helps weak learners but not strong modern classifiers.
Chawla et al., 2002 — the original method, and clear about what it does and does not fix.
The library everyone uses — resamplers, ensembles, and the pipeline API that keeps resampling inside the fold.
scikit-learn — Platt scaling and isotonic regression, which is how you undo the damage above.
Menon et al., 2020 — correcting class-frequency bias in many-class problems by adjusting logits with log priors.

sum: How to estimate performance on data a model hasn't seen: train/validation/test, k-fold and its variants (stratified, grouped, time-based, nested), how big a test set must be, and data leakage — the failure that makes offline metrics beautiful and production metrics collapse — with the reproducibility study that found it in 329 papers.
prereq: ml1
Generalisation means performing well on new data from the same distribution; the i.i.d. assumption justifies random splits into training, validation and test sets.
ml2
Training error is optimistic; the gap between training and validation error signals variance, and repeatedly tuning against one set overfits it.
ml7
Metrics such as AUC, precision and recall are estimates from finite test sets and need confidence intervals.
why:
A team builds a model to predict which hospital patients will be readmitted within 30 days. Under cross-validation it scores an AUC of 0.94 — far better than anything in the published literature. Leadership is thrilled; the model is deployed at a partner hospital, where it scores 0.71. No code changed. What changed is that, at the partner hospital, the model was finally being evaluated the way it would be used: on new patients, with only the information available at the moment of discharge. The 0.94 was never real. Some of each patient's visits sat in the training folds while others sat in the validation folds, so the model had learned to recognise patients; and one feature, a rolling count of visits, quietly included visits that happened after the prediction date.

This is data leakage: information that won't exist at prediction time finding its way into training or evaluation. It is the single most common reason a model looks excellent offline and disappoints in production, and it isn't limited to industry. In 2022, Kapoor and Narayanan surveyed the scientific literature and found leakage-driven errors in 329 papers across 17 fields — this lesson's public case — including an entire research area where the headline claim, that complex machine-learning models beat logistic regression, vanished once the leakage was fixed.

The defence is a discipline of evaluation: holding data back and treating it exactly like future data; choosing a split that matches how the model will be used (random, stratified, by group, by time); putting every data-dependent step inside the split; and knowing how noisy the resulting number is. Interviewers probe this hard because it separates engineers whose models survive contact with production from those whose don't. "Validation 0.94, production 0.71 — find the bug" is one of the most common ML interview questions there is.

This lesson builds that discipline: train/validation/test and why each exists; k-fold cross-validation with fold scores worked through; stratified, grouped, time-based and nested variants with diagrams; how big a test set must be; leakage in its common forms, each with a concrete example (including target encoding computed by hand); pipelines as the structural fix; validation-set overfitting and benchmark contamination in LLMs; and the reproducibility study that found leakage across science.
primer:
The golden rule

A model's score on the data it trained on says little about how it will do on new data — it may simply have memorised (ml2). So we hold back data the model never sees during training and measure on that. The rule that everything in this lesson follows from: evaluation data must be treated exactly like future, unseen data. Not only must the model not train on it; no decision, no preprocessing statistic and no feature may be influenced by it either.

An analogy: exam papers

A teacher who wants to know whether students understand the material sets an exam with questions the students haven't seen. If the students have seen the exact questions — or if the teacher adjusts the course after seeing which questions they got wrong, then re-sets the same exam — the marks go up without understanding going up. Leakage is any way that exam questions reach the students; validation-set overfitting is re-setting the same exam after adjusting the course. The analogy breaks in one instructive place: machine-learning leakage is usually accidental and invisible, like a clue printed faintly on the back of the exam paper, which is why it needs systematic checks rather than good intentions.

Train, validation, test

  • Training set (for example 70%): fit the model's parameters.
  • Validation set (15%): compare models and choose hyperparameters such as tree depth, regularisation strength or the decision threshold.
  • Test set (15%): used once, at the very end, for an honest estimate. If you keep tweaking after looking at the test score, it stops being honest.

Cross-validation

With limited data, one validation split is noisy — you might get a lucky or unlucky split. k-fold cross-validation divides the data into k equal parts called folds, trains on k − 1 of them, validates on the remaining one, and repeats k times so each fold is the validation set once. Average the k scores and look at their spread.

What leakage looks like

Leakage is harder to spot than overfitting because nothing looks wrong: the code runs, the training curve is healthy, the validation score is high. The problem is in what the model was allowed to see. Three classic examples, each of which makes offline scores look better than reality:

  • A feature from the future. A hospital readmission model uses "length of the discharge summary" — written after the stay and correlated with how sick the patient was.
  • Preprocessing that saw the test data. Normalising features with the mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset before splitting: the training process has "seen" test statistics.
  • The same entity on both sides. One customer's transactions in both training and test, so the model recognises the customer rather than learning general patterns.

In each case the fix is the same question asked in advance: when this model is used for real, what will it know, and about whom? The split and the features must reproduce exactly that situation.
body:
1. Reading cross-validation results

Take the five fold scores above: AUC 0.81, 0.84, 0.79, 0.86, 0.80. The mean is 4.10 / 5 = 0.82. The deviations from the mean are −0.01, +0.02, −0.03, +0.04, −0.02; their squares sum to 0.0034, and dividing by k − 1 = 4 gives a variance of 0.00085, so the standard deviation across folds is 0.029. Two readings follow. First, any single split could have reported anything from 0.79 to 0.86 — a team that happened to get fold 4 as its only validation set would have overstated performance by 0.04. Second, a competing model that scores 0.83 is not clearly better; differences smaller than the fold-to-fold spread need more careful comparison (repeated CV with different shuffles, or a paired comparison on the same folds, where each model is evaluated on exactly the same splits and you look at the per-fold differences).

After cross-validation has chosen a model and its settings, the usual final step is to retrain on all the training data with those settings — the k fold models were only for estimation. The test set, untouched throughout, then gives one final number.

Choosing k is a trade-off. Each fold's model trains on (k − 1)/k of the data, so small k (say 2) trains on half the data and underestimates what a full-data model would achieve. Large k trains on almost all the data but costs k model fits, and the fold models are nearly identical, so their scores are highly correlated and the average's variance doesn't shrink as much as you'd hope. Five or ten folds are the standard compromise; leave-one-out (k = n) is reserved for tiny datasets.

2. Choosing the split to match deployment

The most important question in evaluation is: what will the model see when it's used, and does my split imitate that?

Stratified k-fold keeps each class's proportion the same in every fold. With 2% positives and 1,000 rows, a random fold of 200 might contain 1 positive or 8; stratification guarantees 4. Use it whenever classes are imbalanced (ml8).

Group k-fold keeps all rows belonging to one entity — a patient, user, device, document, or all augmented crops of one image — in the same fold. If a model will be applied to new patients, a random split that puts the same patient's visits on both sides measures something easier: predicting a patient it has already seen. In the opening story, 40,000 rows covered 12,000 patients (about 3.3 visits each), so most validation patients had other visits in training. The model learned patient-specific quirks, and the random split rewarded it.

Time-based splits train on the past and validate on the future. If a model will forecast next month, a shuffled split trains on the future to predict the past: trends, seasonality and the similarity of neighbouring days let it interpolate rather than forecast. The standard scheme is an expanding window — train on January to June, validate on July; train on January to July, validate on August; and so on — or a sliding window of fixed length when old data is less relevant.

Leave a gap between the end of training and the start of validation at least as long as the label delay or the longest feature window. If a label ("churned within 30 days") takes 30 days to become known, training rows from the last 30 days before the cutoff have labels that overlap the validation period. Real problems often need several properties at once — grouped by user, ordered in time, stratified for rare labels — and the split then has to be designed explicitly rather than taken from a library default.

3. Nested cross-validation

If you use cross-validation to choose hyperparameters — say, the best of 50 regularisation strengths — the best CV score is optimistic, because you picked the configuration that happened to do best on those particular folds, noise included. Nested cross-validation puts the whole tuning procedure inside an outer loop: for each outer fold, run an inner cross-validation on the outer training part to pick the hyperparameters, train with them, and score on the outer validation fold, which played no part in the choice. The outer scores estimate the performance of the procedure "tune then train". It costs (outer × inner × configurations) fits, so it's used when data is small and an honest estimate matters — typical in medical and scientific studies. With plenty of data, a separate untouched test set does the same job more cheaply.

4. How big must the test set be?

A metric computed on n examples is an estimate with sampling error. For a proportion p — accuracy, recall, precision — the standard error is √(p(1 − p)/n), and a 95% confidence interval is roughly ±1.96 standard errors.

  • 95% accuracy on 1,000 examples: √(0.95 × 0.05 / 1,000) = 0.0069 → about ±1.4 points.
  • The same on 10,000 examples: 0.0022 → about ±0.4 points.
  • Recall of 0.8 measured on 50 positives: √(0.8 × 0.2 / 50) = 0.057 → about ±11 points.

So "the new model improves accuracy from 94.8% to 95.3%" on 1,000 test examples means nothing, and for rare classes the number of positives, not the total, sets the precision of the estimate. Size the test set so its interval is narrower than the smallest difference you'd act on.

5. Leakage, ranked by how often it bites

(a) Preprocessing before splitting. Any step that learns from data — scaling (means and standard deviations), imputation (fill values), encoding (category vocabularies, target encodings), feature selection, dimensionality reduction (ml13), resampling (ml8) — must be fitted on training data only. Fitted on everything, it carries information from validation and test data into training. Sometimes the effect is small (a mean shifted slightly); sometimes it is catastrophic. The textbook demonstration comes from The Elements of Statistical Learning (section 7.10.2): with far more features than rows and labels that are pure noise, selecting the features most correlated with the label on the whole dataset and then cross-validating a classifier on those features reports low error, although no model can do better than chance. Selecting inside each fold gives the honest answer: about 50%.

(b) Target leakage. A feature that exists or changes only because the outcome happened. "Refund amount" in a churn model; "ICU admission date" in a severity model; "account closed flag" in a default model; "number of support calls about cancellation". The test is to ask, for each feature: at the moment we'd make this prediction, would this value already be known, and would it have this value?

(c) Temporal leakage. Aggregates computed over windows that include the prediction moment or later: a "30-day rolling average of visits" computed on the whole table, or "customer's average order value" using all orders ever, including future ones. Fix: compute every feature point-in-time — as of the prediction timestamp — which is what feature stores' point-in-time joins provide (ml14).

(d) Duplicates and entities across the split. Exact duplicates (the same row collected twice), near-duplicates (the same document with a different footer, the same image resized) and shared entities (group k-fold above). For text and images, near-duplicate detection before splitting is standard; for LLMs this becomes benchmark contamination (deep).

(e) Target encoding computed in-sample. Replacing a category with the mean label of its rows is powerful, but computed on the rows being trained on, it leaks each row's own label. Worked: the city "Leeds" appears in two training rows, both churners. Its in-sample encoding is 1.0, so the model learns "encoding 1.0 → churn" — which is just the label reflected back. A category that appears once always gets exactly its own label. The fix is out-of-fold encoding: each row's encoding is computed from the other folds only, plus smoothing towards the global rate for rare categories, e.g. (sum of labels + m × global rate) / (count + m) with m = 10. For Leeds with 2 churners, a global rate of 0.2 and m = 10: (2 + 10 × 0.2) / (2 + 10) = 0.33 instead of 1.0.

(f) Test-set reuse. Covered in section 7 — the slowest, most invisible leak.

6. Pipelines: the structural fix

The reliable way to avoid preprocessing leakage is structural: bundle every data-dependent step with the model into a single pipeline object, and cross-validate the pipeline. Each fold then refits the scaler, encoder, selector and model on its own training part and only applies them to its validation part. In scikit-learn this is make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(k=20), LogisticRegression()) passed to cross_val_score with the appropriate splitter (StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold with a groups array, or TimeSeriesSplit). The same pipeline object is what gets deployed, which also prevents the training/serving mismatch of ml14.

7. Validation-set overfitting

Every time you look at a validation or test score and change something in response, some information about that set flows into your choices. One look is harmless. Two hundred experiments, each kept or discarded based on the same set, add up to an optimisation procedure against that set — including its noise. Picture 200 candidate models that are all truly identical at 80% accuracy, evaluated on 1,000 examples: their measured scores scatter with a standard error of about 1.3 points, so the best of 200 will typically measure around 83–84% — a 3–4 point "improvement" that is pure selection. Defences: a final holdout touched once; refreshing test sets periodically; confidence intervals and paired comparisons for decisions; and, in competitions, the public/private leaderboard split, whose gap is exactly this effect made visible.

8. Putting it together: an evaluation plan

For the readmission model, an honest plan reads like this. Deployment: at discharge, predict whether a new patient returns within 30 days, using only data recorded up to discharge. Features: every aggregate computed as of the discharge timestamp from an event log, never from current-state tables. Split: by time (train on discharges up to a cutoff, validate on later ones, with a 30-day gap so labels mature) and by patient (no patient in both). Preprocessing: imputation, scaling and encodings in a pipeline, fitted per fold. Tuning: hyperparameters chosen on the validation periods; the last three months reserved as a test set, used once. Reporting: AUC and precision at the operating threshold with bootstrap intervals, plus a separate score on a held-out hospital to measure shift. Each line corresponds to one of the failure modes above, and writing the plan down before training is the cheapest leakage defence there is.
deep:
Point-in-time correctness in real data systems

Production data warehouses store the current state of things: today's customer tier, today's account status, the latest address. A training table built by joining events to these tables gives every past event today's values — a customer who became "premium" last week appears premium in all their historical rows, including those that preceded (and perhaps caused) the upgrade. Point-in-time joins look up the value as of each event's timestamp, which requires keeping history (slowly changing dimensions, event logs). Feature stores exist largely to make this automatic. Getting it wrong is the most common form of temporal leakage in industry, and it is invisible in the code, because the join looks correct.

Leakage through proxies and artefacts

Leakage doesn't need an obviously forbidden feature. Row identifiers assigned in order of collection can correlate with the label if positives were collected in a batch; file names or folder structure can encode the class; images of one class may all come from one hospital's scanner, so the model learns the scanner. A useful diagnostic is adversarial validation: train a classifier to distinguish training rows from test rows. If it succeeds well above chance, the sets differ systematically, and its most important features point at the difference — sometimes a leak, sometimes genuine shift that the evaluation should reflect.

Distribution shift is not leakage, but CV can't see it

Cross-validation estimates performance on the distribution the data came from. Deployment often differs: new regions, later time periods, new products, a different hospital. That gap is not leakage — nothing illegitimate reached training — but it's another reason offline scores exceed production ones. Estimate it deliberately with shifted holdouts: hold out a whole region, the latest months, or an entire hospital, and compare with in-distribution CV. The difference is a robustness measurement you can report and track.

Benchmark contamination in LLMs

Large language models are trained on web-scale corpora that may contain the questions and answers of public benchmarks, so a high benchmark score can reflect memorisation — leakage at internet scale, and hard to rule out because training data is often undisclosed. Mitigations include searching training data for n-gram overlaps with test items, building evaluation sets privately or after the model's training cutoff, comparing performance on original items with paraphrased or perturbed versions (memorisation shows as a drop on rewrites), and tracking performance on genuinely new material. For teams fine-tuning models, the same discipline applies locally: deduplicate evaluation examples against fine-tuning data, and keep a private, versioned evaluation set that never enters any training mix.

Adaptive data analysis and the reusable holdout

The statistics of validation-set overfitting has been studied formally as adaptive data analysis: when each analysis depends on previous results from the same data, classical confidence intervals no longer hold. One proposed defence, the reusable holdout (Dwork et al.), answers queries against the holdout only when they differ noticeably from the training estimate, and adds noise to its answers, limiting how much information each query reveals. In practice, most teams approximate it with discipline: pre-registered comparisons, few looks at the final test set, and fresh data for final decisions.

Leakage in feature engineering at scale

In large feature pipelines, leakage hides in shared infrastructure. A feature computed by another team may have been backfilled — recomputed historically with a later version of the logic or with data that arrived late — so the historical values used in training differ from what the live system would have produced at the time. Label-derived features ("number of past fraud reports for this merchant") must exclude the current event and anything reported after it. And features built from model outputs (another model's score) can leak if that model was trained on data that includes your validation period. Lineage tracking — recording for each feature which data and which time window produced it — is the systematic defence.

When cross-validation estimates are biased in other ways

Each fold model trains on less data than the final model, so CV slightly underestimates final performance (the learning-curve effect of ml2). Fold scores are correlated, so the naive standard error of the mean understates uncertainty; repeated CV with different shuffles and corrected tests help. And for very small datasets, the variance of the CV estimate can be as large as the differences being compared, which argues for simpler models and wider intervals rather than finer tuning.
prod:
The public case: leakage across science

In 2022, Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan at Princeton examined how machine learning was being used in scientific research and asked how often reported results were inflated by leakage. Surveying published reviews and their own analysis, they found 17 fields where leakage-driven errors had been identified, collectively affecting 329 papers, in some cases invalidating the papers' main conclusions. They proposed a taxonomy of 8 types of leakage, ranging from textbook errors — no separate test set, preprocessing on train and test together, feature selection before splitting, duplicates — to subtle ones: features that are illegitimate proxies for the outcome, and test sets drawn from a different distribution than the claim concerns, including temporal leakage.

Their case study is striking. In civil-war prediction, a line of papers had reported that complex machine-learning models (random forests, boosting) dramatically outperformed the logistic-regression models political scientists had used for decades. Kapoor and Narayanan reproduced them and found that all the papers claiming superior performance of complex models failed to reproduce because of data leakage — one imputed missing values on the training and test data together, two reused a dataset that had been imputed that way, and one used proxies for the outcome as features — and that once the leakage was fixed, the complex models did not perform substantively better than logistic regression. The headline claim of a whole research strand was an artefact of evaluation. They propose "model info sheets" — structured reporting of how the data was split and what each feature means at prediction time — so reviewers can catch leakage before publication.

For engineers the lesson is the same as the readmission story: an evaluation is only as good as its imitation of deployment. The civil-war models would have been "deployed" on future years; the only honest evaluation trained on the past and tested on later years with features available at the time.

How leakage shows up in production

A dominant feature. One feature carries most of the model's importance and its relationship with the label is almost deterministic. Ask how it's generated and when it's recorded before celebrating.

Offline–online gap. The model's online performance (or its first A/B test) is far below offline. Compare the features the model received in production with the same features recomputed offline for the same requests: differences point to temporal leakage or training/serving skew (ml14).

Performance that decays immediately. A model that is best on the first day and falls quickly may have been evaluated on a period too similar to training — a random split of time-ordered data.

An evaluation checklist

  1. Write down what the model will know at prediction time and what it will be asked to predict; build every feature point-in-time.
  2. Choose the split that imitates deployment: by time for forecasting, by group for new entities, stratified for rare labels.
  3. Put all data-dependent preprocessing inside a pipeline, fitted per fold.
  4. Deduplicate across splits, including near-duplicates.
  5. Tune on validation or inner CV only; touch the test set once; report intervals.
  6. Run a shifted holdout (latest period, new region) to estimate robustness.
  7. Investigate any score that seems too good, starting with the most important features.
myths: A random train/test split is always the right way to evaluate.

Only when examples are independent and the future looks like the past. If the model will predict the future, split by time; if several rows come from the same person, device or document, split by group. A random split in those cases lets the model learn the future or memorise the entity, and the score won't survive deployment.
Cross-validation prevents overfitting.

Cross-validation estimates generalisation more reliably than one split; it doesn't stop a model overfitting, and it can itself be overfitted — tuning hundreds of configurations against the same folds selects the one that got lucky on them. Its estimate is also only honest if every data-dependent step (scaling, feature selection, resampling, encoding) happens inside each fold.
Leakage is rare and obvious.

It is one of the most common reasons models fail in production and it is usually subtle: a scaler fitted on all data, a feature recorded after the outcome, the same user on both sides of a split, near-duplicate documents. Kapoor and Narayanan found leakage-driven errors in 329 papers across 17 scientific fields.
If the validation score is much higher than expected, the model is just very good.

An unexpectedly excellent score is the most reliable sign of leakage. Before celebrating, ask whether any feature could only be known after the outcome, whether any entity appears on both sides of the split, and whether preprocessing saw the validation data. Suspiciously strong single features deserve an explanation.
The test set can be used a few times as long as you're careful.

Every decision made after looking at a test score — a feature, a threshold, a model choice — tunes the process to that set, and its score becomes optimistic. With many experiments the bias can be large. Use validation data or cross-validation for decisions and keep the test set for a final, one-time estimate, or refresh it.
More folds are always better.

More folds use more data for training in each round, reducing the pessimistic bias of a smaller training set, but they cost more compute and the fold scores become more correlated. Five or ten folds are the usual compromise; leave-one-out is rarely worth it except for very small datasets, and with time series or groups the split design matters far more than k.
lab:
Goal: reproduce the classic leak — feature selection before cross-validation on pure noise — and see the honest answer when selection happens inside each fold. NumPy only; written for Python 3.12.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n, p, k = 50, 5000, 20                      # 50 rows, 5,000 noise features, keep 20
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p)); y = rng.integers(0, 2, n)   # labels are pure noise

def top_k(X, y, k):                          # features most correlated with the label
    Xc = X - X.mean(0); yc = y - y.mean()
    corr = np.abs(Xc.T @ yc) / (np.linalg.norm(Xc, axis=0) * np.linalg.norm(yc) + 1e-12)
    return np.argsort(corr)[-k:]

def centroid_acc(Xtr, ytr, Xva, yva):        # nearest class-mean classifier
    m0, m1 = Xtr[ytr == 0].mean(0), Xtr[ytr == 1].mean(0)
    pred = (np.linalg.norm(Xva - m1, axis=1) < np.linalg.norm(Xva - m0, axis=1)).astype(int)
    return np.mean(pred == yva)

folds = np.arange(n) % 5; rng.shuffle(folds)
wrong_feats = top_k(X, y, k)                 # WRONG: selected using all rows
wrong, right = [], []
for f in range(5):
    tr, va = folds != f, folds == f
    wrong.append(centroid_acc(X[tr][:, wrong_feats], y[tr], X[va][:, wrong_feats], y[va]))
    feats = top_k(X[tr], y[tr], k)           # RIGHT: selected inside the fold
    right.append(centroid_acc(X[tr][:, feats], y[tr], X[va][:, feats], y[va]))
print(f"selection before CV: {np.mean(wrong):.2f}   selection inside CV: {np.mean(right):.2f}")

What to look for. The labels are coin flips, so no model can beat about 50%. Selecting features on all rows reports far higher accuracy, because the 20 features were chosen for correlating with the validation labels too; selecting inside each fold gives roughly chance. Try k = 200 or n = 500 and watch how the gap changes.
recap: Performance must be measured on data the model and every choice about it never saw, treated exactly like future data.
The training set fits parameters, the validation set chooses models and hyperparameters, and the test set is used once for an honest estimate.
k-fold cross-validation trains on k − 1 folds and validates on the remaining one, rotating k times, giving a mean and a spread from all the data.
Stratified folds keep class proportions, group folds keep all rows of an entity together, and time-based splits train on the past and validate on the future, with a gap for label delay.
Nested cross-validation tunes hyperparameters in an inner loop and estimates performance in an outer loop, so the estimate isn't biased by the tuning.

All data-dependent preprocessing — scaling, imputation, encoding, feature selection, resampling — must be fitted inside each training fold, which pipelines enforce.

Kapoor and Narayanan found leakage in 329 papers across 17 fields; in civil-war prediction, complex models' claimed advantage over logistic regression disappeared once leakage was fixed.

Area under the ROC curve: the probability a random positive scores above a random negative (ml7).
Evaluation questions (or near-copies) appearing in a model's training data, inflating its benchmark score.

Data set aside and not used for training; the validation and test sets are holdouts.
Splitting data into k folds and training k models, each validated on a different fold.

An outer CV loop for estimating performance around an inner CV loop for tuning hyperparameters.
