sum: Why fewer dimensions can mean better models, how PCA finds the directions of greatest variance (one full PCA on a 3×2 matrix by hand, including projection and reconstruction error), choosing the number of components, PCA via SVD, its uses and traps, and what t-SNE and UMAP pictures do and don't show — with the study where PCA of genomes redrew the map of Europe.
prereq: ml2
Fewer effective parameters mean lower variance; noise directions in the data add variance without adding signal.
ml3
Features should be standardised when their units differ, and ridge regression shrinks directions the data barely explores.
ml11
In high dimensions distances concentrate, but real data often has a low intrinsic dimension.
why:
A manufacturer records 400 sensor readings from every machine each minute: temperatures, pressures, vibration at several frequencies, currents. Engineers want to spot machines drifting towards failure, and data scientists want to predict failures a day ahead. But the 400 readings aren't 400 independent pieces of information. Temperatures in neighbouring parts rise together; vibration at related frequencies moves together; many readings are mostly noise. A model given all 400 has far more inputs than real degrees of freedom, which invites overfitting (ml2), slows everything down, and makes the data impossible to look at.

Dimensionality reduction re-expresses each example with far fewer numbers while keeping what matters. The most important method, principal component analysis (PCA), finds the directions along which the data actually varies. If 20 directions capture 95% of the variation in those 400 readings, each minute can be summarised by 20 numbers; the other 380 directions are mostly redundancy and noise. The summary can feed a model, be plotted, be compressed, or be used to detect anomalies — a reading that can't be rebuilt from the 20 main patterns is one that doesn't fit the machine's normal behaviour.

PCA appears everywhere in AI engineering: compressing embeddings before indexing them (ml11), reducing features before clustering (ml12), removing noise, visualising high-dimensional data, and as the conceptual ancestor of autoencoders. It is also a favourite interview topic because it ties together variance, correlation, eigenvectors and the singular value decomposition, and because its misuses — forgetting to scale, fitting before splitting, reading meaning into components, trusting t-SNE pictures — are common and revealing.

This lesson builds PCA from the idea of spread: the intuition, one complete PCA on a 3×2 matrix by hand (covariance, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, projections and reconstruction error), why the solution is an eigenvector, PCA through the SVD, choosing the number of components, scaling and leakage, uses and failure modes, other methods (t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders, feature selection), and a public case in which PCA applied to the DNA of 3,000 Europeans produced a picture closely resembling the map of Europe.
primer:
Why reduce dimensions

Data often has many features that are redundant — height in centimetres and height in inches, or twenty survey questions that all measure satisfaction. Reducing dimensions can make models faster and less prone to overfitting, remove noise, let distance-based methods work better (ml11), and let you plot high-dimensional data in two dimensions.

An analogy: photographing a statue

You're allowed one photograph of a statue and want it to show as much of the statue's shape as possible. You'd walk around it and choose the angle where it looks widest — the view that shows the most spread. If you're allowed a second photograph, you'd take it from the side, at right angles to the first, to capture the depth the first missed. PCA does exactly this with data: the first principal component is the viewing direction along which the points are most spread out, the second is the most spread-out direction at right angles to the first, and so on. The analogy breaks in one place: a photograph shows the statue from a direction, while PCA's components are directions to measure along; each point's position along a component is one number, its score.

PCA in pictures

Picture a cloud of points shaped like a tilted cigar in two dimensions. PC1 runs along the cigar; PC2 runs across it. Projecting each point onto PC1 alone — replacing its two coordinates with one number, its position along the cigar — loses only the small sideways scatter.

Explained variance

Each component comes with an explained variance ratio: the share of the data's total variance it captures. If PC1 explains 70% and PC2 20%, two components keep 90% of the variance. A common rule is to keep enough components for 90–95%, or to look for the "elbow" where extra components add little.

A small example

Students' scores in maths and physics are highly correlated. PCA gives PC1 ≈ "overall science ability" (both scores rising together), explaining most of the variance, and PC2 ≈ "maths minus physics", explaining the rest. One number summarises most of what two did, and the second number captures the smaller, still-real difference between subjects.

What is kept and what is lost

PCA keeps directions, not features. Each component is a weighted blend of all the original features — its weights are called loadings — so after PCA you no longer have "temperature 3" and "pressure 7"; you have "component 1", which might be mostly a mix of all the temperatures. What you lose is whatever varied only in the discarded directions: small, independent quirks of individual features, which are often noise but occasionally the one signal you needed. That trade — compactness and denoising in exchange for interpretability and possibly some signal — is the decision you make every time you apply it.

The practical rule to remember

Standardise features first (mean 0, standard deviation 1) when they're in different units; otherwise the feature with the biggest numbers dominates the components. And fit PCA on training data only, then apply the same fitted transformation to everything else.
body:
1. The ingredients: centring, variance and covariance

PCA works on centred data: subtract each feature's mean so the cloud sits around the origin. Then the spread of the data is described by the covariance matrix Σ. Its diagonal entries are each feature's variance; its off-diagonal entries are covariances, which are positive when two features rise together, negative when one rises as the other falls, and zero when they're unrelated. For centred data with n rows, Σ = XᵀX / (n − 1).

Now take any direction, given by a unit vector w. Each point's projection onto that direction is the dot product x·w — its coordinate along w. The variance of those projections turns out to be wᵀΣw. PCA asks: which direction w makes this as large as possible?

2. Why the answer is an eigenvector

We want to maximise wᵀΣw subject to w having length 1 (otherwise we could inflate the variance just by making w longer). Using a Lagrange multiplier λ for the constraint, the maximum satisfies:

Σw = λw

That is the definition of an eigenvector: a direction the matrix only stretches, by the factor λ, the eigenvalue. And the variance achieved along it is wᵀΣw = wᵀ(λw) = λ. So the best direction is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, and that eigenvalue is the variance along it. The second component maximises the same variance subject to being at right angles (orthogonal) to the first, which gives the eigenvector with the second-largest eigenvalue, and so on. Since Σ is symmetric, its eigenvectors are orthogonal and its eigenvalues are non-negative, and the eigenvalues add up to the total variance (the sum of the diagonal). The explained variance ratio of component j is λⱼ divided by that total.

3. A full PCA on a 3×2 matrix, by hand

Three points in two dimensions: (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2).

  1. Centre. The mean is (2, 2). Centred points: (−1, −1), (0, 1), (1, 0).
  2. Covariance (divide by n − 1 = 2). Sum of x² = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, so var(x) = 1. Sum of y² = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, so var(y) = 1. Sum of x·y = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, so cov(x, y) = 0.5. 
    Σ = [[1.0, 0.5],
     [0.5, 1.0]]
  3. Eigenvalues. Solve det(Σ − λI) = (1 − λ)² − 0.25 = 0, so 1 − λ = ±0.5: λ₁ = 1.5, λ₂ = 0.5. The total variance is 1 + 1 = 2 = 1.5 + 0.5, as it must be.
  4. Eigenvectors. For λ₁ = 1.5: (1 − 1.5)a + 0.5b = 0 gives a = b, so PC1 = (1, 1)/√2 ≈ (0.707, 0.707). For λ₂ = 0.5: a = −b, so PC2 = (1, −1)/√2. They're at right angles.
  5. Explained variance. PC1 explains 1.5/2 = 75%, PC2 the remaining 25%.
  6. Project onto PC1. Scores are the dot products with (0.707, 0.707): (−1, −1) → −1.414; (0, 1) → 0.707; (1, 0) → 0.707. Their variance is (2 + 0.5 + 0.5)/2 = 1.5 = λ₁. Check.
  7. Reconstruct from PC1 only. Multiply each score by PC1 and add back the mean. −1.414 × (0.707, 0.707) = (−1, −1), plus (2, 2) gives (1, 1): exact. 0.707 × (0.707, 0.707) = (0.5, 0.5), plus (2, 2) gives (2.5, 2.5) for both remaining points, whose true values are (2, 3) and (3, 2). Each is off by (±0.5, ∓0.5), a squared error of 0.5. Total squared reconstruction error = 1.0, which equals the discarded eigenvalue times n − 1: 0.5 × 2.

This small example contains every idea in PCA: the covariance captures how features move together; the eigenvectors are the directions of spread; the eigenvalues are the variance along them; projecting keeps the top directions; and the variance you discard is exactly what reconstruction can't recover.

A general rule hiding in the example. For any two standardised features with correlation r, the covariance matrix is [[1, r], [r, 1]], whose eigenvalues are 1 + r and 1 − r with eigenvectors (1, 1)/√2 and (1, −1)/√2 — whatever r is. So PC1 is always "the two features together", and it explains (1 + r)/2 of the variance. Our example had r = 0.5 and PC1 explained 75%. Maths and physics scores correlated at r = 0.8 give PC1 = "overall ability" explaining 90% and PC2 = "maths minus physics" explaining 10%; uncorrelated features (r = 0) give 50/50, and PCA has nothing to compress. Redundancy is what PCA feeds on: the more correlated the features, the fewer components you need.

4. PCA through the SVD, as software does it

Forming the covariance matrix squares the numbers and loses precision, so implementations use the singular value decomposition of the centred data matrix instead: X = U·S·Vᵀ, where U and V have orthonormal columns and S is diagonal with non-negative singular values. Then:

principal components   = rows of Vᵀ
scores (projections)   = U·S        (= X·V)
eigenvalues            = S² / (n − 1)

In the example, eigenvalues 1.5 and 0.5 with n − 1 = 2 mean singular values √3 ≈ 1.73 and 1. For large matrices you never need the full decomposition: truncated or randomised SVD computes only the top k components, in roughly O(n·d·k) time, and incremental PCA processes data in batches that don't fit in memory. For sparse matrices such as word counts, truncated SVD without centring (to preserve sparsity) is the standard variant, known in text analysis as latent semantic analysis.

5. Choosing the number of components

Suppose PCA on standardised data with six features gives eigenvalues 4.2, 2.1, 1.3, 0.8, 0.4 and 0.2 (total 9.0). The cumulative explained variance is 46.7%, 70.0%, 84.4%, 93.3%, 97.8%, 100%.

  • Variance threshold: 95% needs five components; 90% needs four.
  • Kaiser rule (standardised data): keep eigenvalues above 1 — components that explain more than one original feature's worth of variance — giving three.
  • Scree elbow: the bars flatten after the third, also suggesting three.
  • Downstream validation: sweep k and pick the value with the best validation score for the actual task. When the reduced data feeds a model, this is the rule that matters.

6. Scaling and leakage

Because PCA follows variance, units decide the answer. With income in pounds (standard deviation £20,000, variance 4 × 10⁸) and age in years (standard deviation 15, variance 225), PC1 is essentially "income" regardless of how the two relate. After standardising both to unit variance, the components reflect their correlation instead. Standardise unless all features share units and their raw variances are meaningful (pixel intensities, or embedding coordinates, which are usually left unscaled).

PCA learns means, scales and directions from data, so fitting it on validation or test rows before splitting leaks information about them (ml9). Put it in the pipeline, fit on training data, and apply the fitted transform to new data — including in production, where the stored means and components must travel with the model (ml14).

7. Reading loadings

The loadings of a component say how much each original feature contributes to it, and inspecting them is how you judge whether a component means anything. Suppose PCA on six standardised body measurements (height, arm span, leg length, shoulder width, weight, waist) gives PC1 loadings all positive and roughly equal, about 0.4 each: PC1 is "overall size", and a person's PC1 score says how big they are overall. PC2 might load positively on weight and waist and negatively on height and leg length: "stocky versus slender". That is the best case. More often, later components mix many features with no clear story, and forcing a name on them misleads. A useful check is to list the handful of features with the largest absolute loadings for each kept component and ask a domain expert whether the grouping makes sense; if nobody can tell a coherent story, treat the component as a compression device, not a concept. Two cautions: loadings are only comparable when features were standardised, and a component's sign is arbitrary — a refit may flip all its loadings and scores together.

8. Compressing embeddings, worked

A retrieval system stores 10 million 1,536-dimensional embeddings in 32-bit floats: 1,536 × 4 bytes = 6 kilobytes (KB) each, about 61 gigabytes (GB) in total — too much to keep comfortably in memory on one ordinary server. Fitting PCA on a sample of 200,000 embeddings shows that the first 256 components explain, say, 90% of the variance. Projecting every stored vector (and every query) onto those 256 components cuts storage to 1 KB per vector — about 10 GB — and speeds up distance computations six-fold. Whether 90% of the variance is enough is not a PCA question: measure recall@10 of nearest-neighbour search with the reduced vectors against exact search with the full ones on real queries (ml11), and look at end-to-end answer quality. If recall drops too far, keep more components or use product quantisation instead. Remember to re-normalise the reduced vectors if the index uses cosine similarity, and to refit the PCA whenever the embedding model changes.

9. What PCA is used for

  • Preprocessing for models that suffer from many correlated features or high dimension — k-NN and clustering especially — and for speed.
  • Compression of embeddings before indexing (for example 1,536 to 256 dimensions), validated by retrieval recall (ml11).
  • Denoising: reconstructing data from the top components drops the low-variance directions where much of the noise lives.
  • Anomaly detection: a point with a large reconstruction error doesn't fit the main patterns of normal data — a standard monitor for sensor streams.
  • Visualisation of the first two or three components, which, unlike t-SNE, preserves global distances linearly.
  • Diagnosing structure, as in population genetics (the public case), where the top components can reveal the main axes of variation among thousands of variables.

10. Beyond PCA

PCA is linear. Other methods cover what it can't:

  • t-SNE places points in 2-D or 3-D so that each point's nearest neighbours stay nearby, using a heavy-tailed distribution in the low-dimensional map that pushes moderately distant points apart; its perplexity setting (roughly, the effective number of neighbours, typically 5–50) changes the picture.
  • UMAP builds a neighbour graph and optimises a low-dimensional layout; it's faster, preserves somewhat more global structure and can map new points, but shares t-SNE's distortions.
  • Autoencoders learn non-linear compression with neural networks; a linear autoencoder trained with squared error learns the same subspace as PCA.
  • Kernel PCA, NMF and ICA: non-linear components via kernels; parts-based non-negative factors for counts and spectra; statistically independent sources for separating mixed signals.
  • Feature selection — filter methods such as mutual information, wrapper methods such as recursive elimination, and L1 regularisation (ml3) — when you must keep original, interpretable features.
deep:
Variance is not signal

PCA is unsupervised: it never sees the target. If the feature that predicts churn is a small, low-variance flag, PCA may bury it in the 50th component and a model trained on the top 20 will never see it. Partial least squares (PLS) finds components that both explain the features and correlate with the target; supervised dimensionality reduction more generally exists for this reason. In many modern pipelines the simpler answer is to skip PCA and let a regularised model or a tree ensemble cope with all the features.

Whitening and its cost

Whitening divides each component's scores by its standard deviation (√λ), so every direction has unit variance and the data is uncorrelated with equal spread. Some algorithms benefit — it makes the covariance an identity, which helps certain optimisation and density methods — but whitening amplifies the low-variance directions, which are often mostly noise, by large factors. It's usually combined with dropping the smallest components or adding a small constant to each eigenvalue before dividing.

Instability of components

When two eigenvalues are nearly equal, the data spreads about equally in every direction within their plane, and the individual eigenvectors are poorly determined: small changes in the data rotate them arbitrarily, even though the plane they span is stable. Component signs are also arbitrary (v and −v are equally valid). Code that stores components and compares them across refits must align signs and, for near-ties, compare subspaces rather than individual vectors. Outliers can dominate components too; robust PCA variants separate a low-rank structure from sparse large errors.

Connections: ridge, the SVD and linear autoencoders

Ridge regression (ml3) shrinks the fitted coefficient along each principal direction by the factor d²/(d² + λ), where d is that direction's singular value: directions the data barely explores are shrunk hardest. Principal component regression instead keeps the top k directions fully and drops the rest; ridge is the smooth version. And a linear autoencoder with a k-dimensional bottleneck, trained to minimise squared reconstruction error, learns exactly the subspace spanned by the top k components (though not necessarily the individual orthogonal axes) — the link between classical dimensionality reduction and learned representations.

Probabilistic PCA and factor analysis

PCA can be recast as a probabilistic model: each observation is generated from a few hidden factors through a linear map, plus Gaussian noise that is the same size in every direction (probabilistic PCA). Maximum likelihood recovers the principal subspace, and the model gives a likelihood for new points — a principled anomaly score — and handles missing values. Factor analysis relaxes the assumption so that each feature gets its own noise level, which suits survey and psychometric data where some questions are noisier than others; followed by a rotation (such as varimax) that pushes loadings towards zero or large values, it often yields more interpretable factors than PCA. Both are useful when the goal is to explain correlations with hidden causes rather than just to compress. In interviews, the distinction to state is that PCA summarises total variance, while factor analysis explains shared variance (covariance) and treats each feature's unique variance as noise.

Random projections

The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma says that projecting n points onto about O(log n / ε²) random directions preserves all pairwise distances to within a factor 1 ± ε, with no fitting at all. Random projections are fast, data-independent and useful as a first reduction for enormous datasets or streaming data. They need more dimensions than PCA for the same fidelity, because they ignore where the variance actually lies.

t-SNE and UMAP, more carefully

t-SNE converts distances into neighbour probabilities in both the original and the low-dimensional space and minimises the KL divergence between the two distributions; because this heavily penalises putting true neighbours far apart but barely penalises putting non-neighbours close, local structure is kept and global structure is not. Results vary with perplexity and random seed, and naive implementations scale as O(n²) (Barnes–Hut tree approximations and fast-Fourier-transform-based interpolation scale further, to millions of points). UMAP optimises a similar objective on a fuzzy nearest-neighbour graph; its n_neighbors setting trades local against global structure and min_dist controls how tightly points pack. Both are for looking. Distill's "How to Use t-SNE Effectively" shows random data forming apparent clusters and cluster sizes that mean nothing — a useful exhibit before presenting such a plot.
prod:
The public case: PCA redraws the map of Europe

In 2008 Novembre and colleagues published "Genes mirror geography within Europe" in Nature. They characterised genetic variation in a sample of 3,000 Europeans genotyped at 500,568 positions in the genome (single-nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs) — a data matrix with half a million columns in which, at any single position, differences between European populations are tiny. Before analysis they filtered samples carefully: removing people whose ancestry came from outside Europe, balancing sample sizes across countries, and excluding people whose grandparents came from more than one place; they also removed SNPs that are strongly correlated with their neighbours in the genome, which would otherwise dominate the components.

They then ran PCA. Plotting 1,387 individuals by their scores on the first two principal components — rotated to line up with compass directions — produced a figure that, in the authors' words, "bears a notable resemblance to a geographic map of Europe": individuals clustered by country, and countries sat roughly where they are on a map. The two strongest directions of genetic variation corresponded to perpendicular geographical axes, as population-genetics theory predicts for spatially structured populations. Using the components in a regression, they could place 50% of individuals within 310 km of their reported origin and 90% within 700 km.

Two lessons for engineers. First, PCA can reveal genuine low-dimensional structure hidden in an enormous number of individually weak, noisy features — the same reason it works for sensor streams and embeddings. Second, the result depended on choices that aren't visible in the plot: which samples were included, which correlated features were removed, and a rotation applied for display. Components reflect the data you give them, so the provenance of that data belongs in any interpretation.

Failure modes in production

Refitting silently changes the space. Refitting PCA on new data rotates components and can flip their signs, so models trained on old component scores receive inputs in a different coordinate system. Version the PCA transform with the model, and retrain downstream models whenever it's refitted.

Leaky fitting. PCA fitted on all data before cross-validation or before a time split gives optimistic results (ml9).

Mismatched preprocessing. Serving code that forgets the centring or scaling step, or uses means computed on live data, feeds the model shifted inputs (ml14).

Over-reading plots. Decisions made from t-SNE cluster sizes or gaps; or stakeholders told a component "is" a business concept.

Monitoring with reconstruction error

A PCA fitted on normal operating data gives a cheap drift and anomaly monitor: track the average reconstruction error of incoming data over time. A rising error means new data contains patterns outside the fitted subspace — a new failure mode, a sensor fault, or a shift in the input distribution — and is often visible before any downstream metric moves. Set the alert threshold from the distribution of errors on held-out normal data (for example, its 99th percentile), and when it fires, look at which original features contribute most to the error to see what changed.
myths: PCA keeps the most important features.

PCA doesn't select features; it builds new axes, each a weighted mix of all the original features, ordered by how much variance they capture. It also has no idea what you want to predict: a low-variance direction can carry all the signal for a target. If you need a subset of the original features, use feature selection; if you need directions that predict a target, consider partial least squares or simply a regularised model.
PCA doesn't need scaling.

PCA finds directions of maximum variance, and variance depends on units. Income in pounds (variance in the hundreds of millions) and age in years (variance around 200) put virtually all of PC1 along income. Standardise features to unit variance first unless they share units and their raw variances are meaningful, as with pixel intensities.
Each principal component corresponds to a real-world factor.

Components are forced to be orthogonal and to maximise variance, not to align with anything meaningful; they're usually dense mixes of many features, and their signs are arbitrary. Sometimes a component is interpretable (the 'overall size' axis in body measurements), but naming PC2 'customer loyalty' in front of stakeholders is usually over-reading. Sparse PCA or factor analysis with rotation give more interpretable factors.
Clusters and distances in a t-SNE or UMAP plot reflect real structure.

Both methods preserve local neighbourhoods and deliberately distort global geometry. Cluster sizes, gaps between clusters and overall layout depend on settings such as perplexity or n_neighbors and on the random seed; t-SNE can even show apparent clusters in random noise. Use them to look, not to measure, and never feed their coordinates into a downstream model.
Fitting PCA on all the data before splitting is harmless because it's unsupervised.

It still learns from the data — means, variances and directions — and fitting it on validation or test rows leaks information about them into the features, like any preprocessing done before splitting (ml9). Fit PCA inside the training fold and apply the fitted transform to held-out data.
Reducing dimensions always improves a model.

It helps when many features are noisy or redundant and data is limited, and it speeds up training. It hurts when the discarded low-variance directions carry signal, and modern regularised models (ridge, boosted trees) often handle many features without it. Treat the number of components as a hyperparameter judged on validation performance.
lab:
Goal: reproduce the 3×2 PCA by hand with NumPy, confirm the SVD relationships, then compress correlated data and use reconstruction error to spot anomalies. NumPy only; written for Python 3.12.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# 1. The worked example
X = np.array([[1., 1.], [2., 3.], [3., 2.]])
Xc = X - X.mean(0)
cov = Xc.T @ Xc / (len(X) - 1)
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)                 # ascending order
print("cov", cov.tolist(), "eigenvalues", vals.round(3), "PC1", vecs[:, -1].round(3))
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
print("singular values", S.round(3), "-> S^2/(n-1) =", (S**2 / 2).round(3))
scores = Xc @ Vt[0]
recon = np.outer(scores, Vt[0]) + X.mean(0)
print("PC1 scores", scores.round(3), "recon error", ((X - recon)**2).sum().round(3))

# 2. 50 correlated features driven by 3 hidden factors, plus noise
n, d = 1000, 50
Z = rng.normal(size=(n, 3)); W = rng.normal(size=(3, d))
D = Z @ W + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(n, d))
mu, sd = D[:800].mean(0), D[:800].std(0)          # fit on "training" rows only
Dtr, Dte = (D[:800] - mu) / sd, (D[800:] - mu) / sd
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Dtr, full_matrices=False)
ratio = S**2 / (S**2).sum()
print("explained by first 5 PCs:", ratio[:5].round(3), "cumulative 3:", ratio[:3].sum().round(3))

# 3. Reconstruction error as an anomaly score
k = 3
def err(A): return (((A - (A @ Vt[:k].T) @ Vt[:k]) ** 2).sum(1))
odd = Dte.copy(); odd[:10] += rng.normal(0, 3, size=(10, d))   # corrupt 10 rows
e = err(odd)
print("mean error normal:", e[10:].mean().round(1), " corrupted:", e[:10].mean().round(1))

What to look for. Part 1 prints the covariance [[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]], eigenvalues 0.5 and 1.5, PC1 ≈ ±(0.707, 0.707) (the sign is arbitrary), singular values √3 and 1, and reconstruction error 1.0. Part 2's first three components explain most of the variance and the rest are near the noise level — the three hidden factors. Part 3's corrupted rows have far larger reconstruction errors than normal ones.
recap: Dimensionality reduction represents data with fewer numbers, removing redundancy and noise, speeding up models and allowing visualisation.
PCA centres the data and finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance: the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by their eigenvalues.
Each eigenvalue is the variance along its component, so its share of the total is the component's explained variance ratio.
Projecting onto the top k components gives the best k-dimensional linear approximation in squared error, and the discarded eigenvalues measure the reconstruction error.

In practice PCA is computed with the singular value decomposition of the centred data, whose right singular vectors are the components and whose squared singular values divided by n − 1 are the eigenvalues.
Features in different units must be standardised first, and PCA must be fitted on training data only.
The number of components is chosen by cumulative explained variance, a scree plot's elbow, or best of all by downstream validation performance.
PCA maximises variance, not predictive power, and its components are mixtures with arbitrary sign, not named factors.
t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear methods for visualisation that preserve local neighbourhoods and distort global distances.
PCA of 3,000 Europeans' genotypes produced a two-dimensional summary that closely resembled a map of Europe.
glossary: A neural network trained to reconstruct its input through a narrow middle layer, learning a non-linear compression.
Subtracting each feature's mean so the data is centred at the origin; required before PCA.
A d × d matrix whose diagonal holds each feature's variance and whose off-diagonal entries measure how pairs of features vary together.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule carrying genetic information; genotyping reads it at chosen positions.
For a matrix A, a vector v with Av = λv; v is a direction the matrix only stretches, by the factor λ.
A component's eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues: its share of the total variance.
Keeping a subset of the original features rather than building new combined ones.
Independent component analysis: finding statistically independent source signals that were mixed together.
Keeping components with eigenvalue above 1 on standardised data, i.e. those explaining more than one original feature's worth of variance.
Kullback–Leibler divergence: a measure of how one probability distribution differs from another; t-SNE minimises it.
A penalty on the sum of absolute weights that sets many to zero, performing feature selection (ml3).
The weights that express each principal component as a combination of the original features.
Non-negative matrix factorisation: approximating non-negative data by products of non-negative factors, giving parts-based components.
At right angles; orthogonal components are uncorrelated.
A method that finds components that explain variance in the features and predict the target at the same time.
PC1, PC2, PC3, PC4, PC5, PC6
Shorthand for the first, second, third and later principal components.
A direction in feature space along which the data varies; the first captures the most variance, each later one the most remaining variance at right angles to the earlier ones.
Finding and projecting onto the directions of greatest variance of centred data.
A point's coordinates along the chosen components.
The squared distance between a point and its approximation rebuilt from the top k components.
A plot of eigenvalues (or explained variance) against component number, used to spot where they level off.
Single-nucleotide polymorphism: a position in the genome where individuals commonly differ by one DNA letter.
Factorising a matrix as U·S·Vᵀ; for centred data, V holds the principal components and S² / (n − 1) the variances.
t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding: a non-linear 2-D or 3-D visualisation that preserves which points are neighbours.
Uniform manifold approximation and projection: a faster non-linear embedding that preserves local structure and somewhat more global structure than t-SNE.
Rescaling principal components to unit variance, so all directions count equally.
drill:
Work it out

PCA on a standardised dataset gives eigenvalues 4.2, 2.1, 1.3, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2. How many components for 95% of the variance? What does the Kaiser rule (keep eigenvalues > 1) suggest? And how would you actually decide?

Answer

Total = 9.0 — the number of standardised features, since each contributes variance 1. Cumulative explained variance:

PC1 46.7% · PC2 70.0% · PC3 84.4% · PC4 93.3% · PC5 97.8% · PC6 100%

So 5 components for 95%. The Kaiser rule keeps 3 (4.2, 2.1 and 1.3 exceed 1): on standardised data each original feature contributes variance 1, so a component with an eigenvalue below 1 explains less than a single raw feature.

The two rules disagree, which is the point: 3 components lose 15.6% of the variance and 5 keep almost everything. Neither number is correct on its own — choose by the downstream task, sweeping the number of components as a hyperparameter against validation performance.

Two traps to mention unprompted: standardise first or the largest-unit feature dominates; and fit PCA on the training fold only, because fitting it on train and test together is a quiet form of leakage.
qa: E
What does PCA do, in plain words?

It finds new axes for the data: the first points along the direction in which the data is most spread out, the second along the most spread-out direction at right angles to the first, and so on. Keeping only the first few axes represents each point with a few numbers while keeping most of the variation, removing redundancy between correlated features and much of the noise.
E
Why must you standardise features before PCA?

Because PCA follows variance and variance depends on units. A feature measured in large units — income in pounds — has a variance millions of times larger than age in years, so the first component would simply be income. Standardising each feature to unit variance lets correlation structure, not units, decide the components. Skip it only when features share units and their raw variances are meaningful.
E
How do you choose how many components to keep?

Look at cumulative explained variance (for example, keep enough for 90–95%), look for the elbow in a scree plot, or on standardised data keep eigenvalues above 1 (the Kaiser rule). Best, treat the number as a hyperparameter and pick the value that gives the best validation performance for the downstream task.
M
What is the relationship between PCA and SVD?

PCA on centred data is the SVD of the data matrix X = U·S·Vᵀ: the rows of Vᵀ are the principal directions, the projected data is U·S, and the covariance eigenvalues are S² / (n − 1). Implementations use SVD because it's more numerically stable than forming and diagonalising the covariance matrix, and truncated or randomised SVD computes only the top components for large matrices.
Follow-up: In the lesson's 3×2 example, what are the singular values? — The eigenvalues are 1.5 and 0.5 with n − 1 = 2, so the singular values are √3 ≈ 1.73 and 1.
M
What does the reconstruction error of PCA tell you, and how is it used?

Projecting onto k components and mapping back loses the variance in the discarded directions; summed over the training data, the squared error equals (n − 1) times the sum of the discarded eigenvalues. Per point, a large reconstruction error means the point doesn't fit the main patterns of the training data, which makes it a simple anomaly score — used for fault detection in sensor data and fraud screening.
M
Why can't you interpret a principal component as a real-world factor?

Components are constrained to be orthogonal and to maximise variance, not to align with meaningful concepts; they're usually dense mixtures of many features, their signs are arbitrary, and they change with scaling and outliers. Sometimes the first component has a clear meaning (overall size, overall ability), but later ones rarely do. For interpretable factors use factor analysis with rotation or sparse PCA, and say so.
M
What does it mean that t-SNE distances between clusters aren't meaningful?

t-SNE optimises to keep each point's nearest neighbours nearby, and uses a heavy-tailed distribution in the low-dimensional space that pushes moderately distant points far apart. So the gaps between clusters and their relative sizes are artefacts of the method and of the perplexity setting; two runs on identical data can space clusters differently, and random data can look clustered. Read local neighbourhoods, not global layout.
Follow-up: When would you use UMAP instead? — For larger datasets (it's much faster), when you want somewhat more global structure, or when you need to project new points with the fitted model.
M
Is PCA a good preprocessing step before a supervised model?

Sometimes. It helps with many correlated, noisy features and limited data (reducing variance), with algorithms that suffer from high dimension (k-NN, clustering), and to speed up training. It can hurt because it ignores the target — the discarded low-variance directions may be the predictive ones — and regularised models or trees often do as well without it. Tune the number of components by validation, and fit PCA inside each training fold.
H
Derive why the first principal component is the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix.

Project centred data onto a unit vector w: the variance of the projections is wᵀΣw, where Σ is the covariance matrix. Maximise wᵀΣw subject to wᵀw = 1 with a Lagrange multiplier: the gradient condition gives Σw = λw, so w must be an eigenvector, and the achieved variance is wᵀΣw = λ. The maximum is therefore the largest eigenvalue and its eigenvector. Each later component maximises the same quantity subject to being orthogonal to the earlier ones, giving the next eigenvectors in order.

Follow-up: Why is it also the best reconstruction? — Total variance is fixed, so maximising the variance kept in k directions is the same as minimising the variance discarded, which is the reconstruction error.
H
You need to shrink 1,536-dimensional embeddings to 256 dimensions for a vector index. How would you do it and check it?

Fit PCA (or truncated SVD) on a representative sample of embeddings, keep 256 components, and project both stored vectors and queries with the same transform — re-normalising afterwards if the index uses cosine similarity. Check the explained variance, but judge by the task: recall@k against exact search with the full vectors on real queries, and end-to-end retrieval quality. If the model was trained to be truncatable (Matryoshka-style), simply keeping the first 256 coordinates may work as well. Refit if the embedding model changes.

Follow-up: Why not reduce by random projection instead? — Random projections preserve distances approximately (Johnson–Lindenstrauss) with no fitting, but need more dimensions for the same accuracy because they ignore where the variance is.
H
What are the main failure modes of PCA?

It's linear, so it can't unfold curved structure (a spiral or a swiss roll); it maximises variance, which may not be where the signal is; it's sensitive to scaling choices and to outliers, which can capture whole components (robust PCA variants exist); components with nearly equal eigenvalues are unstable and can rotate between runs; and fitted on data containing a strong common trend, such as prices over time, the first component may just be that trend. It also leaks if fitted before splitting.
H
How did PCA 'redraw the map of Europe', and what does the study teach about interpreting PCA?

Novembre and colleagues genotyped about 3,000 Europeans at over half a million DNA sites and ran PCA; plotting individuals on the first two components (after a rotation) produced a picture closely resembling a map of Europe, and a regression-based assignment placed 50% of individuals within 310 km of their reported origin. It shows PCA surfacing real low-dimensional structure hidden among hundreds of thousands of noisy features. It also teaches caution: the resemblance required careful sample selection (for example, individuals whose grandparents came from one place) and removing correlated DNA sites, and the axes were rotated for display — the components reflect the sampling as much as the population.

The best available explanation of what the components actually are.

t: Feature engineering and the training/serving gap
sum: Turning raw data into features a model can use — encodings, scaling and transforms, time and aggregate features, missing values — each with worked numbers; then the training/serving gap: how the same feature ends up computed two ways, how to detect it (with a population stability index computed by hand), and why logging served features and feature stores exist, as Google's Rules of ML and 'Hidden Technical Debt' describe.
prereq: ml3
Standardisation (mean 0, standard deviation 1) is needed for penalised, distance-based and gradient-trained models; the fitted means and scales are part of the model.
ml9
Every feature must be computed point-in-time from data available at prediction time, and target encodings must be computed out-of-fold, or evaluation leaks.
ml10
Tree ensembles are invariant to monotone transforms of features but can't extrapolate, and high-cardinality categoricals need careful encoding.
why:
A delivery company wants to predict which orders will arrive late. The raw data is an order table — timestamp, warehouse, destination postcode, product weight — and an event log of every scan, dispatch and delivery. Given the raw columns, a model learns almost nothing: a timestamp is just a large number, a postcode is an arbitrary string. Given features — hour of day and day of week, distance from warehouse to destination, whether the date is near a holiday, the warehouse's late rate over the past week, the current backlog — the same model predicts well. Feature engineering, turning raw data into inputs that expose the pattern, is where most of the performance of tabular models comes from.

Then the model ships, and something subtler goes wrong. Offline, the feature "warehouse late rate over the past 7 days" was computed by a nightly warehouse query over complete daily tables. Online, the serving system computes it from a live counter that covers a rolling 168 hours, ignores cancelled orders differently, and lags by an hour when the event stream is busy. Same name, two different features. The model, trained on one and served the other, quietly performs worse than every offline test promised. This is training/serving skew, and it's one of the most common and least visible causes of production ML failure.

Google's "Rules of Machine Learning" — this lesson's public case, alongside the "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" paper — devotes a whole section to it, reporting that teams who measured their skew "were sometimes surprised by the results" and that YouTube's home page gained significant quality improvements, and simpler code, by logging the features actually used at serving time and training on those. Feature stores, shared transformation code and skew monitoring all exist because of this problem.

This lesson covers both halves. First, the feature toolkit with worked numbers: encoding categories (one-hot, smoothed target encoding, hashing with its collision arithmetic, embeddings), scaling and log transforms, cyclical time features, point-in-time aggregates, and missing values. Then the gap: how skew arises, how to detect it (including a population stability index computed by hand), the architectural fixes — logging served features, shared code, feature stores — and how to judge whether a feature is worth its cost.
primer:
Models only see numbers

A model's input is a vector of numbers. Everything in the real world — a product category, a timestamp, a paragraph, a history of clicks — has to be turned into numbers first, and how you do it determines what the model can learn. A good feature makes the pattern simple: if late deliveries happen on Friday evenings, a "day of week" and an "hour" feature let even a simple model see it, while a raw Unix timestamp hides it.

An analogy: preparing ingredients

A chef can't cook a good meal from unprepared ingredients: vegetables must be washed and chopped, meat trimmed, spices measured. The same ingredients prepared differently produce different dishes. Features are prepared ingredients, and the model is the cooking. The analogy extends to the second half of this lesson: imagine the recipe was developed in a test kitchen where onions were diced finely, but the restaurant kitchen slices them thickly because a different cook wrote down "prepare the onions". The recipe is the same, the result is worse, and nobody notices until customers complain. That is training/serving skew.

The common transformations

  • Categories to numbers: one-hot encoding turns "colour = red/green/blue" into three 0/1 columns.
  • Scaling: standardise (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) so features are comparable in size (ml3).
  • Logarithms for skewed values such as income: in natural logs, £20k, £40k and £200k become 9.90, 10.60 and 12.21, so doubling income is the same step (0.69) at any level, and extreme values stop dominating.
  • Dates and times: extract day of week, hour, month, "days since last purchase", holidays.
  • Aggregates: "number of purchases in the last 30 days", "average basket value", "failed logins in the last hour".
  • Ratios and interactions: debt ÷ income; price per square metre.
  • Text: word counts, TF-IDF weights, or embeddings from a language model.
  • Missing values: fill with the training median and add a "was missing" flag — missingness itself is often informative.

A worked example

Predicting late deliveries from order timestamp, warehouse, destination postcode and product weight. Useful engineered features: hour of day and day of week of the order; distance between warehouse and destination; whether the date is within three days of a public holiday; the warehouse's late-delivery rate over the past 7 days; its current order backlog. The raw timestamp alone tells the model almost nothing; the engineered features carry the signal.

Which models need what

Different model families need different preparation. Linear and logistic regression need scaled numeric features, encoded categories and hand-made interactions and non-linear transforms. Distance-based methods (k-NN, clustering) need careful scaling above all. Tree ensembles need none of the scaling but benefit most from aggregates, ratios and history features. Neural networks need normalised inputs and vocabularies for IDs, and learn many interactions themselves. Knowing the model tells you where to spend feature effort.

Training/serving skew in one sentence

If a feature is computed one way when training (from a historical batch table) and another way when serving (from live data), the model sees different inputs in production from the ones it learned from, and quietly performs worse.
body:
1. Encoding categorical features

One-hot encoding creates one 0/1 column per level. It's safe and interpretable for a few dozen levels and the default for linear models. Its problems grow with cardinality: thousands of sparse columns, trees splitting on one rare level at a time, and no column for a level first seen in production. Always define an "unknown" bucket.

Ordinal encoding maps levels to integers. Use it only when the order is real (small < medium < large); imposing a fake order on nominal categories misleads linear models, though trees tolerate it.

Target encoding replaces a level with the average target among its training rows, smoothed towards the global average so rare levels aren't trusted too much:

encoding(level) = (sum of targets in level + m × global rate) / (count of level + m)

Worked: a merchant with 3 transactions, 1 of them fraud, when the global fraud rate is 2% and the smoothing strength m = 20. The raw rate would be 1/3 = 0.33; the smoothed encoding is (1 + 20 × 0.02) / (3 + 20) = 1.4 / 23 = 0.061 — pulled most of the way back towards 0.02, because three transactions is weak evidence. A merchant with 3,000 transactions and 300 frauds gets (300 + 0.4) / 3,020 = 0.0995, essentially its own rate. As ml9 showed, the encoding must be computed out-of-fold for training rows, or each row's own label leaks into its feature; scikit-learn's TargetEncoder does this internally. Unseen levels get the global rate.

Frequency encoding replaces a level with how often it occurs — useful when popularity itself is predictive. The hashing trick maps each level to one of m columns with a hash function, so memory is fixed however many levels appear, and new levels need no vocabulary update. The price is collisions: with n levels hashed into m buckets, the expected number of colliding pairs is about n² / (2m). For 10,000 levels in 2²⁰ ≈ 1,048,576 buckets, that's 10⁸ / 2,097,152 ≈ 48 pairs — a tiny fraction, usually harmless. Learned embeddings give each level a small dense vector trained with a neural network; they're the standard for user, item and word IDs, and need a plan for new IDs (a shared "unknown" vector, or features that describe the new item).

2. Scaling and transforming numbers

Standardisation — (x − mean) / standard deviation, with the mean and standard deviation learned on training data — is needed for regularised linear models (ml3), distance-based methods (ml11, ml12), PCA (ml13) and neural networks. Trees don't need it (ml10). Robust scaling uses the median and interquartile range instead, so a few extreme values don't set the scale. Clipping (capping values at, say, the 1st and 99th percentiles of training data) limits the influence of outliers and protects against absurd serving values.

Log transforms suit positive, right-skewed quantities — money, counts, durations, sizes — where effects are multiplicative. Worked: incomes of £20k, £40k and £200k are 20, 40 and 200 thousand apart on the raw scale, dominated by the largest; their natural logs 9.90, 10.60 and 12.21 put each doubling at the same 0.69 step. Use log(1 + x) when zeros occur. Binning turns a continuous feature into ranges so a linear model can learn a non-linear effect (young drivers and elderly drivers both riskier), at the cost of discarding within-bin detail.

All fitted statistics — means, standard deviations, clip bounds, bin edges, category vocabularies, target encodings — are part of the model. They are learned on training data only (ml9) and must be applied, unchanged, at serving time.

3. Time features

Timestamps carry several kinds of signal. Calendar parts: hour, day of week, month, holiday flags, paydays. Periodic ones should usually be cyclically encoded, because 23:00 and 00:00 are adjacent in reality but 23 apart as numbers:

Worked: hour 23 maps to (sin(2π × 23/24), cos(2π × 23/24)) = (−0.259, 0.966); hour 0 maps to (0, 1). Their distance is √(0.259² + 0.034²) ≈ 0.26, the same as the distance between any two adjacent hours, instead of 23.

Recency — time since the last event (last purchase, last login, last failed payment) — is often among the most predictive features in churn, fraud and marketing. Aggregates over windows — counts, sums, averages, distinct counts over the last hour, day, 7 or 30 days — summarise behaviour. Both must be computed point-in-time (ml9): as of each training example's timestamp, using only events before it.

4. Missing values

Missing values need a decision, and the reason they're missing matters. If income is missing because applicants with irregular income leave it blank, missingness predicts risk. The standard recipe: impute with a statistic from the training data (median for numbers, a dedicated "missing" level for categories) and add a missingness indicator, so the model can learn from both the value and the fact that it was absent. XGBoost and LightGBM learn, at each split, which branch missing values should follow, which often works well. Whatever the rule, serving must apply exactly the same one — a serving path that sends 0 instead of "missing" is a classic skew.

5. Text and embedding features

Text can enter a tabular model in three ways. Counts and TF-IDF weights of words or word pairs are cheap and interpretable, and with a linear model they make a strong baseline for classification. Hand-made text features — length, number of links, presence of certain phrases — capture specific signals. Embeddings from a pretrained language model turn each text into a dense vector that captures meaning; they can be fed to a model directly, reduced with PCA (ml13) first, or used to compute similarity features ("how close is this ticket to known billing tickets?"). Embedding features add their own skew risk: the embedding model's version is part of the feature definition, and serving must use exactly the same model and preprocessing (tokenisation, truncation) as training.

6. A feature review, worked

A team proposes five new features for the late-delivery model. A quick review against the questions of this lesson:

  • "Driver's delivery count today." Available at prediction time? Only up to the moment of prediction — and the training version must use the count as of the order time, not the end-of-day total. Keep, with point-in-time computation.
  • "Delivered on time (yes/no) for the previous order to this address." Useful history, available — keep.
  • "Customer complaint filed." Complaints are filed after late deliveries: target leakage. Drop.
  • "Weather at destination in the next 6 hours." Only available if a forecast (not the observed weather) is used, and training must use the forecast as it was issued, not what actually happened. Keep only with archived forecasts.
  • "Warehouse backlog." Online it comes from a live queue service with a few minutes' lag; offline from end-of-hour snapshots. Two implementations — define it once, or log the served value and train on that.

Every question in the review is about when and how the value is computed, not about whether it's predictive. That's the habit that prevents most leakage and skew.

7. How training/serving skew happens

Google's Rules of Machine Learning defines training/serving skew as a difference between performance during training and performance during serving, caused by (1) a discrepancy between how data is handled in the training and serving pipelines, (2) a change in the data between training and serving, or (3) a feedback loop between the model and the data. The first is the engineering bug this lesson's opening story describes, and it has many forms:

  • Two implementations. A SQL job in the warehouse for training, Java or Python code in the online service for serving, written by different people: window boundaries (calendar days versus rolling hours), whether the current event is included, time zones, rounding, and how nulls and cancellations are treated all drift apart.
  • Freshness. Offline, a feature is computed from complete data; online, the latest events haven't arrived yet, so counts are systematically lower.
  • Preprocessing mismatch. Serving forgets to apply the scaler, uses a different category vocabulary, or maps unseen values differently.
  • Tables that change. A training join reads today's version of a table rather than the version at prediction time (Rule 31 warns that data in a joined table may change between training and serving).

8. Detecting skew

The most direct check: log the feature values actually used for each prediction, then recompute the same features offline for the same entities and timestamps and compare. Any difference is a pipeline discrepancy. The second check compares distributions of each served feature with its training distribution. A common measure is the population stability index (PSI): split the training values into bins, and sum over bins of (actual share − expected share) × ln(actual share / expected share).

Worked. A feature split into quartiles of the training data has expected shares 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25. This week's served values fall into those bins with shares 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40.

bin 1: (0.10 − 0.25) × ln(0.10/0.25) = (−0.15)(−0.916) = 0.137
bin 2: (0.20 − 0.25) × ln(0.20/0.25) = (−0.05)(−0.223) = 0.011
bin 3: (0.30 − 0.25) × ln(0.30/0.25) = ( 0.05)( 0.182) = 0.009
bin 4: (0.40 − 0.25) × ln(0.40/0.25) = ( 0.15)( 0.470) = 0.071
PSI = 0.228

Common rules of thumb treat a PSI below 0.1 as stable, 0.1–0.25 as a moderate shift worth investigating, and above 0.25 as a major shift; 0.23 is a clear signal. PSI doesn't say whether the cause is a bug or real change in the world — the logged-versus-recomputed comparison does. Google's Rule 37 adds a model-level view: track performance on training data, holdout data, next-day data and live data, since each gap points to a different problem (overfitting, time drift, or skew).

9. Preventing skew

Three architectural fixes, strongest first. Train on logged serving features (Rule 29): save the feature values used at prediction time and join them to labels later, so training sees exactly what serving saw. Share transformation code between training and serving (Rule 32), for example by exporting the fitted preprocessing pipeline with the model. Use a feature store: one definition per feature, materialised into an offline store that answers point-in-time queries for training and an online store that serves the latest values in milliseconds, kept in sync by the same logic, streaming updates and backfills. And whichever you choose, monitor: logged-versus-recomputed comparisons, per-feature distribution checks, and performance by data slice over time.
deep:
Logging and waiting: the trade-off

Training on logged serving features removes pipeline skew by construction, and Google reports that YouTube's home page gained significant quality and simpler code by doing so. Its costs are real. A new feature has no history until it has been logged for a while, so you can't train on months of it immediately; logs must be stored, versioned and joined to labels that arrive later; and a serving bug is faithfully preserved in the training data. A common hybrid: backfill a new feature offline with carefully point-in-time code, verify it against a few days of logged values, then switch to training on logs.

Streaming features and event time

Features such as "clicks in the last five minutes" are computed by stream processors (Flink, Spark Streaming) online and backfilled from event logs offline. Two notions of time complicate this: event time (when something happened) and processing time (when the system saw it). Late-arriving events change a window's value after the fact; offline backfills that use event time see complete data, while online computations using processing time don't. Unless both paths use the same windowing semantics and the same rules for late data, the feature is skewed by construction — often by a few per cent, always in the same direction.

Feature crosses and learned interactions

Linear models can't learn interactions unless you create them: a cross of "city × device" lets a model learn that mobile users in one city behave differently. Crosses explode in number and sparsity, which is why they're usually hashed. Tree ensembles learn interactions through nested splits, and neural architectures for tabular and recommendation data (wide-and-deep, deep-and-cross networks) learn crosses automatically — shifting feature work from designing crosses to preparing clean inputs and ID vocabularies.

Features that leak or discriminate

Two kinds of feature are dangerous even when they help offline. Leaky features are updated after the prediction moment — status fields, "last modified" timestamps, aggregates that include the label — and they inflate offline metrics (ml9). Proxy features reproduce the effect of protected attributes the model isn't allowed to use: postcode, name, school or device can stand in for ethnicity or income. Removing the protected attribute doesn't remove the effect; measuring outcomes by group does, and some features must be dropped for legal or ethical reasons regardless of accuracy.

Feature cost and technical debt

"Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" (Sculley et al., 2015) argues that ML systems incur "massive ongoing maintenance costs", and names risks that live in features: entanglement (changing one input changes everything — "changing anything changes everything"), unstable data dependencies (an upstream team changes a signal's meaning), underutilised dependencies (legacy features that add risk without value), and feedback loops. The practical response is a feature inventory with owners and definitions, regular ablation to remove features that no longer earn their keep, contracts with upstream data producers, and alerting on upstream changes. Every online feature is also a serving dependency: if the service providing it is slow or down, predictions degrade.

Automated feature learning versus engineering

Deep learning replaced hand-engineered features for images, audio and text because networks learn better representations from raw inputs when data is plentiful. For tabular and event data the division of labour is different: the most valuable features encode domain knowledge about time and entities — "rate of failed payments for this merchant over 30 days", "days since this customer's last complaint" — that a model can't invent from a raw event table without enormous data. Automated feature generation tools enumerate aggregates and transforms systematically, which helps coverage but multiplies leakage and skew risks and the number of dependencies. The practical balance is to automate breadth, then prune hard with ablations and the feature-review questions.

Feedback loops

The third cause of skew in Google's list is the hardest to see. When a model's decisions affect future data — which items are shown, which transactions are blocked, which customers are contacted — features built from that data reflect the model's own past behaviour. Retraining then reinforces the old policy. Logging the probability with which each action was chosen, keeping a small randomised exploration slice, and correcting for exposure (for example, position bias in rankings) are the standard defences (ml1, ml16).
prod:
The public case: Google on training/serving skew

Google's "Rules of Machine Learning", written from the experience of its production ML teams, devotes a section to training/serving skew. It defines skew as a difference between performance during training and during serving, with three causes: discrepancies in how the training and serving pipelines handle data, changes in the data between training and serving, and feedback loops between the model and the data. Its rules read like a checklist for this lesson:

  • Rule 29: "The best way to make sure that you train like you serve is to save the set of features used at serving time, and then pipe those features to a log to use them at training time." Even if not for every example, do it for a fraction to verify consistency. The guide reports that teams at Google who measured this were "sometimes surprised by the results", and that the YouTube home page switched to logging features at serving time "with significant quality improvements and a reduction in code complexity".
  • Rule 31: beware joining data from a table at training and serving time, because the table may change in between.
  • Rule 32: re-use code between the training pipeline and the serving pipeline whenever possible.
  • Rule 37: measure skew by tracking the differences between performance on training data, holdout data, next-day data and live data.

The companion paper, Sculley et al.'s "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" (NeurIPS 2015), explains why these problems are structural: the ML code is a small part of a real system, surrounded by data collection, feature extraction, configuration, serving and monitoring, and the risks — data dependencies, entanglement, hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers — accumulate there. Together they're the reason feature stores, shared preprocessing and skew monitoring became standard parts of ML platforms.

What goes wrong, and how it shows

A gap between offline and online metrics that appears from day one points to pipeline skew; one that grows over weeks points to drift (ml16).

A feature that is always a little lower online (counts, sums) usually means late-arriving events or a window that ends earlier online.

Sudden jumps in a feature's distribution after a deployment of an upstream service — the meaning of a signal changed without the model's owners knowing.

Predictions that ignore a feature online because serving sends a default value (0, empty string) where training had real values — often a failed lookup silently caught by error handling. Counting how often each feature falls back to its default in production is one of the cheapest and most revealing monitors there is.

A production checklist for every feature

  1. Is it available at prediction time, with the same freshness as in training?
  2. Is it computed by one definition in both paths, point-in-time for training?
  3. How are missing values and unseen categories handled, identically?
  4. Is it logged at serving time and compared with offline recomputation?
  5. Is its distribution monitored (PSI or similar) with alerts?
  6. Does it carry leakage or fairness risk, and who owns it?
myths: With deep learning, feature engineering is dead.

Networks learn features from raw pixels, audio and text, but most tabular production models are gradient-boosted trees that depend on engineered features — aggregates over time windows, ratios, recency, historical rates. Facebook's ad-click paper found historical features dominated everything else. Even for deep models, choosing and preparing inputs (normalisation, ID vocabularies, time features) remains engineering work.
If a feature improves offline metrics, it's a good feature.

Only if it can be computed at prediction time, the same way, with the same freshness. Many offline winners are leaks (computed with data from after the prediction moment) or can't be served in time. A feature is good when it helps offline, is available online, is computed identically in both places, and is worth its latency and maintenance cost.
One-hot encoding is always safe for categorical features.

It's safe for a handful of levels. With thousands of levels it creates thousands of sparse columns, fragments tree splits and memorises rare levels, and unseen levels at serving time have no column. High-cardinality categoricals need out-of-fold target encoding, frequency encoding, hashing or learned embeddings, plus a rule for unseen values.
Training/serving skew is a rare edge case.

Google's Rules of Machine Learning lists it among the most important production concerns and reports that teams measuring it were 'sometimes surprised by the results'; YouTube's home page gained significant quality improvements when it switched to logging features at serving time. Two separately written implementations of the same feature almost always differ somewhere — window boundaries, null handling, time zones, rounding.
Filling missing values with the mean is harmless.

It hides the fact that the value was missing, and missingness is often informative (an applicant who leaves income blank is different from one who reports the average). It also shrinks variance and weakens correlations. Impute with a simple statistic learned on training data, add a 'was missing' indicator, and make sure serving handles missing values identically.
Feature stores are just databases for features.

Their point is a single definition of each feature executed consistently for training and serving: an offline store that produces point-in-time-correct historical values for training, an online store that serves the latest values with low latency, and the machinery (streaming updates, backfills, versioning) that keeps them consistent. Without that, you have two pipelines and skew.

Goal: compute a smoothed target encoding, a cyclical hour encoding and a PSI by hand-checked code, then simulate a skewed feature and watch a model's accuracy drop. NumPy only; written for Python 3.12.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# 1. Smoothed target encoding
def target_encode(n_pos, n, prior, m=20):
    return (n_pos + m * prior) / (n + m)
print("merchant 1/3:", round(target_encode(1, 3, 0.02), 3),
      " merchant 300/3000:", round(target_encode(300, 3000, 0.02), 4))

# 2. Cyclical hour encoding
enc = lambda h: np.array([np.sin(2 * np.pi * h / 24), np.cos(2 * np.pi * h / 24)])
print("dist(23h, 0h) =", round(np.linalg.norm(enc(23) - enc(0)), 3))

# 3. Population stability index
def psi(expected, actual, eps=1e-6):
    e, a = np.asarray(expected) + eps, np.asarray(actual) + eps
    return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e)))
print("PSI:", round(psi([.25, .25, .25, .25], [.10, .20, .30, .40]), 3))

# 4. Skew: train with a 7-day window feature, serve a lagged / undercounted version
n = 20000
spend7 = rng.gamma(2.0, 50.0, n)                        # the feature as computed offline
y = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(spend7 - 150) / 40))).astype(int)
thr = np.quantile(spend7[:15000], 0.5)                   # a one-feature "model": flag above median
acc = lambda f: np.mean((f[15000:] > thr) == y[15000:])
served = spend7 * rng.uniform(0.75, 0.95, n)             # online counter misses late events
print(f"accuracy offline={acc(spend7):.3f}  served={acc(served):.3f}")
bins = np.quantile(spend7[:15000], [0, .25, .5, .75, 1])
share = lambda f: np.histogram(np.clip(f[15000:], bins[0], bins[-1]), bins)[0] / 5000
print("PSI train vs served:", round(psi(share(spend7), share(served)), 3))

What to look for. The encodings print 0.061 and about 0.0995, the hours' distance 0.261 and the worked PSI 0.228. In part 4 the served feature is systematically 5–25% low, so accuracy drops even though the model didn't change, and the PSI between training and served values flags the shift — the kind of silent damage skew does in production.
recap: Feature engineering turns raw data — categories, timestamps, text, event logs — into numbers that make patterns easy for a model to learn, and for tabular problems it often matters more than the algorithm.

Categorical features are encoded by one-hot for few levels, and by out-of-fold smoothed target encoding, frequency encoding, hashing or learned embeddings for many, always with a rule for unseen levels.
Numeric features are scaled for linear, distance-based and neural models, log-transformed when skewed, and clipped or robust-scaled against outliers; trees don't need scaling.
Time features include calendar parts with cyclical encoding, recency and aggregates over windows, all computed point-in-time.
Missing values are imputed with training-set statistics plus a missingness indicator, handled identically at serving time.
Training/serving skew arises when a feature is computed differently in the training pipeline and the serving path, when data changes between training and serving, or through feedback loops.
Skew is detected by logging the features actually served and comparing them with offline recomputations and with training distributions, using measures such as the population stability index.
The structural fixes are shared transformation code, training on logged serving features, and feature stores with point-in-time-correct offline stores and low-latency online stores.
Every feature has a cost — latency, dependencies, maintenance and potential leakage or fairness problems — and should earn its place.

Creating a feature from the combination of two others, such as city × device type.

Filling in missing values, for example with the training median.
Building programs whose behaviour is set by fitting parameters to data rather than by hand-written rules.

The parts of a feature store serving historical values for training and the latest values for real-time prediction.
Turning a categorical variable with k levels into k columns of 0/1, one per level.

Joining each training example to feature values as they were at that example's timestamp.
